Pashhur was one of the leaders and chiefs among the priests, and he heard Jeremiah's prophecies declaring the evil of the priests and the prophets and God's anger against them.
The stocks: a wooden board in which the hands and feet are bound while the man lies on his back, inside the prison.

Pashhur was enraged at Jeremiah's rebukes of the priests and the false prophets. So he struck him and put him in prison and bound him in the stocks, disregarding that Jeremiah was a priest like him, and without any formal trial, relying on the esteem of the priests and rulers for him, so that no one would object to this injustice; and this prison was beside one of the gates of the temple called the Gate of Benjamin, in an upper chamber.

entries.section: (1) Pashhur's trembling over his striking Jeremiah

paragraphs.text: Magor-missabib: terror on every side, or departure.

After Pashhur imprisoned Jeremiah for a day he brought him out, expecting that Jeremiah would have become afraid of the beating and the prison, but he was surprised to find him rebuking him boldly, declaring God's prophecy against him by changing his name from Pashhur to Magor-missabib, that is, from fruitful on every side to terror on every side, and some interpret the name as departure. This means that Pashhur would be greatly terrified before the Babylonian attack and would depart, and they would take him captive far from Jerusalem.

Be courageous however great the threats of those who wrong you, and ask God's help, and you will be able to declare His voice, and people will fear you and your God however strong they appear or weak you seem. For you are stronger than all by the power of God that is with you.

entries.section: (1) Pashhur's trembling over his striking Jeremiah

paragraphs.text: A terror to thyself: the fear comes from within you.
Jeremiah warned him of the great fear that will fill his heart and stir up terror in the hearts of all those around him when the armies of Babylon attack them and kill them with the sword.

entries.section: (1) Pashhur's trembling over his striking Jeremiah

paragraphs.text: And the Babylonians will take possession of all the wealth of the men of Judah and carry it to Babylon, whether silver or gold or precious animals and everything of value, and leave them desolate and destroy them.

entries.section: (1) Pashhur's trembling over his striking Jeremiah

paragraphs.text: It appears from here that Pashhur was not only a priest but also one of the false prophets; therefore Jeremiah prophesied against him that he would be taken captive, he and all his lovers, to Babylon, and would remain there until he died.

Jeremiah grew weak before the beating and the prison and felt that God had forsaken him and had not carried out His promises to protect him, so he rebuked God, who had persuaded him that He would protect him and had urged him to go out to declare His name and rebuke everyone so that they might repent; but sadly everyone mocked him and laughed at him, indeed they resisted him and struck him and imprisoned him, so Jeremiah doubted his mission and tried to give it up.

And whenever Jeremiah proclaimed the word of God and rebuked everyone so that they might repent, everyone became angry with him and mocked his words and persisted in their injustice and evil. And since he found no fruit of his word he felt that his service was in vain, and perhaps he thought of worshiping God quietly and leaving this laborious service.

When Jeremiah tried to be silent about declaring the word of God, he felt the word of God inside him like a fire burning him, so he could not continue to hold it in and not preach it, and he had to yield in the end to God and continue his service, confident that this is the will of God.

If you find no fruit for your service, do not be disturbed, but continue to offer love and to call others to be bound to the Church, and trust that the fruits will come at the right time however late. So ask God's help to support you and comfort your heart.
My halting: my limping, that is, any mistake that comes from me by deviating from what is right.
Will be enticed: oversteps his bounds and errs against God and men.

Jeremiah began to regain his zeal for the service, but he saw many acts of resistance from all around him, who blame him and threaten him and frighten him and try to gather complaints against him and watch him to catch any fault in him so that they may take revenge on him.

Jeremiah lifts his heart in faith toward God, whose power he feels, and calls Him the LORD of hosts after understanding that the afflictions that came upon him were to test his faith and steadfastness, and He knows the hearts of men and is longsuffering but in the end takes vengeance on the wicked. And by this Jeremiah declares his faith in God and his desire to show the wrongness of evil and the steadfastness of goodness and righteousness, and his purpose is not hatred of his enemies, because he loves them with fatherhood, as appears from the previous chapters.

Jeremiah believed that God would save him from the hands of those who resisted him, although they still frighten him and threaten him. And in his joy in his God who supports him he calls all men to praise the Almighty God, who protects His children.

When any affliction comes upon you, stand before God in prayer and ask His help, and He will strengthen your faith and renew your hope, and your heart will be comforted and rejoice, and afterward you can support other afflicted people and strengthen their faith.
Jeremiah was again affected by the resistance of all the people to him, so he wished he had not been born, that he might not meet all these troubles, which he felt were beyond his strength.
Out of his grief he also cursed the man who brought the news of his birth, for from the multitude of his distress he felt that he was born for grief and not for joy.
Cry: noise.

From the multitude of his distress he wished that the one who announced his birth had died and had not announced this birth, and likened his death to the overthrow of the two cities Sodom and Gomorrah (of old) and the hearing of the cry of men as they burned in them.

He wished that God would have killed him as an embryo in his mother's womb, so that her womb would be a grave for him, and it would be said of his mother that she only conceived and did not give birth.
In sorrow Jeremiah says: Why was I born, that I should meet all these troubles and insults and shame from all around me?

The Holy Bible recorded for us the weaknesses of the prophets, so that we do not despair if thoughts of despair and murmuring fight against us, but return to our faith, because the greatest of the prophets were exposed to thoughts of despair yet overcame them. Jeremiah said these words in his heart, but it is not necessary that he declared them to anyone, and the Holy Bible recorded them for us to encourage us whatever our sins.

If thoughts of doubt or despair or murmuring fight against you, do not be disturbed, but ask God's help and resist these thoughts by repeating the Psalms, and you will come out from under them and regain your faith, indeed become stronger than you were. Jeremiah's answer to Zedekiah

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, made Mattaniah king over the kingdom of Judah and named him Zedekiah, after the first Babylonian captivity of the kingdom of Judah; he was 21 years old and reigned 11 years, and he was the last king of the kingdom of Judah, and after him the kingdom of Judah was taken captive and Jerusalem and its surroundings were destroyed.

At the beginning of Zedekiah's reign he sent a letter to the king of Babylon affirming his loyalty to him (Jer 29:3), then in the fourth year of his reign he went himself to Babylon (Jer 51:59). And toward the end of his reign the rulers of Judah encouraged him to rebel against the king of Babylon, because a new king had begun to reign in Egypt and promised the children of Israel to protect them, since he wanted to make the kingdom of Judah a protective shield for Egypt against the kings of Babylon, besides Egypt's attempt to recover some of its lands that the king of Babylon had seized.

So Zedekiah thought of rebelling against the king of Babylon, especially since he had allied himself with the kings of the surrounding lands so that they might stand against the king of Babylon, namely the kings of Edom, Moab, the children of Ammon, Tyre and Sidon. And by rebelling against the king of Babylon Zedekiah meant to be rid of paying taxes to him.

As for the conduct of King Zedekiah, it was wicked, for he introduced the worship of idols into the temple of God, and injustice spread in his kingdom, that is, he walked in corruption and did not obey God's commandments, as appears from (vv. 11, 12). Zedekiah did not rely on God but relied on the power of Egypt, besides that he did not learn from history, for about a century and a half before, in the days of the prophet Isaiah, Egypt made many promises to protect Judah against the Assyrians and did nothing.

The army of Babylon had besieged Jerusalem in the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, and could not enter it because of its strength, and because the king of Egypt moved with his armies toward it, Babylon left it for a time (Jer 37:5), and then returned and besieged it again.

In the eleventh year of Zedekiah's reign, when the siege grew long, the food in Jerusalem ran out, so Zedekiah fled from it with some of his men, but the armies of Babylon seized him and sent him to Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon, who imprisoned him there until he died there (2 Kgs 25:1-7), and Nebuchadnezzar plundered the treasuries of Jerusalem and burned the house of the LORD and destroyed the city and killed many, and took the rest captive (2 Chr 36:11-21) (Jer 39:1-14), and that was in the year 587 B.C.

King Zedekiah sent two of the priests who were attached to him, who hated Jeremiah, for most likely the father of Pashhur the priest is Malchiah, who had cast Jeremiah into the pit, and this Pashhur is not the same as Pashhur the chief priest mentioned in the previous chapter.

Zedekiah told Jeremiah of the king of Babylon's besieging Jerusalem and his intention to make war against it, and asked him to inquire of God; but he did not want to know the voice of God and His guidance, but hoped that God would work a miracle and rescue him from Babylon, because he had relied on Egypt, and Egypt on rebellion against Babylon. So he was not ready to submit to the word of God but was biased and wanted God to give him what he had previously agreed upon with his great men.

Perhaps Zedekiah remembered what happened in the days of King Hezekiah, who asked Isaiah for the word of God, and he encouraged him, and God sent His angel and killed 185,000 of the army of Assyria and the rest fled; but there is a great difference between Zedekiah and Hezekiah, because Hezekiah feared God and was submissive to Him, whereas Zedekiah walked in evil and relied on Egypt.

If you want God's help and desire to hear His voice, be ready to submit to His guidance, repent of your sins, and abide in the Church and her sacraments; then God will keep you and lead your life and guide you in all your steps.
Jeremiah sent the word of God to Zedekiah by the two priests whom he had sent to him to inquire of him.
The word of God did not agree with Zedekiah's purposes, but declared His anger against him because he did not want to repent, so He said to him:

1- The weapons of war in the hands of his soldiers will not profit him, and they will not be able to defend themselves and Jerusalem, but the weapons in their hands will turn back against them because God Himself is against them, that is, they will be defeated in this war.
2- The Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, the enemies besieging Jerusalem, will enter into the midst of it and destroy it.

God declares clearly that it is He who disciplines them, for He is the God of Israel, He is the God of those who disobeyed His commandments, and He will stretch out His hand and His arm, that is, direct His anger and severe discipline at them, because they persist in their sins; and by declaring this discipline He wishes that they fear Him and repent so that He may have mercy on them.
Because God has become against His people, He uses to discipline them not only the armies of Babylon but also the diseases that spread among them as a plague, weakening and killing many.
God's anger comes upon them also through famine, when the armies of Babylon besiege Jerusalem and the food runs out.
And whoever escapes the plague and the famine, the army of Babylon kills, and this includes the king's children, his servants, his great men and his people, so many die by the sword.

Do not persist in or treat lightly or be careless about any sin, because by this you defy God, and then in His love for you He directs His anger against you to discipline you so that you repent. So return quickly to rescue yourself from many troubles, and you will see the face of God, which you hid by your carelessness about sin.

God's word was specific in His counsel to the kingdom of Judah: each one of the people must choose either to live by surrendering to the armies of Babylon, which means submitting to God's discipline in order to repent of sins, or to choose the way of death, which appears in resisting the Babylonians so that they kill him, and this means resisting the word of God, and the result is destruction.
He declared that whoever remains in Jerusalem will die either by famine or plague or the sword of the enemies, but whoever goes out of Jerusalem and gives himself up to Babylon will live and not die.

Jeremiah's words appeared as if he were a traitor to the homeland and loyal to Babylon, but in truth whoever knows that he is a prophet of God will understand that this is God's command, not because Babylon's conduct is good but because submitting to the slavery of Babylon is accepting God's discipline and the beginning of repentance, and then God forgives their sins.
God decides that He is angry with Jerusalem, so He allows evil to come upon her, that is, the discipline of her destruction and burning by Babylon.
God said these words to the people, and their choices were either to submit to Him and believe Him and so rescue themselves, or to oppose Him and He would destroy them.
Do not murmur at afflictions but accept them from the hand of God, and examine yourself so as to repent of your old sins, and know that His mercies are very many and He desires your salvation.

entries.section: (4) A call to repentance for the royal palace and Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: By the house of the king of Judah is meant the royal family and the king's servants, his counselors and his great men, that is, those who help the king in governing the country. These have a great responsibility because they share the rule with the king; if the rule is sound they reward it, or if corrupt they punish it.

entries.section: (4) A call to repentance for the royal palace and Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: It is not only the responsibility of those in the king's palace to be just in their private lives but also to execute justice in all the kingdom, so that they do not keep silent about injustice and extortion but do justice to the wronged. But the king's house did injustice and approved of a man's wronging his brother, so God warned them of His punishment like a fire that burns them for their sins, and this actually happened, for the Babylonians burned the house of the LORD and the king's palace and the palaces of the great men.

Take care to fulfill your responsibilities in caring for and guiding those around you with all your strength, so that you rebuke and warn the offender and punish him if you have authority over him, so that you execute justice and spread purity and draw all to life with God; but if they persist in their sins they will perish, while you will be saved because you were faithful in your duty toward them.

entries.section: (4) A call to repentance for the royal palace and Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: O inhabitant of the valley: Jerusalem was on the top of the mountain, yet he called her inhabitant of the valley and not the level plain.
Rock of the plain: Jerusalem, which is on the mountain, that is, the rock, and surrounded by rocks on three sides except the north.

Jerusalem was proud and thought she was safe from the attack of the enemies because she was situated on a mountain, so that she cried, Who can attack our city and come down with his power upon us, and who can enter into our habitations? for they thought in pride that they were safe from the enemies. Perhaps they thought that as long as the temple of God was in their city no enemy could attack Jerusalem, and they forgot that their sins had separated them from God and deprived them of His protection. Rugged place: the wilderness surrounding Jerusalem where trees grow.
God declares that in His anger He disciplines them, burning them with the fire of the Babylonians, them and their city Jerusalem and the wildernesses and forests around them.
The kings and repentance

God commanded Jeremiah to go down to the king's palace, which lay in a valley surrounded by mountains. This king was Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, the righteous king. Jehoahaz walked in evil and brought idol worship into Jerusalem. God commanded Jeremiah to speak to the king himself so that he might repent, for he had done evil in the sight of the Lord: instead of leading the people to the good, he had turned them away from God. This shows two things:
1- The seriousness of the leader's position, and the importance of using his office to lead the people and not to cause them to stumble.
2- Jeremiah's courage in declaring the truth to the greatest person in the kingdom, bearing the hard consequences if the king became angry with him.

At the beginning of his speech, Jeremiah reminds Jehoahaz, king of Judah, that he sits on the throne of David and is of his seed, so he ought to walk as David did in the fear of God and love for Him. He declares that this word is addressed to him, to his servants who help him in governing, and to all the people he rules; that is, he calls the king to obey the word of God and to direct his people to do so after they had drifted away from Him.

God calls the king and his helpers to hold fast to justice and righteousness in their judgments: not to side against a person and wrong him because of his weakness, and not to favor the stronger party and so help the oppressor seize the rights of others. He gives examples of the weak, namely strangers, orphans and widows: they are to give them their rights and not oppress them by exploiting their weak circumstances. Injustice may even reach the point of killing an innocent person, or at least of stripping him of his rights and pressing him down, as though they had killed him and shed his blood; that is, they took away his right to live and crushed him by their wrongdoing.

Be just in your judgments. Do not be swayed by the position or power of some, so that you deny the wronged his rights and let the wicked and powerful rob him. If you have authority, strive to stop the evil; and if you cannot, at least help the wronged with all your strength.

God promises them as a reward, if they follow justice in their judgments, that the throne of their kingdom will be established, and that strong kings from their offspring will enter this palace to sit on the throne, possessing great chariots and horses, and strong servants and people.

On the other hand, He threatens them that if they do not obey His word and persist in their injustice and in encouraging the unjust, He will lay waste this royal palace, and even what is more important, His own house and temple. The people of the kingdom of Judah and their kings thought that God would protect them because the temple of God was in their city, Jerusalem, and that this temple would remain until the end of days because they were the offspring of David. They forgot that they must walk as David did and offer pure worship in the temple of God in order to enjoy His protection.
Gilead: a fertile region full of high mountains.
The head of Lebanon: one of the high, fertile mountains of Lebanon.

He likens the king's palace, which relies on its strength, to the lofty mountains of Gilead or Lebanon, full of fertility and relying on their greatness, strength and firmness: even so, it will be shattered and laid waste because it disobeyed God. He says "cities" and not "a city" because the whole kingdom of Judah will be shattered because of its evils, and not Jerusalem alone.

God declares that He will appoint and consecrate Babylon to destroy the cities of Judah. The Babylonians were distinguished by felling timber, so they attacked the house of God, the king's palace and the palaces of the great with their axes, to break up their timbers taken from cedar trees and burn them with fire. The Babylonians thought that their god was stronger than the God of Israel, and God tolerated this in order to discipline His people so that they would repent; afterward He would discipline Babylon by the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, who would shatter it.

After the destruction of Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, travelers will pass by these ruins and marvel at their devastation, because they had been very great. Each one will ask his neighbor why they were destroyed, and he will answer him: because of their disobedience to God, their breaking of the covenant with Him, and their turning to worship foreign, pagan gods.
Bewail him: they utter words of lament over him after his death.

The dead man mentioned is Josiah the king, who died in the battle of Megiddo in 609 BC at the age of 38. He was a righteous king, and therefore the people who loved him wept for him when his chariot was brought back to his land, and they buried him with great honor.

But Jeremiah calls the people to weep for his son, the new king Jehoahaz, whom Necho king of Egypt would seize and carry captive to Egypt, where he would die and never return to his land. The last king of Assyria had become very weak and the armies of the Babylonians had begun to grow strong against him, so the king of Egypt went out with his armies to support him. He took possession of Palestine, seized Jehoahaz and sent him to Egypt.

He calls Jehoahaz by his former name, "Shallum," because he was not Josiah's firstborn but the fourth of his sons, and he seized the kingdom by force. He sat on the throne only three months and ten days; the king of Egypt seized him and sent him there, where he died and never returned to his land. So he calls him by his former name because he was a usurper of the kingdom, and he was wicked and not righteous like his father; this evil came upon him in his captivity to Egypt.
Jehoahaz died in Egypt and never returned to his land; that is, he died in exile because of his evil.

Do not rejoice in seizing the rights of others who cannot resist you, for God, who is able to do all things, sees you and will punish you if you do not repent. So remember always that you stand before God, and fear Him in all your works, words and thoughts, and live in purity, so that you may enjoy His care and love.

entries.section: (3) Pride and love of material things

paragraphs.text: Chambers: upper rooms in the house.

Jeremiah addresses his words to King Jehoiakim, whom Necho king of Egypt made king over the kingdom of Judah after Jehoahaz his brother was carried captive to Egypt. Sadly, Jehoiakim did not learn or benefit from what happened to his brother by returning to God in repentance. Instead he was concerned to build himself a house, that is, a great palace of several stories. For this he used his poor people, who were pressed by the heavy taxes the king collected to pay tribute to the king of Egypt and to enjoy the pleasures of life himself. The word "neighbor" means the Jewish people: he wronged his people and exploited them in building without wages. He was unjust and unfair in order to satisfy his pride and his love of material things, which appeared in the building of the great palace, built with the money of injustice which he took from the people.

entries.section: (3) Pride and love of material things

paragraphs.text: Windows: openings for light.
Ceiled: he makes the roof of the palace.
Vermilion: a paint for walls.

He describes the details of the great palace which Jehoiakim took care to make spacious, with its roof of the most precious timber, the wood of cedar trees. He also took care to paint it with materials containing glue so that they would stick to the walls; that is, he took care to erect a palace of the highest standard to satisfy his lust and his pride.

entries.section: (3) Pride and love of material things

paragraphs.text: Closest to: on a level with.

Jeremiah rebukes him for his pride, which he compares to his rising high to be on a level with the tall cedar trees. He calls him to humility, following the example of his father Josiah, who was content with necessary food and drink and not with a palace and luxurious foods; so God blessed him and he lived in much prosperity.

entries.section: (3) Pride and love of material things

paragraphs.text: He praises King Josiah, the father of Jehoiakim, calling his son to imitate him, for Josiah took care to provide for the poor, not to wrong them, and to give them their rights, as well as every needy and destitute person; by this he demonstrated his knowledge and fear of God.

entries.section: (3) Pride and love of material things

paragraphs.text: He rebukes Jehoiakim for the shocking injustice into which he had fallen: he snatched the rights of others and exploited the poor in building his palace, exhausting their strength until they fell dead from weariness and overwork.

entries.section: (3) Pride and love of material things

paragraphs.text: His glory: his greatness.

Because of Jehoiakim's great injustice to his people, they hated him. So when the king of Babylon attacked Jerusalem and killed Jehoiakim, no one grieved for him; they did not weep for him or lament him; the people did not say to one another, "Ah, my brother!" or "Ah, my sister!" and ask why this had happened; nor did they cry out in sorrow that they had lost their lord and their great man, but they made light of his death. When Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon killed him, he threw him outside the city without burial, and they dragged his body as the carcass of a dead donkey is dragged, and buried him without any honor. This was the result of his injustice to his people and his using the money of his subjects to build his palace and satisfy his pleasures.

Do good to all those around you as far as you are able, even to those who wrong you and treat you unjustly and do not thank you for your kindnesses. Be sure that all your works are precious to God. And after you depart from this life, those who wronged you may be moved and return to God, because deep within they cannot deny your love.
Bashan: lies to the northeast of Jerusalem.
Abarim: lies to the southeast of Jerusalem.

Jeremiah calls on rebellious Jerusalem, persisting in her sins, to go up on the mountains in the regions surrounding her, namely Lebanon, which lies to her north, and likewise Bashan and Abarim, to weep over the evil that will come upon her, just as the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite went up to weep over herself before she died (Judg 11:37, 38). Jerusalem is to weep not only over her coming destruction, but also over the surrounding countries that allied themselves with her, such as Egypt, because it fell into the hand of Babylon, who shattered it; for Babylon overcame Egypt in the battle of Carchemish in 605 BC (Jer 46:2-12). That is, no one was found to help Jerusalem in her affliction; she was destroyed together with all her lovers because she had rebelled against the Lord.

God punishes Jerusalem because He called her to repentance at a time when she was at rest from the wars of her enemies, but she refused to listen to Him and repent. This has been her nature for many years, so she persists in disobedience even when the time of her ruin draws near, and she refuses God's warnings to her.

Do not accept any sin, even a small one such as a thought or an evil word, lest you become accustomed to it and it leads you to greater evils that destroy your life, as you do not benefit from God's warnings because of your negligence. He loves you, so why do you neglect His voice and despise His love?...!
The wind shall feed them: they lose all shepherding, and the wind scatters them.
By "your pastors" is meant your kings, O Jerusalem, and your rulers, who will lose all care and protection because they forsook God.

By the shepherds is also meant the kings of the countries surrounding Jerusalem, who will lose their strength before the king of Babylon and so be unable to support Jerusalem. Then she will be put to shame when Babylon attacks and destroys her, and there will be no one to rescue her, because the countries around her will themselves have been carried captive to Babylon.

God addresses Jerusalem, which dwells on the mountain like the mountains of Lebanon, which built palaces within her of the wood of the strong cedars of Lebanon, and felt secure within them, declaring that she will be destroyed by the hands of Babylon and her pains will be very severe, like the pains of a woman who travails at childbirth, and all who are around her will pity her.

After Nebuchadnezzar killed King Jehoiakim, his son Jehoiachin, who is also called Coniah, reigned. He reigned for three months and walked in evil like his father (2 Kgs 24:8-17). Nebuchadnezzar seized him and carried him captive to Babylon, where he died.

Here God swears by Himself, to confirm His word, declaring that however great Coniah may be as king, God will pluck him from his kingdom and carry him captive to Babylon, even if he were firm and great like a signet on the right hand of God, that is, in perfect strength, for the right hand signifies strength.

God warns Jehoiachin through the mouth of Jeremiah, that perhaps he may repent and turn back from his evil. He tells him that He will deliver him into the hand of the king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar (Nebuchadrezzar), the strong and dominant king of whom Jehoiachin was afraid, who will carry him captive to the land of the Chaldeans, that is, Babylon.

He also warns him that he will be carried captive to a foreign land in which he was not born, namely Babylon, he and his mother, who is called Nehushta (2 Kgs 24:8, 15), and they will not return to their homeland but will die in captivity, as a symbol of the eternal destruction that awaits the wicked.

Jehoiachin and his mother longed to return from Babylon to Jerusalem, but they did not return because of their evil. This shows that the whole family lived in evil: King Jehoiakim, his wife Nehushta, and their son Jehoiachin, the young man of eighteen years (2 Kgs 24:8-9).
A vessel wherein is no pleasure: God takes no pleasure in it.

God looks with sorrow and fatherly love at King Jehoiachin (Coniah), how he was carried captive to Babylon and cast down there in humiliation, as a broken earthen vessel of no use is cast away. The great man became lowly, and all this because of sin. So the wrath of God came upon him and his offspring.

God calls the earth to witness against Jehoiachin's evil and his humiliating end as a punishment for him. He says that although Jehoiachin has offspring, none of them will reign after their father or recover their father's throne, and so he is considered "childless" in that none of his sons will reign. Thus the reign of the descendants of David over the kingdom of Judah comes to an end; but in the fullness of time Christ, the Son of David, comes to reign over the hearts of those who believe in Him, not only from among the Jews but from the whole world.

Consider the consequences of your sins, which lead to destruction and separate you from God, so that you hasten to repent of them. Then you will gain the salvation of your soul and rejoice the heart of God.
Christ the Savior and the false prophets

God warns the rulers, the priests and all those responsible for His people in the kingdom of Judah, because instead of gathering God's people they scattered them and drove them away from Him; indeed they led them astray and destroyed them by spreading idol worship among them and encouraging them in evil. This was at the end of the kingdom of Judah in the days of King Zedekiah, when Babylon began to attack Jerusalem and the kingdom of Judah.
God threatens these wicked shepherds that He will punish them for their walking in evil, their failure in shepherding, and their leading His people astray.
Folds: their pens.

God Himself intervenes to gather His people who walked in evil. God disciplines them with captivity and dispersion in the kingdom of Babylon, then brings them from the land of Babylon and restores them from captivity to Jerusalem and Judea, and blesses them so that they increase and multiply.

God promises to raise up shepherds who will care for His flock. These are His righteous men who brought them back from captivity, Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah, and He also means the Apostles of the New Testament and the bishops and priests in the Church. Thus the flock is reassured and the devil cannot snatch it away.

Here he speaks clearly about the awaited Messiah, the true Shepherd of the people of God. He likens Him to a Branch because He is joined to the root, that is, the "tree of David," being of his seed, and because He became incarnate in order to grow in our midst and complete our righteousness by our redemption on the Cross. Christ shepherds His people successfully and rules with truth and justice.

Here he speaks of Christ the Savior, who saves His people by His death on the Cross, and so saves the two kingdoms of the Jews, Judah and Israel, and even the whole world of those who believe in Him. God justifies His children by taking their sins away from them and granting them His virtues, so that we become righteous by the grace of God; that is, Christ becomes the cause of our righteousness.

He prophesies about the return from captivity, that is, from Babylon to Jerusalem, which will be a very great and unexpected event, its report rising above the report of the exodus from Egypt and its bondage. All this is a symbol of liberation from sin by the redemption of Christ, and then of liberation from the burden of the body and the passing world by entering the Kingdom of Heaven.

If you find no one to listen to you or guide you, and you find a shortcoming in the spiritual care offered to you, do not be troubled. Be sure that God is able to shepherd and guide you by different means, so that you are saved and find your place in heaven.

Jeremiah looked at the evil of the false prophets, which deserved God's wrath against them. Before he utters the words of God for their punishment, his fatherly love for them appears in the breaking of his heart for them, that is, the anguish of his feelings over what would come upon them, and likewise the shaking of his bones, that is, the weakness of his body in its strongest part, the bones. Indeed, from grief over their evil end he came to stagger like a man drunk with wine.

Be compassionate toward sinners even while you call them to repentance. Your tenderness wraps around your rebuke of them, and as they feel your fatherly love their hearts are moved to return to God. God looks upon your prayers for them, forgives them, and leads them to the way of the new life with Him.
Adulterers: the disobedient who walk in uncleanness.

Through the prophecies of the false prophets, evil, idol worship, adultery and every uncleanness spread in Jerusalem and around it. So the curse of God came upon them and the land lost its fertility and its pastures; that is, neither man nor beast found food, and man's effort turned to worshiping idols and doing uncleanness with all his strength.
The prophets and priests also shared with the people in these evils, so much so that they set up images of foreign gods in the house of the Lord and engraved them on its walls.

God punishes them, since the way of their adultery made them slide from evil to evil, like one who slips on a slope in the dark, stumbles and cannot rise. God allows them to be driven out of their land at the hand of Babylon and to fall slain by the sword, and He punishes them in the year of Babylon's attack on them, in which they destroy Jerusalem and burn it.
(3) The prophets and lying (vv. 13-22)

13- And I have seen folly in the prophets of Samaria; they prophesied in Baal, and caused my people Israel to err. 14- I have seen also in the prophets of Jerusalem an horrible thing: they commit adultery, and walk in lies: they strengthen also the hands of evildoers, that none doth return from his wickedness: they are all of them unto me as Sodom, and the inhabitants thereof as Gomorrah. 15- Therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts concerning the prophets; Behold, I will feed them with wormwood, and make them drink the water of gall: for from the prophets of Jerusalem is profaneness gone forth into all the land. 16- Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD. 17- They say still unto them that despise me, The LORD hath said, Ye shall have peace; and they say unto every one that walketh after the imagination of his own heart, No evil shall come upon you. 18- For who hath stood in the counsel of the LORD, and hath perceived and heard his word? who hath marked his word, and heard it? 19- Behold, a whirlwind of the LORD is gone forth in fury, even a grievous whirlwind: it shall fall grievously upon the head of the wicked. 20- The anger of the LORD shall not return, until he have executed, and till he have performed the thoughts of his heart: in the latter days ye shall consider it perfectly. 21- I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran: I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied. 22- But if they had stood in my counsel, and had caused my people to hear my words, then they should have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their doings.

The false prophets walked in lying to please the kings, and by their prophecies they helped spread the worship of Baal in the northern kingdom, the kingdom of Israel, whose capital was Samaria. All this led the people astray and drew them away from God.

The false prophets in Jerusalem also shared in lying, and led the people of God astray like the prophets of Samaria. They walked in disobedience and uncleanness, and even encouraged the wicked instead of rebuking them. So they became brothers of Sodom and Gomorrah; that is, their evil increased greatly and they deserved destruction like Sodom and Gomorrah.
Wormwood: an extremely bitter plant.
The water of gall: very bitter water.

God expresses His punishment and discipline of the false prophets by making bitter wormwood their food and the water of gall their drink, that perhaps they may repent, especially since the lying of the prophets of Jerusalem spread to the neighboring lands and led everyone astray.

The false prophets persist in their lying and attribute their words to God, while God is utterly innocent of them. Therefore God speaks with power, declaring His title the Lord of hosts, that is, the Mighty One, and commands His people not to listen to the false prophets, because what they say is vain and useless: it is what they themselves see, and not God.

Sadly, the false prophets encourage the wicked to persist in evil, so that they despise God, worship idols and stubbornly insist on sin; yet the false prophets promise them peace, security and blessings.
Jeremiah asks whether there is a single one of these prophets who has stood in the council of God with His saints, or whether all of them lie and claim to have heard from God.
Whirlwind: a storm.
Tempest: a violent wind.

Since the prophets persisted in their lying, God was angry with them and threatened them with discipline like the blowing of a whirlwind and a violent wind upon them and upon their heads, to trouble and destroy them.

The latter days: the end of their opportunity for repentance, when His wrath rises against them, as happened in the Babylonian attack and the captivity. God declares that His wrath will continue to destroy the disobedient until God makes manifest the punishment of sin and everyone who is ready to repent repents.
God repeats that He is innocent of all that the false prophets said.

God affirms that these prophets are liars, for if they were true prophets they would have stood in the council of God through their prayers and holiness, and they would have heard the voice of God and spoken His words.

Do not teach others anything you have not heard in the Church, lest your teaching be false and cause others to stumble and drive them away from God. Be humble and be a disciple in the Church, and declare your lack of knowledge if you do not know, so that you may ask and learn the sound teaching.
(4) Dreams and the claim to prophecy (vv. 23-40)

23- Am I a God at hand, saith the LORD, and not a God afar off? 24- Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the LORD. Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the LORD. 25- I have heard what the prophets said, that prophesy lies in my name, saying, I have dreamed, I have dreamed. 26- How long shall this be in the heart of the prophets that prophesy lies? yea, they are prophets of the deceit of their own heart; 27- Which think to cause my people to forget my name by their dreams which they tell every man to his neighbour, as their fathers have forgotten my name for Baal. 28- The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD. 29- Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces? 30- Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, saith the LORD, that steal my words every one from his neighbour. 31- Behold, I am against the prophets, saith the LORD, that use their tongues, and say, He saith. 32- Behold, I am against them that prophesy false dreams, saith the LORD, and do tell them, and cause my people to err by their lies, and by their lightness; yet I sent them not, nor commanded them: therefore they shall not profit this people at all, saith the LORD. 33- And when this people, or the prophet, or a priest, shall ask thee, saying, What is the burden of the LORD? thou shalt then say unto them, What burden? I will even forsake you, saith the LORD. 34- And as for the prophet, and the priest, and the people, that shall say, The burden of the LORD, I will even punish that man and his house. 35- Thus shall ye say every one to his neighbour, and every one to his brother, What hath the LORD answered? and, What hath the LORD spoken? 36- And the burden of the LORD shall ye mention no more: for every man's word shall be his burden; for ye have perverted the words of the living God, of the LORD of hosts our God. 37- Thus shalt thou say to the prophet, What hath the LORD answered thee? and, What hath the LORD spoken?

38- But since ye say, The burden of the LORD; therefore thus saith the LORD; Because ye say this word, The burden of the LORD, and I have sent unto you, saying, Ye shall not say, The burden of the LORD; 39- Therefore, behold, I, even I, will utterly forget you, and I will forsake you, and the city that I gave you and your fathers, and cast you out of my presence: 40- And I will bring an everlasting reproach upon you, and a perpetual shame, which shall not be forgotten.

God asks in astonishment: Am I like the limited pagan gods who exist in a particular place?! Of course not. Am I a God at hand, and not present in distant places?! God answers that He is present everywhere, so He sees everything that is hidden and concealed, and He fills heaven and earth.
God declares His displeasure with the false prophets who claim to have seen dreams and relate them to people as divine revelations.
God declares that these prophets are liars and deceivers.

God rebukes these prophets: their false dreams and their claim to prophecy draw them away from God and bind them to idol worship such as Baal, and this is a grave sin because it leads the people astray from God.

God asks the true prophet, to whom God reveals a vision, to speak it, like the prophet Jeremiah; as for the liars, let them fall. God marvels at the existence of the false prophets, whom He likens to chaff, alongside the true prophet Jeremiah, whom He likens to wheat.

Then God continues, declaring that His word is like the fire that consumes chaff, that is, it exposes the deceit of the false prophets who are likened to chaff, and thus God exposed these false prophets. God also likens His word to a hammer that breaks the stony hearts of these prophets.

These prophets also fell into the sin of stealing, for they heard the prophets of God such as Jeremiah or Baruch, took their words, and claimed that God had guided them to them by dreams and visions, adding their own thoughts to them.
God declares His war on the false prophets who claim private thoughts, uttering them with their tongues and saying that God is the one who said them; they falsely ascribe themselves to God.
God affirms that He is against the false prophets who boast of their claims and their false dreams; they did not profit my people in anything, but led them astray.

Do not ascribe the thoughts of others to yourself in order to find greater honor, lest you bring upon yourself the wrath of God because of your pride and your lying. Be humble, and God will grant you great and deep knowledge.
When the people, or the prophets, or the priests ask Jeremiah about the burden of the Lord, he is to say that the Lord has declared it and that He rejects them because of their evils.
God repeats that He will punish everyone who claims prophecy and knowledge of the burden of the Lord, whether among the false prophets, the priests, or any individual of the people.
He requires the people to seek out the word of God which His true prophets declare, such as Jeremiah or Baruch, and no longer to claim knowledge of the burden of the Lord.
God reproaches them in sorrow, saying that what they speak is their own burden and their own thoughts, and not the burden of the Lord and His word.

God mocks the claims of the false prophets, and requires Jeremiah to confront them and say to this deceiving prophet, "What has God said to you?", that perhaps he may take heed and repent of his deceit and lying.

God ends His speech by threatening the false prophets who persist in claiming prophecy that He will punish them by forgetting them, that is, abandoning them and their city Jerusalem. The Babylonians will attack it, destroy it and burn it, and the city of the fathers, Jerusalem, in which is the temple of God, will become a reproach and a shame before all peoples because of the evil and disobedience of the people of God.
The baskets of figs
Jeconiah: he is King Jehoiachin, who reigned three months over the kingdom of Judah and was then carried captive to Babylon.

Jeremiah saw a vision of two baskets of figs set before the temple of the Lord. He fixes the time of the vision: it was after Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away Jeconiah king of Judah, and had taken with him the great men of the Jews and the craftsmen skilled in the various trades from Jerusalem, and carried them all captive to Babylon.

The presence of the two baskets before the temple of God means that the Jews, of their different kinds, stood before God for Him to judge them, since everything is naked and open before His eyes. God allowed Jehoiachin to be carried captive to Babylon because of his evil. The king of Babylon carried away the best of the Jews to work in the capital of his kingdom, which made it flourish and grow strong, and among them were prophets and godly men. The fig fruit signifies unity, for it contains small seeds, none of which has any value in itself, but gathered together within a single skin they give it a sweet taste, just as the believers are gathered into one body, which is the Church, the Body of Christ.
Although the two baskets contain one fruit, the fig, there are two entirely different kinds inside them, and figs are of three kinds:
1- The first-ripe fig: the firstfruit of the fig, which appears in the month of June. It is a very good fig, that is, the best kind of fig.
2- The summer fig: a good fig which ripens and is gathered in the month of August.
3- The winter fig: the fig which remains on the tree throughout the winter until the beginning of spring. It is a very bad fig which cannot be eaten.
Of the two baskets before the temple of the Lord, one had very good figs, that is, of the first kind, while the other had very bad figs, of the third kind.

God asked Jeremiah what he saw in the vision, and he answered that he saw very good figs in the first basket and very bad figs in the second. God asked this so that the prophet would declare his clear distinction between the two kinds. The two kinds are the righteous Jews and the wicked Jews. The first kind are those who obeyed God, went into captivity and kept His commandments; the second, bad kind are those who remained in Jerusalem and held fast to idol worship and all their evils.

God is the searcher of hearts and minds, and we are all exposed before Him. So do not persist in sin, for He sees you; and at the same time He greatly values your repentance, your striving and your attempt to draw near to Him. Remind yourself every day that you stand before Him to give an account of your stewardship, so that sin may not seduce you and you may not lose your crown.

God declares that the good figs are the Jews who were carried captive to Babylon. They lost their place beside the ruined temple, but they held fast to the commandments of God. So God blesses them with good because of their obedience to Him and their acceptance of discipline for their sins, since they listened to His prophets; God accepted their repentance and blessed them.

If affliction comes upon you, accept it as discipline from God for repentance and for the correction of your faults, and know that God is able to bless you within the affliction, so that you experience Him and behold Him more than at any time in your life.

God promises those who obeyed Him and came into captivity that He will bless them for accepting discipline, that He will reward them by returning them to Jerusalem and establishing them there, that He will build the temple for them and build them up in a strong spiritual life, for He is God, who is able to do all things.

God also promises His repentant children that He will give them a heart inclined to Him, that is, feelings of love directed toward Him. He also declares that He sets them apart as His people and cares for them because of their repentance.

God speaks of those who will disobey Him and cling to material things and evil, such as Zedekiah the king, the last king of Judah, and his close servants who govern the land, and the remaining people in Jerusalem and Judea who refused to go into captivity. They will be in a wretched state like the bad figs, because in their hypocrisy they thought that their remaining in Jerusalem was good and right, while their hearts were full of evil and idol worship.

Jeremiah prophesies about the wicked who remained in Jerusalem that God will abandon them and they will be in anxiety, because they relied on themselves and rejected God. In their weakness they will even become an example of contempt and mockery among the peoples, all because of their disobedience to God. They will also be driven out of Jerusalem and subjected to many troubles, for some of them went to Egypt and suffered many hardships there.
God decrees that He will punish them with three afflictions:
1- The sword, that is, death.
2- Their extreme poverty and their hunger even for necessary food.

3- Their being struck with severe diseases through pestilences that weaken them and destroy some of them. By these blows they will die and will not benefit from being in the Promised Land, because being in holy places without walking in holiness is of no benefit.

Benefit from every spiritual opportunity offered to you, so that you may know God through it and enjoy fellowship with Him, lest all these opportunities condemn you; for God sent them to you because He loves you.
The cup of wrath

Jeremiah fixes the time of the prophecy mentioned in this chapter as the fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah, which is at the same time the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, namely 604 BC, after Nebuchadnezzar's victory over Necho king of Egypt at the battle of Carchemish in 605 BC, by which Babylon took possession of all Judea. He speaks of the Babylonian attack, coming swiftly to destroy Jerusalem and Judea, and warns his people for the last time so that they may repent.

This prophecy is addressed to those who dwell in Jerusalem and Judea, that is, the whole kingdom of Judah. Jeremiah dictated this prophecy to his scribe Baruch the prophet, who presented it to King Jehoiakim, and he burned it (Jer 36:1-26); Jeremiah wrote a second copy of it. This prophecy comes in order after the first twenty chapters of this book, and this book, or scroll, became the nucleus for the gathering of the rest of his prophecies (Jer 36:27-32).

Jeremiah declares that the beginning of his prophecies was in the thirteenth year of Josiah the king, the son of Amon, which is 627 BC. They continued for 19 years, then three months for the reign of Jehoahaz; after that Jehoiakim reigned for four years, and we reach the year 604 BC. That is, Jeremiah's prophecies have extended up to now for 23 years, during which he warned them to repent and spoke to them the word of God. He says "rising early" because Jeremiah began his prophecies at an early age.

Pay attention to God's messages, in which He calls you to repentance in different forms, so that you respond to His love. And in proportion to your care for prayer and for obeying Him before your own desires, you will hear His voice clearly.

There is no excuse for the disobedience of the Jewish people, because God did not send them one prophet only, Jeremiah, but many prophets went before him, such as Elijah, Elisha and Isaiah; yet they rejected the word of God spoken by their mouths.
The prophecies of the prophets are summed up in a call to repent of the evil, which appears in two things:
1- Idol worship.
2- Evil lusts.

If they repented of their sins, they would enjoy the good things of the Promised Land which God promised to the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; indeed it was in His eternal plan and love to give it to them. This land is a symbol of the new earth, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven, which God prepared in His first plan from eternity for the believers, that they might dwell in it with Him forever.

Consider God's love for you from eternity and what He has prepared for you in the Kingdom, so that you may reject all your sins, however beloved or habitual they are or however much all those around you walk in them, and thank Him for His love, and live for Him so that you may enjoy Him now and forever.

He clearly warns against the idol worship which the Jews made with their own hands in the form of various images, and warns them that by this they defy Him and provoke Him to anger, that perhaps they may repent and return to Him; and if they insist on worshiping idols, He will be compelled to punish them.
Sadly, the people insisted on worshiping idols and provoked God to anger by their evil, so they deserved every punishment.
God shows one of His attributes, "the Lord of hosts," to declare His power, which is able to punish them for their evils.
The families of the north: the armies of the Babylonians.
Utterly destroy them: kill them.
An astonishment: they will be in terror.
An hissing: all people mock them for what has happened to them.

God declares His punishment for their disobedience: it is the use of the mighty Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon with his armies to attack the kingdom of Judah and shatter it, and to take possession of all the surrounding countries, laying them waste and killing those in them. Those who remain in them will be in terror and fear, and any who pass by them will mock and despise them for what happened to them because of their sins.
The millstones: the plural of the mill, the stones used anciently to grind grain. The punishment will include many things:

1- The banning of joy and gladness, represented by the joy of new marriages and the use of musical instruments in merrymaking. This is a symbol of the absence of joy in God, and sorrow takes its place because of sin.

2- Hunger: the mill will not be used to grind grain for the food of man and beast, since there will be no grain to grind, so they suffer hunger and die. This is a symbol of hunger for the word of God.
3- The absence of light because of the destruction, which is a symbol of the darkness of sin.

Here he fixes the duration of the captivity of the kingdom of Judah, or the Babylonian captivity, when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon occupied all the land of the Jews and the countries around it. He fixes this period at seventy years, beginning in 609 BC when Jeremiah announced this prophecy, to 536 BC when the first group of Jews returned to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel in the days of Cyrus king of the Medes and Persians. That is, the seventy years are approximately the duration of the Babylonian kingdom; then Babylon fell and the kingdom of the Medes and Persians arose, at the beginning of which the return of the Jews to Jerusalem from captivity began.

God used Babylon to discipline His people so that they would repent, although the Babylonians were wicked and worshiped idols. After the people of God repented, He brought them back from captivity, and punished the Babylonians for their evils and their wrongs against His people, so that great Babylon was destroyed by the hand of the Medes and Persians, who reigned in its place.
He affirms that He will fulfill the prophecies of Jeremiah recorded in his book concerning the people of God and the Babylonians.

He decrees that the kings who enslaved His people and wronged them, and everyone who walked in evil, He will repay for their sins: Babylon will be overturned, and after it the Medes and Persians, and then the Greeks, that is, the Ionians.

Do not become proud if God blesses you and you become stronger than those around you. Rather, thank Him and repent of your sins, because if God disciplined another for his evil, He will discipline you also if you do not repent. So live with God and hold fast to His commandments, and you will live in security.

God declares His wrath in order to discipline all the peoples of the earth for their evil, that they may repent, for God is the God of the whole world and desires the salvation of all, even though He chose a people for Himself, the Jews, to be an example to the rest of the peoples, so that all may return to Him and believe in Him. This is what was accomplished in Christianity, as mankind from all lands believed in Him.

The "cup" he calls a cup of wine that makes a person lose his balance, and he means divine discipline; when the wrath of God comes upon them they lose their strength. Christ before the Cross called the sufferings a cup, that is, He drank the cup for our sake and died to redeem us, bearing the wrath of God and the punishment of sin on His head to free us from it (Mt 26:39). The law of Moses decreed that a woman accused of unfaithfulness to her husband was given holy water by the priest in an earthen vessel, with some of the dust of the tabernacle of meeting put upon it, and she drank this water, which was called the water of the curse. If her belly swelled and her thigh fell away, she was judged unclean and became a curse among the people for her evil. So this cup proclaims the wrath of God against the unclean.

The effects of God's wrath on the nations are that they reel, that is, lose their balance, and go mad, that is, lose their minds, because of the many slain among them. This declares that God's wrath will be severe because of their many sins.

Jeremiah took the cup, that is, the word of God from the cup of wrath, and made all the peoples drink by announcing this prophecy before God, His servants and all the people, and the news of this prophecy passed to all the peoples.

He begins with Jerusalem and the kingdom of Judah because they are the people of God who knew much about Him. He disciplines them before others, because they have no excuse if they reject God and walk in evil and idol worship despite their knowledge of God.

After this comes the discipline upon Egypt and its princes, because it was the power on which the people of God tried to rely. Egypt was proud and did not submit to God but walked in idol worship, so the wrath of God came upon it after Jerusalem.

The mingled people: those of the Egyptians who joined the children of Israel and lived with them. Uz: a country lying east of Egypt and south of the kingdom of Judah, where Job dwelt (Job 1:1). Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and the remnant of Ashdod: the most important cities of Palestine, that is, the discipline will come upon the Philistines.
The wrath of God comes upon the countries neighboring the Jews that lie to their east, namely: Edom: they are the descendants of Esau, living in the mountains of Seir.
Moab: they are the descendants of Lot by his elder daughter.
The children of Ammon: they are the descendants of Lot by his younger daughter.
All these peoples were hostile to the people of the children of Israel on many occasions.
The wrath of God extends to the countries lying west of the land of the Jews, namely:
1- The Phoenicians (Lebanon), including:
a- Tyre: it lies on the coast of the Mediterranean and is famous for commerce.
b- Sidon: it lies on the coast beside Tyre and is famous for fishing.
2- The isles: those in the Mediterranean, such as Malta and Crete.
The wrath of God also extends to the Arab tribes dwelling south of the Jews, namely:
1- Dedan: descendants of Abraham, famous for commerce (Gen 25:3).
2- Tema: they dwell in the desert regions beyond Haran (Gen 25:15).
3- Buz: descendants of Nahor, Abraham's brother (Gen 22:21); they dwell on the road between Damascus and Mecca.

4- All that are in the utmost corners: those with the hair cut round; it was among the rites of worship of some gods to cut the hair in a circle, leaving a round area on top of the head, and these are Arab tribes.

The wrath of God includes all the kings of the Arabs and their tribes spread throughout the Arabian peninsula, and likewise "the mingled people," that is, those of the Arabs who attached themselves to the Jews and lived with them.
Zimri, Elam and the Medes: countries lying in the far east, upon which the wrath of God will also come.
Sheshach: Babylon.

The wrath also includes the countries north of the land of the Jews, whether near to them or far from the Jews; these countries will rise against one another, so the wrath of God will include all people because of their evil. In the end, the wrath of God comes upon Babylon, as the kingdom of the Medes and Persians lays it waste.

God declares His wrath against the peoples of the earth for their sins, so He says to them through Jeremiah: drink the cup of wine, that is, your evil lusts and idol worship, until you lose your balance like drunkards, and vomit, that is, come to a base and wretched state, and become empty after what is within you is brought out, that is, you become weak; then you will fall silent because of your shame and terror before the many slain among you.

And if they refuse to drink the cup, that is, refuse to hear the teachings and prophecies of Jeremiah, he assures them that the punishment is certain, that is, they will drink the cup of divine wrath.
The city which is called by my name: Jerusalem, because the temple of God is in it.
You: all the pagan peoples of the world.

God declares that His wrath will come upon His children who worship Him in His temple in Jerusalem because of their evils, and all the more will His wrath come upon all the peoples of the world because of their evil. Although He permits the wicked, such as Assyria and Babylon, to discipline His children, or the countries surrounding the Jews, such as Edom, Moab and the children of Ammon, to wrong them, all this is temporary; afterward He disciplines all who wronged His people, because they are wicked and pagan.
As they that tread the grapes: the shout of those treading grapes in the winepresses after they have been gathered is strong.

God likens Himself to a lion that lets out his fearful voice to all the animals; that is, God declares His wrath against all the peoples of the world and punishes them all, that they may believe in Him and return to Him. He also likens Himself to the shout of those who tread grapes in the winepresses.

God expresses the intensity of His wrath by the noise; that is, the loud voice and the great tumult heard everywhere in the world, because God stands as an adversary before the peoples of the world and judges and tries them, showing their deserving of punishment, and punishes them for their evil.
Tempest: a violent wind.

God declares that His wrath will fall on all the lands of the world because they are wicked, so the wrath comes upon one country after another to alert everyone to faith and repentance. By the great whirlwind he means the Babylonian attack, which sweeps over the whole earth and kills many.

Today you have an opportunity to repent before the day of judgment comes or severe afflictions befall you and you become preoccupied with them and it is hard for you to return to God. Offer your repentance today before God, and pledge to live for Him and remain steadfast in His Church.
Dung: human waste.
Lamented: people mourn them with the well-known words of lamentation.
Gathered: their corpses lying in the streets are collected.

He describes the Babylonian attack that will cover the whole earth, that is, most of the countries known at that time, and kill many of them. Because of the multitude of the slain there is no opportunity to mourn the dead or even to lift up their bodies and bury them, because the living who remain flee from the face of the sword; so terror is in every heart, and the corpses become putrid, giving off foul odors everywhere, as human waste has a foul odor.

By the shepherds he means the leaders of the people, the teachers and those responsible for guiding and caring for the people of God. He warns them that their punishment has come, and they will be broken like a precious vessel and shattered. In another translation, instead of "a pleasant vessel" it says "the desirable rams," that is, they will be slaughtered like fattened rams. In sum, they will perish for their evils and their neglect of teaching the people the commandments of God. Therefore God calls them to weep and to humble themselves in the dust in repentance before Him before God strikes them by the hand of Babylon and scatters them far from their land.
A way to flee: a resolution and a rescue.
And if these shepherds try to flee from the Babylonian attack, they will find no opportunity, for it will overtake them and kill them, or seize them, humble them and enslave them.

These shepherds weep and cry out because they found no pasture for their flocks because of the Babylonian devastation that comes upon them; what is meant is that they will be in severe hunger and distress.

Peaceable folds: the green pastures in which the flocks graze quietly and securely. Terror and fear prevail because of the Babylonian attack, so everyone is disturbed and flees, and there is no opportunity for quiet work such as shepherding; consequently the sheep grow weak and die, and man is exposed to hunger.
His covert: his den.

He likens Babylon to a young lion that has come out of his den to prey on and shatter the nations of the world, and he describes it as oppressive because it plunders the spoils of all the lands and lays them waste.
Take care to shepherd those around you and draw them to Christ, show them love and warn them to guard against mistakes, so that you keep them and keep yourself from the wars of the devil.
Jeremiah's sermon in the temple and the attempt to kill him

entries.section: (1) Jeremiah's sermon in the temple and his arrest

paragraphs.text: After the death of the righteous King Josiah, his son Jehoahaz reigned a few months and was then carried captive to Egypt, and his brother Jehoiakim reigned in 609 BC. He had to pay a heavy tribute to Necho, Pharaoh of Egypt, yet he did not repent and fear God but was concerned to gather money to build a great palace for himself, and he opposed Jeremiah the prophet. So at the beginning of his reign, when his evil appeared, God commanded Jeremiah to stand in the house of the Lord, where many gather, to declare this prophecy, since the inhabitants of Jerusalem and all Judea come to the house of the Lord; and He emphasized to him that he must not diminish a word of the word of God, which shows the importance of this prophecy. Note that in this chapter and the following three chapters Jeremiah addresses his words to the people, the priests, the false prophets and the rulers, to call them to repentance.

entries.section: (1) Jeremiah's sermon in the temple and his arrest

paragraphs.text: God's purpose in the warning that comes in this prophecy is not vengeance on His children but to alert them to repent, so that He may forgive them all their sins.

entries.section: (1) Jeremiah's sermon in the temple and his arrest

paragraphs.text: God warns them and cautions them of woes that will come upon them if they do not obey His commandments.

entries.section: (1) Jeremiah's sermon in the temple and his arrest

paragraphs.text: God declares His word through His prophets, but sadly the people rejected their word.

entries.section: (1) Jeremiah's sermon in the temple and his arrest

paragraphs.text: Shiloh: the place where the tabernacle of meeting and the ark of the covenant of God were in the days of Samuel the prophet; the Philistines destroyed this city and seized the ark of the covenant of God from the children of Israel. God reminds them that He allowed the enemies to demolish the place of His house at Shiloh, and now He will allow the demolition of His temple in Jerusalem and her destruction if they do not repent, return to Him and obey His commandments.

entries.section: (1) Jeremiah's sermon in the temple and his arrest

paragraphs.text: The Holy Bible affirms that the words of this prophecy were heard by the people with their various leaders, the priests and the false prophets.

Do not rely on the outward forms of your spiritual life, as the Jews anciently relied on having the temple and Jerusalem, the city of God. All outward forms of piety are of no benefit without living their depths and without repentance.

entries.section: (1) Jeremiah's sermon in the temple and his arrest

paragraphs.text: After Jeremiah declared this prophecy, all the people, led by the priests and the false prophets, rose against him and seized him to kill him because of his prophecy about the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple. It was an uprising of the whole people against Jeremiah.

entries.section: (2) Jeremiah warns the princes against shedding his blood

paragraphs.text: The princes of Judah: he means the judges and civil rulers responsible for leading the people. When the princes of Judah, who helped the king in governing the kingdom, heard all of Jeremiah's prophecy about the destruction of the temple and Jerusalem, they were greatly troubled. They went up from the royal palace, where they do their work of administering the affairs of the kingdom, to the temple of God, because it is built on a hill, and gathered at one of its gates, called "the new gate," to try Jeremiah, as was the ancient custom of holding trials at the gates and squares of cities so as to have room for the crowds to gather and follow the trial (Gen 23:10-20) (Ruth 4:1).

entries.section: (2) Jeremiah warns the princes against shedding his blood

paragraphs.text: When the judges and princes reached the gate of the house of the Lord, the priests and the false prophets hurried to them, holding Jeremiah, and repeated to them what he had said in his prophecy about the destruction of the house of the Lord, and announced the verdict before the trial: the necessity of putting him to death. This shows their evil and their unwillingness to examine matters, because they hated Jeremiah on account of his earlier prophecies against them.

entries.section: (2) Jeremiah warns the princes against shedding his blood

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah affirmed before the princes and all the people that he is a prophet sent by God to declare the prophecies they hear; therefore they must obey the words of this prophecy.

entries.section: (2) Jeremiah warns the princes against shedding his blood

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah summed up what was required of his hearers: repentance and return to God, and the amendment of their faults, that is, leaving their lusts and their worship of idols. Then God would forgive them all their sins and turn back from the punishment He had decreed against them, namely the destruction of Jerusalem.

entries.section: (2) Jeremiah warns the princes against shedding his blood

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah was not afraid of the threat to kill him, and declared his readiness to die for God's sake, saying that it was in their power to put him to death.

Do not fear the threats of the wicked, and trust in God's protection of you. Then you will proclaim the voice of God and live faithfully, confident that evil has no authority over you unless God permits it for your benefit; and He will be with you and support you in all your afflictions.

entries.section: (2) Jeremiah warns the princes against shedding his blood

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah warned them against killing him, for by this they would fall into the sin of killing without cause that a man deserves, and God would be angrier with them and with their city because of the shedding of his innocent blood.

entries.section: (3) The princes against the priests and the prophets

paragraphs.text: God intervened and convinced the princes of Jeremiah's innocence, and that he is a prophet sent by God who fulfilled his mission and intends no personal evil against Jerusalem. Thus they turned away from the hatred of the priests and the false prophets, and rejected their mistaken counsel which wanted to put Jeremiah to death.

entries.section: (3) The princes against the priests and the prophets

paragraphs.text: God also sent the elders and heads of the people, that is, the foremost of the people at hand, and they supported the words of the judges and princes in the king's palace against the priests and the prophets by reminding them of ancient events that support Jeremiah's innocence and his rescue from death.

entries.section: (3) The princes against the priests and the prophets

paragraphs.text: Plowed: tilled with the plow, that is, demolished and leveled with the ground.

The high places of a forest: hills of ruined buildings like the hills found in the wilderness. The elders reminded the judges, the priests and all the assembled people of what happened about a century earlier, when a prophet named Micah the Morasthite, that is, from a town called Moresheth, arose and prophesied the destruction of Jerusalem and her complete ruin (Mic 3:12).

entries.section: (3) The princes against the priests and the prophets

paragraphs.text: King Hezekiah, who was reigning at that time, did not become angry and take vengeance on Micah by killing or torturing him; on the contrary, he feared God and offered repentance, he and his people (2 Kgs 18:14), so God forgave them and postponed carrying out the destruction of Jerusalem. Consequently, taking vengeance on Jeremiah and killing him would cast the whole people into a great sin, because by this they would be resisting God.

God is able to rescue you at the right time, however much enemies rise against you and however great their strength. So do not be terrified of them: He sends you help in due time from where you do not know. God is with you, so do not fear any man.
Kirjath-jearim: a city of the Gibeonites lying northwest of Jerusalem at a distance of eight miles.

Jeremiah tells us a story that shows how fierce King Jehoiakim was and how he was led along behind the priests and the false prophets. It happened at the same time that a prophet of God arose in the village of Kirjath-jearim and prophesied the destruction of Jerusalem exactly as Jeremiah prophesied. God sent him, as He sent Jeremiah and, anciently, Micah, to confirm what would happen so that the Jews would repent and not rely on having the temple, for this is not enough for their salvation as long as they are in sin.
Jehoiakim and all his helpers were greatly angered, and made war on Urijah the prophet, and he commanded that he be killed, so he fled to Egypt.

There were treaties and an understanding between Jehoiakim king of Judah and Necho, Pharaoh of Egypt, so Jehoiakim sent men, and they seized Urijah in Egypt and brought him to Jehoiakim, who killed him and cast his body with contempt into the graves of the common people, and not with the honor given to prophets.

Do not persist in sin, insisting on it and trying to carry it out by every means, lest you bring upon yourself the wrath of God. He is long-suffering but at the same time just, so do not make light of His long-suffering.

Ahikam the son of Shaphan: one of Jehoiakim's helpers. His father Shaphan was one of Josiah's helpers and was godly and loved Jeremiah. The discussions were still heated, the priests on one side and the false prophets on the other, over killing Jeremiah or acquitting him. So God moved the heart of one of the godly, Ahikam, one of the king's helpers, and he interceded and confirmed the words of the judges, and so rescued Jeremiah from being put to death.
Submission to Babylon

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Many think that King Jehoiakim is mentioned here by mistake and that the correct name is King Zedekiah. In the Arabic and Syriac translation the first verse reads: "Zedekiah reigned in place of Jehoiakim." This was in 597 BC. Babylon made this king reign in place of Jehoiachin, whom it carried captive to Babylon after he had reigned a few months. So at the beginning of Zedekiah's reign Jeremiah spoke this prophecy. In those days the kingdom of Babylon, only four years after its rise, faced wars in the east from Elam and unrest in Syria, so some kings west of the kingdom of Babylon, around Jerusalem, gathered and organized an alliance to resist Babylon. The false prophets in the kingdom of Judah affirmed that Babylon would collapse, and encouraged King Zedekiah and the kings allied with him to fight Babylon because it would fall and collapse. Only one person stood against all this current, demanding that the people submit to the bondage of Babylon, and he was Jeremiah the prophet, as the Lord commanded him.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem
