paragraphs.text: Bonds: straps of leather or ropes tied around the neck of an animal.

Yokes: the plural of yoke, a piece of wood placed on the necks of two animals, tied with ropes or leather around the neck and fastened there; a crosswise beam is mounted on the yoke and draws at its end the farming implements such as the plow.

God asked Jeremiah to make yokes with ropes fastened to them and to put them on his neck as a visual aid by which he declares his submission to the king of Babylon, as an example before the messengers of the kings and before King Zedekiah, that they might submit to the king of Babylon.

Jeremiah bore the yoke, which signifies the bondage of sin, although he is a godly man far from evil. By this he is a type of Christ, who is without sin and bore the Cross for us to die in our place and redeem us.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Edom: the descendants of Esau, living in the mountains of Seir.
Moab: the descendants of Lot by his elder daughter.
The children of Ammon: the descendants of Lot by his younger daughter.
Tyre: a large commercial city on the coast of the Mediterranean in Lebanon.
Sidon: a city on the coast of the Mediterranean south of Tyre.

There were messengers from the countries of Edom, Moab, the children of Ammon, Tyre and Sidon who had come to King Zedekiah to ally with him against Babylon. He gave each of them a yoke to bind and carry to his king as a visual aid of the necessity of his submission to the king of Babylon, as an animal submits to the yoke placed on its neck.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: God sent a message through Jeremiah, with the messengers of the kingdoms mentioned above, declaring in it that He is God, the Creator of the earth and of the man and beast upon it, that is, that He has complete authority, and gives the kingdom to whom He wills of mankind to carry out the will of God.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: God continues His speech: He uses Nebuchadnezzar His servant to carry out His will by possessing all the lands of his kingdom, as an instrument to discipline His people and the other peoples for their disobedience and evils.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: His son and his son's son: either he means his sons and grandsons, or he means his son Evil-merodach and his son's son Belshazzar (Dan 5:11). The time of his land: the time when the kingdom of Babylon collapses and the kingdom of the Medes and Persians rises against it. Many nations and great kings: the kings of the Medes and Persians who laid Babylon waste and took all their lands.

God declares that the peoples of the earth will submit not only to Nebuchadnezzar but also to those who succeed him from his seed up to his grandson Belshazzar, and this was for seventy years. After that the kingdom of the Medes and Persians arises, a union between two kingdoms, to enslave Babylon and take all its possessions and use them as it wishes.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: God adds that whoever disobeys and resists the king of Babylon will die either by the sword, by disease, or by hunger, which is the opposite of all that the false prophets claimed.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Your prophets: he means the false prophets.
Your diviners: the plural of diviner, one who claims knowledge of the unseen in any form.
Your dreamers: one who claims to have dreams that tell him the future.
Your enchanters: the plural of enchanter, who likewise claims knowledge of the unseen.
Your sorcerers: the plural of sorcerer, who likewise claims, by the power of Satan, to know the future and to be able to work wonders.

God also forbids them to listen to those who claim prophecy and knowledge of the unseen, whether false prophets or others, and who prevent them from submitting to the king of Babylon and encourage them to resist him.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: He also warned the peoples of these kingdoms that their believing the words of the false prophets would make the king of Babylon attack them, drive them out of their lands and destroy them, as God permitted him. It is remarkable that God says He will drive out these peoples; what is meant is that He will accomplish this by the hand of the king of Babylon.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: On the contrary, God gives good news to whoever obeys His word and submits to the king of Babylon, that he will dwell in his land, do his work and be settled in his life.

Accept the word of God even if it is hard, such as keeping the difficult commandments, so that you may find your salvation, and do not be deceived by the words of the people of the world, which deceive you that sin gives you comfort and makes you succeed in life.
(2) Warning to King Zedekiah (vv. 12-15).

12- I spake also to Zedekiah king of Judah according to all these words, saying, Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and live. 13- Why will ye die, thou and thy people, by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, as the LORD hath spoken against the nation that will not serve the king of Babylon? 14- Therefore hearken not unto the words of the prophets that speak unto you, saying, Ye shall not serve the king of Babylon: for they prophesy a lie unto you. 15- For I have not sent them, saith the LORD, yet they prophesy a lie in my name; that I might drive you out, and that ye might perish, ye, and the prophets that prophesy unto you.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah repeated the same words to King Zedekiah, to submit to the king of Babylon so that he and his people might live. This time he responded and left this alliance, but he returned and rebelled against the king of Babylon, relying on Egypt, so the king of Babylon seized him, killed his sons, and then put out his eyes.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: He assured him that if he did not obey God and submit to the king of Babylon he would die by one of three means, namely the sword, disease or hunger.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: He warned him against being influenced by the words of the false prophets, because they claim that God sent them while God is innocent of their words; they intend to lead you astray so that you are driven out of your land, you and also these prophets.

The children of God ought to hold fast to His commandments before the children of the world, and indeed be an example of obedience to God, so that they escape the evil of the world and are a model for others.
(3) Warning to the priests and the people (vv. 16-22).

16- Also I spake to the priests and to all this people, saying, Thus saith the LORD; Hearken not to the words of your prophets that prophesy unto you, saying, Behold, the vessels of the LORD'S house shall now shortly be brought again from Babylon: for they prophesy a lie unto you.

17- Hearken not unto them; serve the king of Babylon, and live: wherefore should this city be laid waste? 18- But if they be prophets, and if the word of the LORD be with them, let them now make intercession to the LORD of hosts, that the vessels which are left in the house of the LORD, and in the house of the king of Judah, and at Jerusalem, go not to Babylon. 19- For thus saith the LORD of hosts concerning the pillars, and concerning the sea, and concerning the bases, and concerning the residue of the vessels that remain in this city, 20- Which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took not, when he carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah from Jerusalem to Babylon, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem;

21- Yea, thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that remain in the house of the LORD, and in the house of the king of Judah and of Jerusalem; 22- They shall be carried to Babylon, and there shall they be until the day that I visit them, saith the LORD; then will I bring them up, and restore them to this place.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: God exposes the lying of the false prophets who claim the collapse of Babylon and the return of the vessels of the house of the Lord that the king of Babylon had taken.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: He calls them to obey the king of Babylon so that they do not die and Jerusalem is not destroyed. And Jeremiah, of course, is not an agent of Babylon, as the false prophets claim, but is the one speaking the word of God, that they may accept their discipline and so repent of their sins.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: God gives proof of the lying of the false prophets: if they are sent by God, let them intercede with Him so that the rest of the vessels of the Lord and the contents of the temple which the king of Babylon had not taken may not go.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: The pillars: the two bronze pillars which King Solomon made and set in the outer court (1 Kgs 7:15-22). The sea: it corresponds to the laver in the tabernacle of meeting, and its form is a round bronze basin about five meters in diameter in which water is placed for washing.

The bases: twelve bases, each in the form of an ox, made of bronze, on which rested the bronze sea mentioned above (1 Kgs 7:23-25). These parts of the temple, which are the pillars, the sea and its bases, and other contents of the temple, Nebuchadnezzar did not take when he carried captive Jeconiah, or King Jehoiachin, and the nobles who were in Babylon. So Jeremiah asks the false prophets to pray to God that they may not be taken to Babylon too, if they are truly real prophets; but what will actually happen is that they will be taken in the second attack of the king of Babylon on Jerusalem.

entries.section: (1) Warnings to the neighboring kings in Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: The day that I visit them: when Babylon collapses before the kingdom of the Medes and Persians and Cyrus the Persian king orders the return of the vessels of the house of the Lord to Jerusalem.

God declares that the rest of the contents of the temple will be taken by the king of Babylon and remain there until the end of the Babylonian kingdom and the rise of the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, when everything will be returned to the house of the Lord in Jerusalem.

God permits affliction for a temporary period so that you repent, and then He lifts it from you and restores to you all your glory. So do not be troubled by the affliction, but hasten to repentance and to holding fast to God.
Hananiah the false prophet
Gibeon: a city inhabited by priests, lying about 5 miles northwest of Jerusalem.

In the fourth year of King Zedekiah, at the beginning of his reign (he means the first half of his reign, since he reigned eleven years, and the fourth year corresponds to 593 BC), one of the false prophets came forward, called Hananiah the son of Azur, from the city of Gibeon, which is inhabited by priests, so he is thought to have been a priest. Because Gibeon is a city in the tribe of Benjamin and near Jerusalem, Hananiah came to Jerusalem and stood in the house of the Lord, where many gather, to declare his false prophecy. This was in the presence of Jeremiah, to make the people doubt the prophecies of Jeremiah.
Note the power of deception in Hananiah's prophecy, which relies on:
1- His being a priest.
2- He speaks in the house of the Lord before the crowds with boldness.
3- He speaks in the presence of Jeremiah, declaring the error and mistake of his prophecies.

4- He uses the same expressions that Jeremiah uses: "Thus speaketh the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel... I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon...", using the same visual aid that Jeremiah used.
5- He fixes a time for the fulfillment of his prophecy, namely after two years.

Be careful before strange, misleading teachings, for they have a logical form and a dazzling appearance; but as long as they conflict with the teachings of the Church and the holy Fathers, they are misleading. Do not rush after them, but lift up your heart in prayer and hold fast to what you have, that is, what you learned from the Church, lest you go astray.

The summary of the prophecy is the end of Nebuchadnezzar's enslavement of all the lands he occupied, including the kingdom of Judah, after two years' time, the breaking of Babylon, and the return of the vessels of the house of the Lord which Nebuchadnezzar had seized from the temple in Jerusalem. Note his preoccupation with material things, namely the vessels of the house of the Lord, before the captives, who are more important. Of course his prophecy is false, because Jeremiah declared that the Babylonian captivity would continue for 70 years (Jer 25:12).

He gives a second proof of the end of Babylon's enslavement of the kingdom of Judah, that is, the breaking of its yoke: the return of King Jeconiah king of Judah, who was carried captive to Babylon, and all the captives with him, to Jerusalem and Judea.
Jeremiah was not troubled by the deceit of the false Hananiah. He stood before him in the house of the Lord and answered him calmly and with power.

Jeremiah declared his agreement, not with Hananiah's prophecy, but with the return of the captives and of the vessels of the house of the Lord. This will indeed happen, but after 70 years; it is the wish of the whole kingdom of Judah, but it will not be after two years as Hananiah said.
Jeremiah qualified his words to Hananiah: although he agrees with this wish, he shows his lying in what follows in the next two verses.

Jeremiah said to Hananiah that any prophet is known to be truthful by the fulfillment of his prophecy in its time. So it was with the ancient prophets who preceded him: if his word is true, what he says will come to pass. The truth is that Hananiah's word conflicts not only with Jeremiah's word but with many earlier prophets such as Joel, Amos, Hosea, Micah, Zephaniah, Nahum, Habakkuk and others.

Do not be troubled by the error of false teachers, and be sure that your God is with you, supporting you, and will fulfill what you believe. Satan is not only a liar and the father of lies, but he speaks with boldness and impudence, so pay no attention to his words.

entries.section: (3) The breaking of the wooden yoke

paragraphs.text: Hananiah supported his words with a visual aid: he took the yoke which Jeremiah wore on his neck and broke it before the assembled people to prove his prophecy that the bondage of Babylon would end, using the moving visual aid to mislead the people.

entries.section: (3) The breaking of the wooden yoke

paragraphs.text: Hananiah affirmed that Babylon's enslavement of the kingdom of Judah and all the lands around it would end after two years. When Jeremiah saw his insistence on error, he left him and went his way: the servant does his duty and is not troubled by the abundance of evil, even if the wicked persist in it.

Do not deceive others by letting them hear what they want to hear, even if it is against the truth, and do not believe what you wish, lest others lead you astray and you drift from the truth. Rather, seek God and accept His word, so that you repent of your sins and are ready at all times.

Jeremiah did not rush to utter words to rebuke Hananiah but turned to God and prayed until it was revealed to him what to say to Hananiah, for he speaks with the voice of God and not with his own personal words.

Make sure that what you say is the voice of God. Do not be hasty in answering, and seek God to guide you, however much others provoke and threaten you, and be reassured, for God will teach you the truth and keep you from the evil of enemies.

Jeremiah declared the word of God to Hananiah: that in haste and deceit he broke the wooden yoke to proclaim falsely that the bondage of Babylon would end, but the truth is that this word is a deception of the people, and God will allow yokes of iron in place of the wooden yokes; that is, the bondage of Babylon will be harsh and cannot be escaped except after the fullness of time, that is, after seventy years.
God will allow Babylon to enslave all the peoples, and likewise all its possessions, like the animals.

Jeremiah declared the word of God clearly in a specific rebuke of Hananiah the false prophet, for Jeremiah said to him: you are not a prophet from God, but you came of yourself and falsely claimed that your words are from God.

The second divine declaration to Hananiah is his punishment for his false prophecy: he will be cast off, not from his country as the Babylonians will do to the inhabitants of the kingdom of Judah, but from the face of the whole earth, that is, he will die as the recompense for his lying, as happened with Ananias and Sapphira, who lied and died at once (Acts 5:1-11).

God's word was indeed fulfilled: Hananiah died in the same year, two months after his false prophecy, which was in the fifth month of the fourth year of King Zedekiah; Hananiah died in the seventh month. Here we see the mercy of God, who gave him two months as an opportunity to repent, and that is better than the case of Ananias and Sapphira, who died at once. He prophesied that after two years the bondage would end, but only two months passed and he died, while the Babylonian bondage lasted seventy years.
God gives you the opportunity of this life for repentance and returning to Him, so do not be negligent and neglect it, and accept rebuke from others, for it may be a divine message to you.
A letter to the captives

After Nebuchadnezzar carried captive Jeconiah the king, who is also called Jehoiachin, and with him the great men who were in Jerusalem, Jeremiah sent this letter, and this was in 597 BC. Jeremiah sent this letter from Jerusalem to the leaders of the captives, the priests and the prophets, to read it to all the people.

With Jeconiah the captive king were his wife the queen and also some men whom the king of Babylon had made eunuchs to work for him, especially in the palaces of his wives, in addition to the Jews distinguished in the various trades.

King Zedekiah king of Judah sent two of his officials, Elasah and Gemariah, to establish a good relationship with Nebuchadnezzar, who had heard of the attempt to form an alliance against him in the west of his kingdom, among whom was the king of Judah. So Jeremiah sent his letter with these two messengers, who were friends of his.

The speaker is the God of Israel, that is, the God of the people captive in humiliation and bondage. He declares His fatherhood and care for them to reassure them, and confirms this reassurance by describing Himself as the Lord of hosts, that is, the Mighty One, able to do all things.

If affliction passes through your life, be sure that your God, who always loves you, will not forget you. He is the Mighty One, able to rescue you when you return to Him in repentance, and He fixes the right time to lift all your troubles from you; and also during the affliction He will not leave you but will comfort your heart as long as you hold fast to Him.

God commands them to settle in Babylon and not be deceived by the errors of the false prophets, who make them imagine that the return from Babylon will be after two years. He confirms this settling through two things:
1- Building private houses for themselves in which to dwell.

2- Planting gardens of fruit trees to eat their fruit, which will ripen after years. This means that He calls them to accept divine discipline, which helps them to repent, and afterward God will return them to Jerusalem, after seventy years, so that their repentance may be complete.

He confirms their settling by a third thing, which is calling the young people to marry, establish new families and bear children. There is no need to postpone marriage, since they have seventy years ahead of them in captivity. Of course the marriage will be to believing Jews and not to pagans.

He also confirms their settling by a fourth thing, which is that they pray for the kingdom of Babylon, so that when it has peace they enjoy peace and settled life. This is what the Church does in praying for the city in which she is established and for the civil rulers, in the prayers of the Liturgy and the various ritual prayers (the Litany of Peace, the Litany for the Ruler)...

God warns them against listening to the lies of the prophets, diviners and dreamers, for it is their words of deception and not the word of God; Babylon will not be destroyed after two years as they claim.
If God has allowed His people to be disciplined so that they repent, it is for a fixed period, seventy years in captivity, and after that He returns them to their land to enjoy their worship of Him.
God's plan is the salvation of His children, and afflictions are one link in the links of this plan, so that they may be with Him in heaven.
I will be found of you: you will feel My presence in your midst.

God encourages His children that when their repentance is complete and they pray to Him, not only with their lips but with their faith and all their feelings, God hears them and makes them feel His presence in their midst, and brings them back from captivity to their land.

God rebukes His people captive in Babylon for describing the two false prophets, Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, mentioned in (v. 21), as prophets from God, and consequently believing their lies that Babylon would be overturned after two years, which hindered them from repentance and returning to God.

Then God speaks to the captives about their brothers who are still in Jerusalem and with whom King Zedekiah dwells; that is, He gives the captives a message from God about those who remain in Jerusalem.

Those who remained in Jerusalem thought that they were righteous and those in captivity wicked, so God declared to those remaining in Jerusalem that His wrath would come upon them, to die in three ways:
1- Death by the sword.
2- Death by disease, that is, by pestilence.
3- Death by hunger.
Their state will be very wretched and no one will accept dealing with them, like the bad winter fig which could not be eaten, explained earlier in (ch. 24).
To be removed: a cause of trouble.
A curse: the alliance of the nations against them.
An astonishment: the nations marvel at their humiliation and their God's abandonment of them.
An hissing: they hiss at them in mockery.
A reproach: an example of humiliation and ridicule.

God completes His punishment of those remaining in Jerusalem and Judea by the continuance of His wrath upon them: they die by the sword, famine and pestilence even after the Babylonians drive them out and transfer them from their land to other lands, and they become a cause of trouble in the lands to which they go; everyone mocks them and marvels at the humiliation into which they have fallen.

He continues his words to those remaining in Jerusalem, rebuking them for not obeying His prophets whom He sent early, that is, for many years up to now, to call them to faith and repentance; because of this disobedience the wrath of God came upon them.

He returns to direct his words to the captives in Babylon and gives them a new message, making clear in his words that it is He who sent them to Babylon, that is, He allowed this discipline so that they might accept it, submit to God and repent.

Jeremiah prophesies about the two false prophets whom the captives thought to be prophets from God, declaring that the king of Babylon will kill them, and that is a divine punishment because of the multitude of their sins, especially their leading the people astray.

The king of Babylon will kill them, not with the sword, but he will torture them by burning them with fire or boiling oil, so that they die a horrible death which becomes an example of shame and cursing. God allows this so that the people may fear and keep away from error.

God adds another reason, beside the lies and the leading of the people astray by these two prophets: that they committed adultery with their neighbors' wives, which is the sin of adultery and betrayal.

God asked Jeremiah to speak to one of the false prophets in Babylon, who was called Shemaiah the Nehelamite. The details of this letter are not given, but in essence it is a rebuke of Shemaiah for the letter he sent to Zephaniah the priest to stir people up against the word of God through the mouth of Jeremiah.
Jeremiah's letter to Shemaiah shows the following:
1- The speaker, the author of the letter, is God, the Lord of hosts, that is, the Mighty One, that Shemaiah may fear and repent of his evil.
2- Zephaniah had a distinguished position among the priests in Jerusalem, so Shemaiah sent his letter to him.

3- Shemaiah wanted to stir up all the priests against Jeremiah, so he directed his letter not only to Zephaniah but to all the priests; but he sent it to Zephaniah because he was foremost among them and their chief, and he attached to it letters with the same words to the priests.

4- The Lord of hosts is the God of Israel, that is, the One who shepherds him, and the letters of false prophets such as Shemaiah cannot change His plan: He disciplines them so that they repent and then brings them back from captivity.
5- These letters are in the name of Shemaiah and not in the name of God, so they are his own words and not, as Shemaiah claims, from God.
The stocks: a piece of wood with a place to fasten the hands and feet, where the person is laid on his back and his hand and foot are bound in it so that he cannot move inside the prison.
Shemaiah's letter to Zephaniah contains the following:

1- Shemaiah's claim that God made him chief priest, and not Jehoiada, about whom we know nothing, though he is thought to have been a high official among the priests and known to all; he died, and Shemaiah set himself up in his place and claimed that God had appointed him.
2- He describes Jeremiah the prophet as mad, and therefore his words are unsound and are not the word of God.
3- He claimed that God gave him the right to arrest the wicked who speak against the temple, like Jeremiah.

4- He calls the priests to seize Jeremiah, bind him in the stocks and put him in prison. From this it is understood that this Jehoiada was the chief of the guard responsible for protecting the temple and that Shemaiah took his place, so he commands the priests and their assistants to seize Jeremiah and throw him into prison.
All this, of course, is lies and claims of Shemaiah, and God is utterly innocent of them.
Shemaiah says in his letter to Zephaniah, reproaching him for his failure to rebuke Jeremiah, who is from the village of Anathoth near Jerusalem.
It is long: the stay in Babylon will be for a long time.

Shemaiah's letter to Zephaniah makes clear that Jeremiah erred because he sent a letter to Babylon asking the Jews to settle in it, build houses, plant fruit gardens and wait to eat from them. In Shemaiah's opinion this is against the people of God and an alliance with the Babylonian enemies.
But the truth is the word of Jeremiah and the word of God to discipline His people by staying in captivity for 70 years so that they repent.

When Shemaiah's letter reached Zephaniah the priest, he made it known not only to all the priests and those working in the temple, but also declared it to Jeremiah so that he would stop his prophecy, for it was a kind of threat to him. But Jeremiah did not fear, and God revealed to him to send a letter to him rebuking him for his letters and his lies, so he sent him a letter as we have mentioned.

Do not fear the threats of the wicked, for they have no authority over you; God alone has authority, and He protects you. So continue to hold fast to His commandments and to proclaim the truth, and do not fear anyone.

entries.section: (3) A second letter to the captives

paragraphs.text: God commanded Jeremiah to send a second letter to the captives in Babylon in which He declares His punishment of Shemaiah, who led the captives astray and also those in Jerusalem. What is meant by declaring God's punishment is that the Jews should keep away from these errors and repent, so that God may forgive them.

entries.section: (3) A second letter to the captives

paragraphs.text: The divine punishment of Shemaiah is that he will have no offspring living to see the return from captivity after 70 years; that is, his sons, his daughters and his offspring die and leave no offspring after him, so his offspring will not enjoy God's blessing for His people returning from captivity.

God had already declared His punishment through Jeremiah on another false prophet, Hananiah (ch. 28:15-16), by his death, and he died quickly. The divine purpose is also that the lies of the false prophets not be listened to.

Keep away from any strange teachings you hear outside the Church that conflict with her teachings, and consult your father of confession about these gatherings, so that you do not expose yourself to thoughts that draw you away from God, however beautiful and attractive their form, because the devil is a deceiver who can take the form of an angel to lead the children of God astray.
The return from captivity

God declares Himself as the God of Israel, that is, its Shepherd and Defender, and commands Jeremiah to write His coming prophecies in this chapter, because these prophecies will be fulfilled after a time and not now; but He declares them now to give hope to His people, captive and humiliated under the hand of Babylon. Chapters 30-33 are a message of consolation to encourage the people, full of hope.

God promises His people to bring them back from captivity. Although they had been divided into two kingdoms, Israel and Judah, after enduring the affliction of captivity the two become one kingdom after the captivity, to possess the Promised Land as a gift from God. The return from captivity is a renewal of their possession of it, after they had lost it through captivity because of their sins. They possess it from God and so thank Him, and it does not possess them, that is, it does not take hold of their hearts by its material things.
Accept affliction for God's sake, purify your heart in it, and forgive those who wronged you, so that love may return and reign over your heart, and you may possess many virtues which God grants you.

entries.section: (2) Salvation by the hand of the Medes and Persians

paragraphs.text: This prophecy concerns the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, which were exposed to captivity, and He wants to give them hope of deliverance from this affliction. He begins with Israel because it was carried captive first and has suffered for a long time the pains of bondage.

entries.section: (2) Salvation by the hand of the Medes and Persians

paragraphs.text: He expresses the feelings of the captives in Babylon when they heard of the attack of the Medes and Persians upon it. They feared greatly because they were humiliated under the hand of Babylon, and they felt a new affliction coming upon them, the attack of the Medes.

entries.section: (2) Salvation by the hand of the Medes and Persians

paragraphs.text: His loins: his belly and middle.
In travail: a woman whose delivery is near and who is in pain.

He likens the fear of the captive men, when they put their hands on their middle, to a woman whose delivery is near and who suffers her pains... And he says, does a man lay an egg like a hen, or give birth like a woman? Of course not, but it is the appearance of intense fear, which also showed on the faces that turned yellow as the blood fled from them because of terror.

entries.section: (2) Salvation by the hand of the Medes and Persians

paragraphs.text: God reassures His people, the descendants of Jacob, that although this day is difficult, the day of the Medes' and Persians' attack on Babylon to destroy it and kill those in it, among whom were the Jews, God will turn this day into salvation for His people; for after Cyrus, the first of the kings of the Medes and Persians, took possession, he ordered the return of the captive Jews to Jerusalem.

entries.section: (2) Salvation by the hand of the Medes and Persians

paragraphs.text: His yoke: a crosswise piece of wood placed on the necks of the two animals that draw the farming implements.
Thy bonds: the rope with which the yoke is tied on the neck of the beast.

God gives His people the good news that by the attack of the Medes and Persians the people of God are freed from the bondage of captivity and return to Jerusalem and begin worship in the temple, which signifies faith in Christ and worshiping Him in the Church. Then no one enslaves the people of God, since they have been freed from sin, and sin does not enslave them afterward; that is, strangers, who are the demons, cannot enslave them. The people of God were delivered by the Medes and Persians from captivity, but after a time the Greek kingdom arose and enslaved them, and after it the Roman kingdom, so deliverance from bondage was temporary; but spiritual salvation by faith in Christ lasts forever.

entries.section: (2) Salvation by the hand of the Medes and Persians

paragraphs.text: David their king: Christ, who is of the seed of David.

With the return of the people of God from captivity to Jerusalem, they began the worship of God in the temple, which was a preparation for their faith in Christ, who is of the seed of David, so that they serve Him forever with praise.

Do not be troubled by the afflictions that pass through your life, for they are the beginning of many blessings you will receive and they free you from many sins that enslave you, and you set out in worship and love, and enjoy fellowship with God more than before.

entries.section: (3) Healing from wounds that cannot be cured

paragraphs.text: God repeats His promise that He will deliver His people from the Babylonian captivity and bring them back to Jerusalem and Judea, and He calls it "My servant" to declare His responsibility for it, so that it may trust in God's promise and be reassured despite the afflictions surrounding it in captivity.

entries.section: (3) Healing from wounds that cannot be cured

paragraphs.text: God affirms His care and concern for His people and His promise of salvation to them, and reassures them that He punishes the nations that carry them captive and destroys them for their evils, while His people He disciplines only that they may repent, and then He saves them.

entries.section: (3) Healing from wounds that cannot be cured

paragraphs.text: The splint: a support for a fracture in the bones by means of pieces of wood or plaster so that the fracture knits. Grievous: hard and severe and impossible to heal.

God makes clear His feeling of the harshness of Babylon's bondage to His people, which is like a break in the bones that no splint can heal, or a very deep wound from which recovery is impossible. But despite the impossibility of escaping the bondage of Babylon, God, who is able to do all things, intervenes and delivers them; He makes clear the difficulty of the situation in order to show the power of His salvation.

entries.section: (3) Healing from wounds that cannot be cured

paragraphs.text: Pressing: squeezing the part afflicted with deep pus to bring out the pus within it and clean it.
Medicines: drugs.

Healing plaster: a strip of cloth (gauze) bound on the wound after the medicines are put on it. He also shows the misery and humiliation of the bondage of his people in Babylon, likening them to a person with pus in his body who finds no one to treat him and bring it out, for he has no medicines or cloths with which to bind his wounds; he is gravely ill and has no one to treat him or any medicines that would help him.

entries.section: (3) Healing from wounds that cannot be cured

paragraphs.text: Because of the harshness of the bondage, which is a severe discipline from God, the people of God not only suffered but everyone who had shown them an old friendship, such as Egypt, kept away from them, which increased the feeling of despair within the people of God, and nothing remained but hope in God alone.

entries.section: (3) Healing from wounds that cannot be cured

paragraphs.text: God addresses His people as a rejected bride and says to her: Do not cry out asking for someone to heal you, for there is no healing for your wounds, that is, no hope of your deliverance according to human thought, since God is the One who struck you, so who can rescue you from His hand unless you offer repentance, and He forgives you and lifts it from you.

entries.section: (3) Healing from wounds that cannot be cured

paragraphs.text: Every one: all together.

When the people of God repent, their God delivers them by humbling those who humbled them, who were devouring them by killing them to wipe them out: they themselves are exposed to death and to captivity to far-off lands, their spoils are seized and their houses plundered. This is what actually happened to the Babylonians when the Medes and Persians attacked them.

entries.section: (3) Healing from wounds that cannot be cured

paragraphs.text: God promises to heal her incurable wounds, healing her by His power which is able to do all things; she will no longer be called exiled and captive, but returns as His bride to her land, that is, to Jerusalem.

If you are passing through hard afflictions with no hope of resolution, or unbearable problems, do not be troubled, because your God watches over everything. He will heal you, treat your problems and lift every affliction from you, so that you praise Him always.

entries.section: (4) The return to Jerusalem and the change of conditions

paragraphs.text: The people of God left the tents in which they dwelt during the captivity and returned to Jerusalem to build its walls and palaces and dwell in them, and to bless God, who restored glory to Jerusalem, built on a high hill.

entries.section: (4) The return to Jerusalem and the change of conditions

paragraphs.text: The people praise God, and the children go out to play in the streets, rejoicing in their city. God blesses them so that they multiply and their number increases, and gives them standing and greatness among the peoples.

entries.section: (4) The return to Jerusalem and the change of conditions

paragraphs.text: The people of God return to their strength and standing in Jerusalem, and whoever among the surrounding peoples tries to trouble them, God punishes.

entries.section: (4) The return to Jerusalem and the change of conditions

paragraphs.text: Engaged his heart: he gave up his heart's attachment to material things, relied on God and held fast to Him; that is, he sold himself to the love of God.

Among God's blessings upon them is that one of themselves rules them and not enemies, serving as governor over them like Zerubbabel, Nehemiah or Judas Maccabeus; and God promises to bless their ruler because he drew near to God and asked His help and blessing.

entries.section: (4) The return to Jerusalem and the change of conditions

paragraphs.text: In the end the people of God enjoy His care and fatherhood, and become a people peculiar to Him, and He is their God who defends them.

God is able to restore your glory to you, honor you and bless you, however much sin has wearied you, the sin you held to and which caused you any losses. Your God is rich and loves you, and He will compensate you for everything as long as you have returned to Him.
A continuing whirlwind: a violent wind that sweeps away everything in its path.

God declares that He has allowed a severe whirlwind and tempest which express His wrath that He pours out on the wicked, namely the Babylonians who humiliated His people. God allowed this discipline for His people so that they would repent, but afterward He disciplines those who disciplined them and were harsh to them, namely the Babylonians.

The latter days: after the accomplishment of His purposes, that is, after the collapse of Babylon and the return of His people from captivity. God declares that His wrath will not cease against Babylon until it collapses, and the kingdom of the Medes and Persians comes and restores His people to their land.

If you do not understand God's purposes in the afflictions that pass through your life, know that He will make them clear to you afterward; but trust in His fatherhood, which cares for you and permits nothing for you except for the salvation of your soul.
The New Covenant
At the same time: the return from captivity, or faith in Christ.
The families: the tribes.

God promises to bring His people back from captivity, so that they are one people and He is their God. This also signifies the faith of, not only the tribes of Israel, but the whole world in Christ, so that they become one people, the new Israel.
The people which were left of the sword: those who were not killed and did not die in captivity.

God speaks of His people scattered in the world in the bondage of captivity, far from their land as though in a wilderness, and declares that they have found grace in the eyes of God. God shows His love in that He is the One who takes the initiative to give His people rest, saying "I went to cause him to rest"; for God is the One who goes after His children to free them from the bondage of sin if they repent and cry to Him, and this is the meaning of the affliction of captivity or of any affliction we pass through.

The captive people felt that God was far from them, so God declares that He appeared to His people, whom He thought far from Him although He is very near to them, and it is He who allowed their discipline that they might repent. He even declares that His love for His people is everlasting, that is, it does not pass away but continues forever. Therefore, if He allows them affliction and discipline, He returns and has mercy on them; indeed He is ready to have mercy on them many times as long as they repent and return to Him. Mercy is perpetual, that is, it continues throughout life.

God continues His promises, speaking of His people as His virgin, that is, His bride, and promises to build her again, and moreover she will be adorned with joy and rejoice like one who plays musical instruments and dances like the players in the dancing grounds; that is, His people praise Him with joy.
Shall eat them as common things: they rise early, that is, they get up energetically from early morning to work.

God also promises her fertility and good things: vineyards will be planted in Samaria, the capital of Israel, and the farmers rise early with energy to plant the trees and gather the fruit. This signifies the spiritual fruits with which the children of God are adorned.
The watchmen: the guards, that is, the servants.
There shall be a day: the day of the return from captivity.

After their return from captivity, they all worship God in Jerusalem, that is, Zion, because they have been disciplined by the affliction of captivity and have returned to God with all their hearts. The servants do their work, which is calling all the people to the worship of God.

If only you would understand that affliction is a temporary period which God allows for you to review yourself, bind yourself to Him and renew your vows, and then you will enjoy God's infinite love, His wide mercy and His beautiful promises.

God calls the peoples of the world to rejoice and sing for His people, who are the chief of the peoples because of their faith in God. He also calls His people to praise Him and asks them to be saved. God wants to save His people, but He waits for them to repent and seek Him, and then He saves them from all their enemies and gladdens them from all their hearts.

God also promises that He will gather His people scattered in the north at Babylon and from the ends of the world, however weak they are because of the humiliation of bondage. He expresses this weakness in four states: "the blind," that is, one who has lost the ability to discern and needs someone to lead him; the second state is "the lame," unable to walk except with the help of another; the third state is "the woman with child," who walks slowly because of her pregnancy; and the fourth state is "her that travaileth," that is, one who has come into birth pains and is unable to walk. God gathers His people in great numbers with all their weakness and delivers them and brings them back to their land.

From the abundance of affliction, the people weep to God and make supplication to Him to save them, so He brings them out of captivity by His power and leads them in clear, straight ways full of water, that is, life, which signifies the work of the Holy Spirit in the Church, to which unbelievers return and find their salvation.
And as God leads them they do not grow weary on the way or fall, for He keeps them.

All this shows the fatherhood of God toward His people, whom He considers His firstborn among the peoples of the earth. When He says "Ephraim," He means all His people, because Ephraim possessed a large region in the Promised Land. The people of God in the Old Testament were the firstborn, but in the New Testament, as all peoples believe, the believers in Christ are in all the countries of the world.

God addresses the peoples of the earth because He wants the salvation of all, and began with His people the children of Israel as an example so that all may come to Him. He says to all the peoples that if He has scattered His people by captivity in order to discipline them so that they repent, then He returns and gathers them and delivers them from the bondage of captivity.

Here He clearly declares His redemption of His people and their deliverance from the hand of Babylon, which is far stronger than His people. All this is a symbol of Christ's redemption of mankind on the Cross and its deliverance from the hand of one stronger than it, namely Satan.
Zion: a Hebrew name meaning fortress; it is one of the summits of the hills on which Jerusalem was built, and by Zion is meant all of Jerusalem.
Goodness: blessings and graces.

When the people of God reach Jerusalem, which is Zion built on a high hill, they sing with joy at their return to their land, and God pours out on them many blessings from the produce of the field such as wheat, and from trees such as the vines from which they take wine, and the olives from which they take oil. He also blesses their cattle, the sheep and the oxen, so they are many, and their land becomes like a garden from the abundance of water, fertility and many good things. God does not allow them captivity afterward and assimilation among the peoples of the earth, and this is what actually happened, for the children of Israel were not carried captive again until the coming of Christ, in whom all the previous types are fulfilled, who gives the believers in Him many spiritual blessings, and their souls become like a garden, that is, they become temples of the Holy Spirit.

He expresses the joy of His children after their return from captivity by the young women of His people who dance, and the young men and the old whose weeping during the captivity turns to joy. He also likens His people to a virgin who rejoices like a bride in her bridegroom, and God also shows His fatherhood by comforting His children and compensating them for all they endured in captivity. This signifies God's comforts to His children in heaven, compensating them for all their toils on earth.

The people turn to the worship of God and offer many sacrifices in His house, from which the priests take their share and are satisfied; thus God satisfies the people with all their leaders. This signifies the Holy Spirit's satisfying of the believers, the priests and the servants by His work in the Church, and He gives special blessings to the priests for their pastoral responsibility in leading the people.

Thank God for His gifts and praise Him in His Church and in every place, so that you feel His presence with you and are occupied with Him rather than with every sin and the various enticements of the world.
(3) The end of the pains of captivity (vv. 15-20)

15- Thus saith the LORD; A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not. 16- Thus saith the LORD; Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD; and they shall come again from the land of the enemy. 17- And there is hope in thine end, saith the LORD, that thy children shall come again to their own border. 18- I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself thus; Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised, as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke: turn thou me, and I shall be turned; for thou art the LORD my God. 19- Surely after that I was turned, I repented; and after that I was instructed, I smote upon my thigh: I was ashamed, yea, even confounded, because I did bear the reproach of my youth. 20- Is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child? for since I spake against him, I do earnestly remember him still: therefore my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him, saith the LORD.
Ramah: a city in the north of Judea near the kingdom of Israel, near which Rachel the wife of Jacob died and was buried.
Rachel: the wife of Jacob, who signifies the mother of all the Jews.

Jeremiah expresses the sorrow of the captives, whom the Babylonians probably gathered in the region of Ramah before transferring them to Babylon and the surrounding countries, and their mothers, symbolized by Rachel, weep for them and cannot be comforted because they will not return to them. Matthew the Evangelist borrowed this prophecy at the massacre of the children of Bethlehem, because their mothers would not see them again (Mt 2:17, 18).
Thy work shall be rewarded: your tears and your supplications to God for your children.
God declares through the tongue of Jeremiah hope to all these mothers: that despite the might of Babylon, God will bring His people back.
Thine end: after years.
Thy border: your boundaries.

God promises His people hope of the return, but not soon; rather at the end of the lives of those who are in Jerusalem, for the captives will return to their land within their borders after 70 years, and the aged, who have passed ninety or a hundred years of age, will receive them with joy.
Unaccustomed to the yoke: the animal trained in sound habits and conduct.

He borrows the name Ephraim, which represents the largest of the tribes, as a figure for all the Jews. The captives weep, and their kin also weep over them, and they humble themselves before God, feeling that their sins are the cause of this discipline, as Jeremiah informed them many times, so they ask God for feelings of repentance that they may obtain His mercies, because they walked in many sins and deviations like an untrained animal, and so deserved this discipline.

The people of God declare their regret and repentance: when the Babylonians attacked them and they saw the force of the treatment, they came to themselves and regretted their sins, and expressed their grief by striking the thigh, a custom that still occurs today in Egypt and the East, where people strike the cheeks and thigh in intense sorrow. They also remembered their former shameful sins, full of disgrace, and were ashamed of themselves.

Before the regret of the people of God, during their captivity, the fatherhood of God toward them appears, and He declares that His people are dear to Him, indeed the joy of His heart, so God's bowels yearn over them and He has mercy on them and brings them back from captivity.

God's tenderness toward you is wonderful: His heart does not change however much you sin, and He keeps waiting for you until you repent, then His bowels yearn over you, and He hastens to forgive you and embrace you, and restores you to your great place in His Church.

entries.section: (4) Blessings for those returning from captivity

paragraphs.text: Waymarks: pieces of stone.
High heaps: a pillar of stone.

God likens His people to a virgin because He loves her as a bride, and says to her: set up stone pieces and stone pillars on the road from the countries to which you were carried captive as far as Jerusalem, so that your children returning from captivity to their land may be guided by them. It is a clear divine promise to bring His people back from captivity.

entries.section: (4) Blessings for those returning from captivity

paragraphs.text: God requires His captive bride to turn back from her sins, and the captivity to be an opportunity for repentance, so that she turns from her apostasy from God; and God promises her to bring her back from captivity when she repents, and declares a strange fact as a clear prophecy, namely a woman shall compass a man, which has three meanings:

(1) The female is characterized by physical weakness, and the man, on the contrary, by strength. The female signifies the captive children of Israel, who are weak, and the man signifies strong Babylon. The situation will be reversed and the weak female will overcome the man, who returns by means of the Medes and Persians, who bring back the people of God with honor and strength, while Babylon is shattered, taken captive and enslaved.
(2) The female signifies the people of God who embrace the man, who is their God, when they repent and embrace their God, who lifts them up, saves them, and brings them back from captivity.
(3) The female signifies the Virgin Mary, who embraces in her womb the strongest man in the world, who is Christ her Son, to offer salvation to the whole world.

entries.section: (4) Blessings for those returning from captivity

paragraphs.text: Among God's blessings to His people after the return from captivity is that righteousness, that is, God, dwells in their midst, so they, as His children, are characterized by righteousness, that is, purity and good works. Likewise Jerusalem and Judea are called the holy mountain, that is, they are characterized by steadfastness in God and spiritual strength.

entries.section: (4) Blessings for those returning from captivity

paragraphs.text: He also promises them that they will sow their land, gather its fruit and be satisfied, and likewise shepherd their cattle so that they grow fat and increase in number; that is, their material prosperity increases. This signifies spiritual satisfaction, and Christ, His Apostles, His priests and His servants, who sow the word of God in people's hearts and care for the shepherding of their souls, enjoy fellowship with God.

entries.section: (4) Blessings for those returning from captivity

paragraphs.text: God declares the joy of His heart at the rest of His people, and likens Himself to a man who awoke and saw the good of his people, so he rejoiced and slept with pleasure, delighting in his sleep. This is a prophecy about Christ, who died, that is, slept, on the Cross delighting in His sleep because He had completed our redemption.

God rejoices in your good, your walk with Him and all your virtues. So take care to walk uprightly, and try to acquire one virtue that you need, to rejoice the heart of God, so that you rejoice with Him.

entries.section: (4) Blessings for those returning from captivity

paragraphs.text: God also promises that He Himself will sow man, that is, bless His children who return from captivity, multiply them and give them many blessings. Likewise He sows beast, that is, blesses and multiplies their cattle.

entries.section: (4) Blessings for those returning from captivity

paragraphs.text: Pluck up: that is, destroy.

God likens Himself to a man who watches, that is, is occupied, concerned and persevering in disciplining His people with all the severe ways of discipline. His aim in this, of course, is their repentance, because of their violent insistence on sin; they needed this severe discipline, and they actually responded to the discipline of the captivity, and repented. Therefore God promises them that He will build not only their cities but their spiritual life with Him.

entries.section: (4) Blessings for those returning from captivity

paragraphs.text: There was a common proverb that the fathers eat sour grapes, which are small, sharp-tasting grapes, and then the children's teeth are set on edge by this taste and knock against one another; that is, some of them thought that the discipline that came upon them in captivity was because of the sins of their fathers. God clearly declares that every person is responsible for his own sin and perishes because of it: if the fathers are wicked and the children righteous, the children do not perish, but if they imitate their fathers and become evil, they perish like their fathers. In sum, he means that the discipline that came upon them in captivity is because of their own evils, and the solution is repentance, and then God has mercy on them.

At the end of this chapter, God declares that He will make a covenant with His people returning from captivity. This covenant means a commitment from God, as one party, to care for His people, protect them and bless them, and the second party is His people, who are committed to obeying His commandments.

This covenant is new, and is not the first covenant which He made with His people when He delivered them from the bondage of Egypt and brought them through the Red Sea; this is a new covenant after He rescued them from the harshness of the Babylonian bondage. But even more, this covenant signifies the covenant which Christ makes with us by His blood on the Cross by His redemption of us.
The characteristics of this new covenant are:

1- The people keep the Law of God and His commandments in their hearts; that is, they do not carry them out only literally but commit themselves to their spirit. This is what those returning from captivity did in part, and it was fulfilled even more in those who believe in Christ.
2- They worship God and abandon the worship of idols; and in the New Covenant they are not occupied by material things and lusts, but by the love of Christ the Redeemer.
In the New Covenant God adds two other things:

1- God becomes known and clear to all His children, so they discern that He is the only God and do not need anyone to teach them to abandon the idols. And in the Church the Holy Spirit descends on all the believers and guides them to the truth and to life with Him within His Church.

2- God forgives all the repentant and lifts from them the debt of their sins, which He bore on the Cross; and in the case of those returning from captivity, He does not discipline them for their sins but blesses them with many material good things.

God wants to renew His covenants with you, and gives you more abundant blessings when you take care to keep His commandments and prefer Him to anything of your material affairs. Then He reveals to you, and you experience, an inexpressible delight which is a pledge of the glories of the Kingdom that have not entered into the heart of man.
Who divideth: the One who firmly restrains.
Roar: the waves surge with a strong sound.

God declares that He is steadfast in His promises with the whole creation. He appointed the sun to light the day, and the moon and the stars come after it to light the night, and He set boundaries for the sea so that it does not cover the dry land: it moves by the property of the tide, but despite the power of its waves its waters return inward by the property of the ebb. The One who set all these laws and governs them is God, who is able to do all things, and so He shows us His power by describing Himself as the Lord of hosts.

Because the order of nature is made firm by the power of God, He is also able to establish His people as a nation before Him throughout life; that is, this people will never become extinct. This actually happened, for the children of Israel remained as a nation throughout the Old Testament although exposed to the rule of the Medes and Persians, then the Greek and Roman states. But what is more important than this is that through Christ the Christians became the new Israel, the nation that lives not only throughout earthly time but extends into eternity.

God shows His pleasure and love for His people throughout life by proofs: it is impossible for man to measure the dimensions of heaven, however much he advances in science; he merely knows a little about it, but it is impossible for him to know everything about it and measure it. Likewise no one can know the foundations of the earth, that is, the depths of the globe; however much research advances, only some information about them is known. So, if it is impossible for anyone to measure heaven or to know the foundations of the earth, then God will not cast off His people but will keep them as a nation before Him until He takes them with Him in the Kingdom.
The tower of Hananeel: it is in the northeast of Jerusalem.
The corner gate: it is in the northwest of Jerusalem.
God affirms His establishing and keeping of His children who return from captivity by building for them their city Jerusalem, in which is His temple, from its east to its west.
The measuring line: the line used to set the stones and bricks in building; what is meant is the extent of the building.
The hill Gareb: a hill lying in the west of Jerusalem.
Goath: a region in the southwest of Jerusalem.

The valley of the dead bodies and of the ashes: it is the valley of Hinnom, or the one called the son of Hinnom, into which the remains of animals and all the waste of the city of Jerusalem were thrown to be burned there; it lies in the southwest of Jerusalem. From it the word Gehenna was taken.
The brook Kidron: a valley that passes around Jerusalem from its west, then its south, then turns toward its east.
The horse gate: one of the gates of Jerusalem, lying on the eastern side.

To complete God's affirmation of the rebuilding of Jerusalem, He mentions in detail many places in it through which the builders pass to rebuild it. After they begin from the northeast and extend toward the northwest (v. 38), they complete the western side and head toward the southwest, passing through the whole southern part until they reach the eastern region of Jerusalem; that is, all of Jerusalem is built.
Jeremiah buys a field
The time of the prophecy is given as the tenth year of King Zedekiah of Judah, which corresponds to the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, that is, the year 588 BC.

At the time of this prophecy, which God sent to Jeremiah, Jerusalem was besieged by the armies of Babylon. They then withdrew for a short time as the armies of Egypt advanced toward Jerusalem, after which Babylon returned and besieged Jerusalem with the final siege, then destroyed it and completed the last captivity of the Jews.

At this time Jeremiah was imprisoned in a special prison belonging to the palace of the king of Judah, and he had some freedom of movement, as is shown by his weighing out the silver and buying the land in his town of Anathoth. Although this prison was hard for Jeremiah as an affliction, it was an opportunity to keep Jeremiah safe from the abuse of his enemies and a protection for him.
The reason for Jeremiah's imprisonment was the anger of Zedekiah king of Judah against him, because he had prophesied several things. The first was that the king of Babylon would take Jerusalem.
Jeremiah continues his prophecy and announces a second matter, that the king of Babylon would seize Zedekiah king of Judah.
And a third prophecy, that Zedekiah would meet the king of Babylon.

Jeremiah adds to his prophecy a fourth matter, that the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, would carry King Zedekiah away to Babylon. He says “carry” because they would put out his eyes and lead him to Babylon, which he would not see, as the prophet Ezekiel said (Ezek 12:13), but he would remain there for the rest of his life.
And he prophesies a fifth matter, that Zedekiah would remain in Babylon until the end of his life, where God would visit him, that is, he would die and be removed from our land.

A sixth and last prophecy that Jeremiah spoke is that Judah's attempt to resist Babylon would fail, and Babylon would kill many of the Jews, take captive those it chose, and leave the weak in the land.

In the afflictions that God allows for you, His love and care for you are hidden. Just as Jeremiah was imprisoned in the palace of the king of Judah to protect him from his enemies, so God also protects you from many troubles by means of the afflictions that you pass through. So thank God for everything, even afflictions.

God commanded Jeremiah to buy a field in his town of Anathoth, where he and his family were born and lived, a town of the priests near Jerusalem. It appears that Jeremiah's cousin, who owned this field, had fallen into financial difficulty and so had mortgaged it. To preserve the inheritance of the land, one of his relatives could buy the field so that it would remain the property of the family, as the Law stipulated in (Lev 25:25), because the Promised Land was a type of the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the eternal inheritance, and so it must be preserved.

It appears that Jeremiah's cousin did not find anyone to buy this field from the person with whom it had been mortgaged and to pay the price of redeeming it and returning it to the family. Perhaps this was because of the captivity that was coming upon them, and therefore there was no benefit in such a purchase, since Babylon would take possession of all the lands. So he came to Jeremiah in the prison and offered him the field to buy, in order to restore the inheritance to the family.
Shallum was Jeremiah's uncle and Hanamel was his cousin.
God had informed Jeremiah of Hanamel's coming to him before he arrived, and commanded him to buy the land.

Here God uses a visual aid to declare before the Jews that the captivity would come but that they would return from it. So He had His prophet Jeremiah buy the field as a confirmation that their return from the captivity was certain. It is a clear hope and a consolation that God offers to His children.

If God allows afflictions for you, He shows you at the same time His power and His care for you. So do not be grieved because of the affliction, but seek God, and He will show you His presence with you, and your heart will be comforted.

God's word was fulfilled when Hanamel, Jeremiah's cousin, arrived at the prison where Jeremiah was held, and offered him to redeem his mortgaged field and to buy it for himself so that it would return to the ownership of the family. So Jeremiah was assured of what God had told him beforehand.
For God prepares and guides His children who cling to Him, so that they are not troubled by the events coming upon them, and when they are reassured they become an example to those around them.
From another side, God guides His children in the details of their lives as long as they hold fast to Him.
A shekel of silver: equal to about fifteen grams.
Jeremiah obeyed God's word and bought his cousin's field, and paid him its price, which was seventeen shekels of silver.

Jeremiah wrote a deed for the purchase of the field in order to establish his ownership of it, and this was done before witnesses, both from the relatives who came with Hanamel and from those imprisoned with him.
He sealed this deed, that is, the contract, and weighed the silver before the witnesses as proof of his ownership.

The custom in buying in ancient times was to write two copies of the contract, either both exactly identical or one a summary of the other. One was closed and sealed, while the other remained open, to confirm ownership.

After the witnesses had signed the deed of purchase and Hanamel had received the price, Jeremiah gave the deed to his disciple “Baruch,” who was the scribe of his prophecies and helped him in writing any matters that concerned him. All this was as proof before many witnesses, and a declaration to the people that Jeremiah had bought a field even though Babylon was besieging Jerusalem and the captivity was drawing near them, in order to declare, as we mentioned, that they would return from the captivity and enjoy their lands.
Baruch, the disciple of Jeremiah, was also a prophet, and he has a prophecy in his name among the canonical books, which the Protestants removed.

Jeremiah commanded him to put the two copies of the deed in an earthen vessel. This was the custom for preserving important documents: they were placed in an earthen vessel, which was closed over them and the seal was fixed with pitch. This was a declaration from Jeremiah that the captivity would last for many years, but that after it the Jews would return from the captivity.
God confirms the return from the captivity and the Jews' buying of houses and fields.

All this is a type of Christ, who bought us with His blood and wrote the deed on the Cross. The accomplishment of complete salvation will come after the years of our earthly life, when we are lifted up to the heavenly Jerusalem and reign with Him forever. The two copies of the contract of purchase signify, the open one, the blessings that we receive now on earth, and the sealed one, the blessings that we shall receive in heaven, which cannot be expressed. Christ took our nature by His Incarnation to be near to us and to complete our redemption, so that He frees us from the hand of Satan, to whom we sold ourselves because of our spiritual poverty. The price of redemption was paid openly before many witnesses, namely all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, outside which Christ was crucified.
(3) The prayer of Jeremiah (vv. 16-25)

16- Now when I had delivered the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed unto the LORD, saying, 17- Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee: 18- Thou shewest lovingkindness unto thousands, and recompensest the iniquity of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them: the Great, the Mighty God, the LORD of hosts, is his name, 19- Great in counsel, and mighty in work: for thine eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of men: to give every one according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings: 20- Which hast set signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, even unto this day, and in Israel, and among other men; and hast made thee a name, as at this day;

21- And hast brought forth thy people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs, and with wonders, and with a strong hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with great terror; 22- And hast given them this land, which thou didst swear to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey;

23- And they came in, and possessed it; but they obeyed not thy voice, neither walked in thy law; they have done nothing of all that thou commandedst them to do: therefore thou hast caused all this evil to come upon them: 24- Behold the mounts, they are come unto the city to take it; and the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans, that fight against it, because of the sword, and of the famine, and of the pestilence: and what thou hast spoken is come to pass; and, behold, thou seest it. 25- And thou hast said unto me, O Lord GOD, Buy thee the field for money, and take witnesses; for the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.

After the procedures for buying the field were finished, Jeremiah stood to pray. This was his first concern; indeed, the goal of all the matters of his life was his attachment to God. In his prayer he reviews God's kindnesses and His provisions for His people and His care for them even in afflictions.
At the beginning of his prayer he glorifies God, the Creator of all things, and also describes Him as the One who is able to do all things.

He describes God by the love that appears in His gifts to His people, who number in the thousands, for He cares for all His children. Then he presents a fourth attribute of God, which is His justice, which appears in His recompense, not only to the wicked fathers but also to their children if they walk in the sins of their fathers.

He describes a fifth attribute of God, that He is strong and mighty, and calls Him “the LORD of hosts” to show His power. Let us notice that Jeremiah's prayer is praise of God and a review of His many attributes, for praise is love of God and attachment to Him.
He continues his praise of God and describes Him with a sixth attribute, His greatness in guiding His children. His counsel is the true counsel, because He knows everything and loves His children.

Then he describes Him with a seventh attribute, His knowledge of everything, which he expresses by saying that His eyes are open upon all that happens on the earth. This reassures His children and those who fear Him, since He protects them and blesses them, and at the same time it troubles the wicked, because He will punish them for their sins.

He reminds God of His power by which He saved His people when they were enslaved in Egypt, when He struck the Egyptians with the ten plagues, brought them through the Red Sea, and destroyed the army of the Egyptians. So he praises His divine power and His care for His people, of which the whole world has spoken to this day, because what happened will never be erased from the minds of men because of its greatness.

He thanks God, who fulfilled His promises to Abraham and the fathers. This is an eighth attribute of God, the truthfulness of His promises, since He gave His people to possess the land of Canaan, which was full of good things.

Jeremiah makes a confession before God, on behalf of his people, that after they possessed the land of Canaan they left God's commandments and walked in their evil lusts, so they deserved that God should punish them with the captivity, that is, with this evil.

The mounts: the soldiers who build the siege mounds. The word is the plural of a mound, which is a wall of brick or stones, or any obstacles that the enemies build around besieged cities to hinder the fighting of the besieged if they try to escape.
The city: Jerusalem.
The Chaldeans: the Babylonians.

After that he declares the truthfulness of God in His word that He sent to Jeremiah to proclaim as prophecies before the people. For God had said that Jerusalem would be besieged by the Babylonians and would fall into their hands, not only because of the Babylonians' cruelty in killing the Jews, but also because of the Jews' weakness, as diseases attacked them and they found no food to eat during the siege. All this was a discipline from God for His people who had rebelled against Him.
Thus a ninth attribute of God appears, which Jeremiah praises, namely the truthfulness of His word and His prophecies.

He praises God, who comforts His people, which is a tenth attribute in God, for He gave them hope of returning from the captivity and presented to them a real story, namely Jeremiah's buying of a field even though Babylon would shortly take possession of the whole kingdom of Judah, yet they would return and enjoy their lands. Jeremiah did not benefit from this land because he died before the return from the captivity, but he obeyed so as to declare by this act the love of God, who would bring His people back from the captivity.

How beautiful it is for you to contemplate the attributes of God, and to praise Him and thank Him for His gifts and care. May you learn even a small part of the Church's Midnight Praise (Tasbeha), or listen to it on recordings, to take part in praising His holy name, and your heart will be filled with joy.
(4) The reasons for the discipline (vv. 26-35)

26- Then came the word of the LORD unto Jeremiah, saying, 27- Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me? 28- Therefore thus saith the LORD; Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the Chaldeans, and into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and he shall take it: 29- And the Chaldeans, that fight against this city, shall come and set fire on this city, and burn it with the houses, upon whose roofs they have offered incense unto Baal, and poured out drink offerings unto other gods, to provoke me to anger. 30- For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have only done evil before me from their youth: for the children of Israel have only provoked me to anger with the work of their hands, saith the LORD. 31- For this city hath been to me as a provocation of mine anger and of my fury from the day that they built it even unto this day; that I should remove it from before my face, 32- Because of all the evil of the children of Israel and of the children of Judah, which they have done to provoke me to anger, they, their kings, their princes, their priests, and their prophets, and the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
33- And they have turned unto me the back, and not the face: though I taught them, rising up early and teaching them, yet they have not hearkened to receive instruction.

34- But they set their abominations in the house, which is called by my name, to defile it. 35- And they built the high places of Baal, which are in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to cause their sons and their daughters to pass through the fire unto Molech; which I commanded them not, neither came it into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.

After God listened to Jeremiah's prayer, He declared to him that He is the Creator of all creatures and able to do all things, and that He disciplines His people so that they repent, then brings them back from the captivity and comforts their hearts.
God carries out His discipline by allowing Babylon to take Jerusalem.
God continues His words by saying that Babylon would burn Jerusalem and its houses, on whose roofs the Jews had worshiped idols.
Here He begins to show the reasons for His discipline of His people. The first is their worship of idols on the roofs of their houses, that is, their worship of the heavenly bodies.

The second reason for God's discipline of His people is their continuing in evil for a long time. They began it from their youth and not only now, for they worshiped idols from the time they were in Egypt, even before they entered Egypt, and God bore with them throughout this long period so that they would repent.

He adds a third reason for the discipline of Jerusalem, that it worshiped idols and walked in evil from the time when the Jebusites, the original pagan inhabitants of the land, lived in it. Then after the Jews possessed it, they completed the evil in it, so Jerusalem deserved to be destroyed at the hand of Babylon.

A fourth reason for the discipline of God's people is that everyone shared in the evil, the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel, the leaders such as the kings and the ordinary people. This evil is directed against God, a provocation to Him, and disobedience and defiance.

The fifth reason for the discipline is the insistence on not obeying God and hearkening to His commandments, and even treating Him with neglect and coldness, which is expressed by giving God the back and not the face.
