Take care lest you fall into neglect of God and give Him the back and not the face, when you neglect your prayer, or your reading of the Holy Bible, or coming to the house of God.
The sixth reason for the discipline is the audacity of placing idol images inside God's temple in Jerusalem, for this is the utmost defiance of God.

The seventh reason for the discipline is their loss of natural human affection, for in their immersion in the worship of the pagan gods they offered their sons to them as burnt offerings, like the god Molech, and sacrificed their children out of love for idol worship, in addition to building temples for the worship of the god Molech on the hills and high places.
(5) The return from the captivity (vv. 36-44)

36- And now therefore thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel, concerning this city, whereof ye say, It shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence; 37- Behold, I will gather them out of all countries, whither I have driven them in mine anger, and in my fury, and in great wrath; and I will bring them again unto this place, and I will cause them to dwell safely: 38- And they shall be my people, and I will be their God: 39- And I will give them one heart, and one way, that they may fear me for ever, for the good of them, and of their children after them: 40- And I will make an everlasting covenant with them, that I will not turn away from them, to do them good; but I will put my fear in their hearts, that they shall not depart from me. 41- Yea, I will rejoice over them to do them good, and I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul. 42- For thus saith the LORD; Like as I have brought all this great evil upon this people, so will I bring upon them all the good that I have promised them. 43- And fields shall be bought in this land, whereof ye say, It is desolate without man or beast; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans. 44- Men shall buy fields for money, and subscribe evidences, and seal them, and take witnesses in the land of Benjamin, and in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, and in the cities of the mountains, and in the cities of the valley, and in the cities of the south: for I will cause their captivity to return, saith the LORD.
This city: Jerusalem.

Although God allows His people to be disciplined by the captivity, with all the killing, hunger and disease that it brings, when He finds His people accepting the discipline He returns and has mercy on them and brings them back from the captivity. For God is not cruel but a tender Father who disciplines His children so that they repent and return to His embrace.

God promises to gather His people who were scattered in the captivity, and then to bring them back to their land, and more than that, that they will live in security in their land, because when they repent they obtain all mercies.

God's mercies are waiting for you to repent of your sins, and they will pour out upon you countless blessings. So do not delay repentance, and do not despair because of the multitude of your sins, and do not be led away after passing pleasures.
God makes a fourth promise, that He will give His people the enjoyment of special care because they believe in Him, and He will reign over their hearts.

The fifth promise is the unity that He gives to His people, so that the division of the two kingdoms, Israel and Judah, ends. This is a type of unity in Christ, where the believers in the whole world are united in Christ. The sixth promise is that God gives them His fear in their hearts, so that they reject sin and enjoy His abundant goodness.

The seventh promise is God's care for His children forever, so that He establishes His fear in their hearts, and good things continue for them as long as they believe in Him and hold fast to His commandments. This is fulfilled in Christ, who gives us the eternal Kingdom.

The eighth promise that God gives His people after their return from the captivity is that He will establish them in faithfulness and upright conduct toward Him and toward one another, and God will work in them with all power and rejoice in their response to Him. This is the true divine kindness, not only material good things but faithfulness in carrying out His commandments.
Thus, in proportion to the discipline and afflictions they endured in the captivity, God compensates them after the return from the captivity with many good things.
The ninth promise is the fertility of the land that had been desolate, so that the Jews eagerly buy it to enjoy its good things.

He confirms their concern for the process of buying fields with all its procedures, including writing documents for this purchase and sealing them with seals. That is, the land is of great value, so they make sure of their ownership of it after paying high prices for it in silver and gold. This would be not only in Jerusalem but in all the regions around it in the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. This signifies the enlightenment of the believers in the New Testament and their concern to buy the new land, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven, and to exert every effort to acquire it through their worship in the Church and their spiritual striving.
God's blessings for those who obey Him

The king seized Jeremiah and cast him into prison because he had prophesied the destruction of Jerusalem. But the tender God spoke to him in the prison to make him feel His presence with him, so that he would be reassured and comforted.

God reveals Himself to you in afflictions to reassure you, guide you and gladden your heart. So do not be disturbed by the affliction, for it may be the best time in which you experience God's love and know Him closely.

The Lord declares that He is the maker of the earth and its former, in order to reassure the imprisoned Jeremiah. For although Jeremiah was bound in a dark chamber, God declares to him that He is the maker of the whole earth upon which all men live, so he need not be troubled by the chains, because God, the Ruler of all, upholds him and speaks with him. This is the second consolation in the prison, after the first mentioned in (v. 1). The third consolation is that God declares His name to him, which is “Jehovah,” that is, God is, and exists. He thereby assures him of His presence with him so that he does not feel loneliness and isolation inside the prison. For though he has been cut off from men, he enjoys the fellowship of God.
Hidden things: the plural of a hard thing, that is, something difficult to perceive and understand.

The fourth encouragement is God's invitation to Jeremiah to speak with Him in prayer, so that he is comforted and feels the presence of God. Even greater than this, God promises him to reveal to him wonderful and lofty things of His wisdom that a man, however intelligent, cannot know.
Thus we sense the distinction of the spiritual man, in the hardest circumstances, because God blesses him and magnifies him.

entries.section: (2) The blessings of those who return from the captivity

paragraphs.text: The mounts: the plural of a mound, which is a wall built around a besieged city to prevent those in it from escaping. The enemies build them so that everyone in the city perishes, and the enemies take cover behind these mounds. The engines: long tubes from which they hurl stones or flaming fire onto the besieged cities to burn them.

God speaks to Jeremiah, while he is in prison, about the destruction of Jerusalem, and specifies the houses and palaces of the great men and kings in it, which will all be destroyed when the Babylonians besiege it, build mounds around it, and hold in their hands the engines with which to demolish Jerusalem and burn it.
And when He says “thrown down by the mounts,” He means thrown down because of the mounds.

entries.section: (2) The blessings of those who return from the captivity

paragraphs.text: The carcases of men: the stinking corpses of men whom the Babylonians killed.

God calls to His people who come to fight the Babylonians who are attacking them, and tells them that the Babylonians will kill many of the Jews and throw their corpses in the streets until they become putrid and their smell foul.

God allowed the Babylonians to strike them, for they are the rod of God with which He strikes His people in His anger, and hides His tender face from them because of the multitude of their sins and their disobedience to God. He disciplines them severely so that they repent, and when they repent He forgives them and blesses them.

entries.section: (2) The blessings of those who return from the captivity

paragraphs.text: Health: a strip of linen cloth with which a wound is bound, similar to medical gauze today. Cure: various ointments and medicines for treating wounds and diseases.

God shows His mercies to His people whom He brings back from the captivity. He heals their wounds by putting medicines on the injured place, binding it and covering it with the bandage. By this comparison He means that He treats their sins and moves them to repentance, and purifies their senses and thoughts so that they regain their peace. God puts in their hearts the love of faithfulness, that is, truth, so that they hold fast to God's commandments and are mindful of their God in all their conduct, and He increases for them feelings of reassurance and inclination to the truth.

God is ready to heal all the problems you have caused by your falling into sin, if you repent and return to Him. So do not be disturbed by the bad state you have reached, but rise quickly and offer repentance and contrition before God to begin a new life full of peace, joy and pure conduct.

entries.section: (2) The blessings of those who return from the captivity

paragraphs.text: God promises His repentant people that He will bring them back from the captivity, build their cities and strengthen them spiritually and psychologically, because the discipline was because of sin, and if they repent He will restore to them all their glory.

entries.section: (2) The blessings of those who return from the captivity

paragraphs.text: After God had treated the problems of sin that had resulted in the souls of His children, the blessings began, as He filled them with peace and security. After that He restored to them their building and their glory, and in this verse He added a fourth blessing, the forgiveness of their sins and their cleansing from all evil, that is, the removal of the inclination to sin from within them, and not only the blotting out of their sins and forgetting them, so that they enjoy a new heart inclined to a pure life with God.

entries.section: (2) The blessings of those who return from the captivity

paragraphs.text: The fifth blessing for those returning from the captivity is that they become God's witness among the Gentiles because of God's care for them and His making them happy with His gifts, so they become a light to the world, calling to faith in God. For the Gentiles sense God's power in His people, so they fear Him and glorify Him together with His people, who praise Him and rejoice in Him.

entries.section: (2) The blessings of those who return from the captivity

paragraphs.text: The sixth blessing is the turning of the sorrow over Jerusalem and its surroundings, destroyed by the hand of the Babylonians, into joy over its rebuilding and glory, and the multitude of its inhabitants and their possessions of cattle. They express this joy in four ways:
1- They sing songs of victory with joy.
2- They hold marriages and the bridegroom and the bride rejoice. This is a type of the joy of the people, as a virgin, in God, the Bridegroom of their souls.
3- They praise the merciful God, who restored glory to His repentant children.
4- They offer peace offerings in thanksgiving to God on the bronze altar in the temple, which are a type of the sacrifice of Christ, His Body and Blood, on the altar of the New Testament.

entries.section: (2) The blessings of those who return from the captivity

paragraphs.text: The seventh blessing is the multitude of their possessions of sheep and cattle. Instead of the total destruction of the cities and pastures, the folds, that is, the dwellings of the shepherds, will increase, and their flocks will multiply, so that the shepherd counts them one by one. This will be in all the cities of the Jews returning from the captivity, of which He mentions examples, namely the cities of the mountains, and likewise the cities of the valley and the cities of the south, and also in the cities of Benjamin, and not only the tribe of Judah. This is a type of Christ the Good Shepherd, whose believers multiply, and He counts them and cares for them one by one.
Days: what is meant is the days of the return from the captivity or the birth of Christ.
The good thing: God's promises to the fathers.

These are prophecies about the return from the captivity, and this is the near meaning of the prophecy, for God in His goodness grants His people that a Branch of righteousness should grow up to them, that is, the life of righteousness begins in them, so that after their return from the captivity they live in purity of heart, in unity and not as two separated kingdoms.

As for the far meaning of the prophecy, it speaks of the awaited Messiah, and the days are the fullness of time when Christ is born. He likens Him to a branch that grows from the tree, which is the Jewish nation, but He is a Branch of righteousness, that is, without sin, and righteous and holy, to lead His people who believe in Him in the life of righteousness. He rules with justice and uprightness, for He rejects evil and rewards His children in the Kingdom of Heaven, while the wicked are cast into eternal torment. With the coming of the awaited Messiah, God's promises that He spoke to the fathers are fulfilled.

Christ gives to those who believe in Him salvation from sin and its punishment, that is, eternal torment, and gives to Jerusalem, that is, His Church, peace and righteousness. His children trust that their righteousness is from Him and rejoice to be named Christians, after Christ, the cause and source of their righteousness; that is, they call us “The LORD our righteousness.”

Thus God's promises are fulfilled that the reign of the offspring of David will continue through Christ, who reigns over the hearts of those who believe in Him forever. What is meant by Israel is not only the people of the Jews of old but the new Israel, that is, those who believe in the awaited Messiah, who are the Christians.

God also promises the continuation of the priesthood among His people, not only through their return from the captivity and the renewal of the temple and the offering of the burnt offerings, sacrifices and oblations that they offer and burn on the bronze altar, but also the priesthood and the ministry of the Levites continue in the New Testament in the form of priests and deacons, not after the order of Aaron, but the priests of the Church who offer the sacrifice of Christ, His Body and Blood. The work of the priesthood continues in a spiritual form in the Kingdom of Heaven in the form of the twenty-four elders, and the unceasing praise of the believers forever.

God's promises are true and He cannot break them. This should reassure you greatly however much the afflictions around you increase. So trust that He is with you, upholding you, and even turning all your afflictions into blessings, spiritual growth, and peace and joy that cannot be expressed.

The wicked Jews raised doubts about God's promises of His care for His people when they saw the Babylonian attack and Jeremiah's prophecies about the destruction of Jerusalem, and they said that God had broken His covenant with His people. So God sent His word by the mouth of Jeremiah, addressing these wicked people and telling them: if you doubt the succession of night and day, then you doubt My promise to My people that the offspring of David will be king over them.

And He says “you have broken,” that is, by the words of your doubts you speak against God. Just as the order of night and day is fixed, so My covenant is fixed with My people and with the offspring of David, and also with the priesthood that I placed among them.

God confirms His promises to His people, not only by the firmness of the kingdom for the offspring of David and likewise the priesthood, but also by the multitude of the people like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea, and He will also multiply the Levites, the servants of God.

God continues His words with Jeremiah about the murmuring people who spread doubts that God had broken His covenant with them and that He would destroy the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah and scatter them among the Gentiles, so that they would no longer be a nation and a people before Him. This will of course not happen, because God will bring them back from the captivity with great power and restore to them their glories after they repent through the disciplines of the captivity.

God confirms a second time that if the order of nature, which is the succession of night and day, were to change, then God would break His covenant with His people and destroy them. This will of course not happen. Just as God preserves the order of night and day until the end of the world, so He also makes the offspring of David kings over His people Israel. God will bring His people back from the captivity, and in the fullness of time Christ will come and reign over the hearts of those who believe in Him, His new people.
Be faithful in your promises to God, and if you have been careless in them, return again and renew your vows to live with Him and serve Him, whatever your weakness, relying on His power and help.
The breaking of the covenant by freeing the slaves

Jeremiah specifies the time of the prophecy, which is the final siege of Jerusalem, when Nebuchadnezzar besieged the city with his army, and with him were soldiers from the lands he had conquered. He had triumphed in all his battles, and Jerusalem remained, which he was now besieging to take it, together with all the cities belonging to it in the kingdom of Judah. This was accomplished in the year 587 BC.

God commanded Jeremiah to go and meet Zedekiah king of Judah and to repeat to him God's decision that Nebuchadnezzar would take Jerusalem and burn it. This was a last attempt by God that Zedekiah and all his people might repent, so that God would have mercy on them and deliver them. But despite the king's respect for Jeremiah, he was not obedient to God's word and did not repent of his sins.

This prophecy adds a second matter, after the decision to burn Jerusalem, which is the seizing of King Zedekiah by the soldiers of Nebuchadnezzar. The third matter is Zedekiah's standing before Nebuchadnezzar and seeing him, and the fourth matter is the carrying of Zedekiah to Babylon, which he would not see with his eyes because they put out his eyes when they seized him.

As a result of Zedekiah's listening to Jeremiah's words and honoring him, God gives him grace, so that he does not die by the sword but remains in Babylon until he dies a natural death. This is the fifth matter.

God does not forget any virtue that you do. If He rewards the wicked with material blessings in this world, then all the more will He reward you for every good work you do with blessings that are not only earthly but rather heavenly.

The burnings of your fathers: it was the custom in ancient times, when one of the kings of the Jews died, that they made a burning for him (2 Chr 16:14) and (2 Chr 21:19). They will lament: they say words of mourning.
Ah lord: they glorify you and magnify you.
The sixth prophecy is the honoring of Zedekiah at his death as follows:
1- A burning is made for him, as is the custom for great kings.
2- They lament him.
3- They magnify him at his death.
Jeremiah told Zedekiah these six prophecies in Jerusalem.
Lachish and Azekah: two fortified Jewish cities lying south of Jerusalem.

While Nebuchadnezzar was besieging Jerusalem in its final siege, he was also fighting the two cities of Lachish and Azekah, because they alone remained of the cities of Judah, since Nebuchadnezzar had taken the whole kingdom of Judah, and it remained for him to take Jerusalem, Lachish and Azekah.

The Jews were negligent in carrying out the Law of freeing Hebrew slaves in the seventh year (Deut 15:12). When Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem and death drew near them, “King Zedekiah” commanded the Jews to free their brothers who were slaves with them, in the hope that God might remove His anger from them and protect them from Nebuchadnezzar.

Zedekiah gathered the leaders of the people, and they swore before God to carry out the Law by freeing their brothers who were slaves, and they carried out the king's command and released the slaves. This shows their obedience to the commandment in the hour of affliction and their taking refuge in God.

During Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem, Hophra, Pharaoh of Egypt, advanced with his armies toward the armies of Babylon that were besieging Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar was afraid and withdrew from Jerusalem to complete his war preparations, that is, he left Jerusalem for a time to return to it. The Jews thought that the crisis had ended, and they saw their fields, in which the soldiers of Babylon had been encamped, empty, so they felt their need of their slaves to cultivate them. During the siege the slaves did not work and cost their masters their food, so they did without them and carried out the commandment because it saved them the expense of feeding the slaves. But after the fields were vacated, it was in their interest to bring back their slaves, so they went back on their oath and their covenants with God and abandoned the commandment, and brought back their Hebrew slaves by force.

Submit to God's commandments, even if they are against your material interests, for the commandment is for your good even if you are not convinced of it. And if you have offered repentance, do not go back on it, and if you fall again, repent and return quickly to God.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of those who violate the covenant

paragraphs.text: God reminds them of His freeing them from the bondage of Egypt, and calls it the house of bondmen, and He also reminds them of the covenant that He made with their fathers in the wilderness of Sinai after their exodus from Egypt, when He appeared on the mountain and gave them the commandments and the Law.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of those who violate the covenant

paragraphs.text: The covenant between God and His people was in the words of the Law, which commands that if a Hebrew, because of his poverty, is compelled to sell himself, or his family sells him, as a slave to one of his Hebrew brothers, he shall work for his master six years, and his master must release him in the seventh year. But sadly the fathers did not commit to carrying out this covenant and enslaved their brothers by force for more than six years. This law is mentioned in (Ex 21:2; Deut 15:12).

entries.section: (3) The punishment of those who violate the covenant

paragraphs.text: God commends His people in the kingdom of Judah in the days of Jeremiah because they renewed the covenant with God in His house, that is, the temple in Jerusalem, declaring their return to carrying out the Law and freeing the Hebrew slaves in the seventh year.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of those who violate the covenant

paragraphs.text: God rebukes them because they turned back from their covenant with Him and took back the Hebrew slaves whom they had released because they had completed more than six years, and so they enslaved them again by force and thereby violated the Law of God.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of those who violate the covenant

paragraphs.text: God declares His punishment of His people who refused to obey His Law and did not free their Hebrew brothers who worked as slaves for them. So God looses the sword to kill them, and likewise the pestilence to strike them down sick, and the famine to destroy them, and they become an example of a troubled and distressed nation among the nations of the earth because they violated the commandments of their God, so He disciplines them severely. God intends by this that they fear Him and repent of their sins.

When you read God's commandments in the Holy Bible that command you to keep away from evil and make you afraid of the divine punishment, return to Him quickly with repentance and shake off every evil pleasure, so that you save your soul and gain your eternity.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of those who violate the covenant

paragraphs.text: The way of making a covenant that was prevalent at that time was to slaughter animals such as a calf, cut it into two halves, and have those making the covenant pass between the two pieces of the sacrifice. This is what the leaders of the Jews did: they passed between a calf slaughtered into two halves, declaring their covenant with God to free the Hebrew slaves, but they turned back and violated this covenant. Abraham made a covenant with God in the same way (Gen 15:9-10, 17). The leaders and all the people passed between the two pieces of the calf, and then when they violated their covenant, God punished them by delivering them into the hand of Babylon, which would kill them by the sword, pestilence and famine.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of those who violate the covenant

paragraphs.text: The horror of the divine punishment of God's people who violated the covenant appears in Babylon's fierce attack upon them, the killing of many and the throwing of their corpses in the streets, where they are eaten by birds of prey and beasts of the earth, since there is no one to bury these corpses because of their great number and because the rest flee in fear.

entries.section: (3) The punishment of those who violate the covenant

paragraphs.text: After Babylon withdrew from its siege of Jerusalem, and God's people thought they had been rid of them and violated their covenant with God and took back their Hebrew brothers as slaves with them, God allows Babylon to return and besiege Jerusalem and destroy it and burn it and seize King Zedekiah and the leaders of the kingdom of Judah, and even kill many of them. It destroys all the cities of the kingdom of Judah, because God commanded their punishment for their disobedience to His Law.
The Rechabites

In the days of Jehoiakim king of Judah there were raids by the Babylonians on Judea, which made the inhabitants of the villages and the open country take refuge in Jerusalem to shelter inside its walls. Among them were the Rechabites, who lived in tents in Judea near Jerusalem.

The Rechabites: they are one of the tribes of the Kenites, and of Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, who accompanied the Jews to the Promised Land and were influenced by the character and conduct of the Jews.
The chambers: the side rooms of the temple of the Lord.
God commanded Jeremiah to bring a group of the Rechabites who lived in tents inside Jerusalem, and to bring them into one of the chambers of the house of the Lord and offer them wine to drink.

Jeremiah took one of the leaders of the Rechabites, who was called “Jaazaniah,” and his household and those of the Rechabites who were with him, and brought them into the chamber of the sons of Hanan in the house of the Lord.
Pots: large vessels.
Cups: drinking vessels.
Jeremiah offered them wine in large vessels and cups so that they might fill them and drink as they wished.
Jonadab the son of Rechab: he is the father of the Rechabites. He lived in the days of the prophet Elijah, that is, about two and a half centuries before the time of Jeremiah.
The Rechabites refused to drink wine because their ancestor Jonadab had commanded them not to drink wine forever, that is, never to drink at all, because wine represents the pleasures of the world.
Jonadab also commanded them to live as strangers to the world, by the following:
1- Living in tents.
2- Not owning fields and gardens to plant with vineyards and olives.
And this is in addition to not drinking wine, which is the third proof of their estrangement from the world.
The Rechabites declared their obedience throughout their lives to their father Jonadab in not drinking wine, living in tents, and not owning lands to cultivate.
When the armies of the Babylonians moved and attacked Judea, the sons of Rechab took refuge in Jerusalem to shelter in it.

If the sons of Rechab became strangers to the world in obedience to their father “Jonadab the son of Rechab,” how much more should we become strangers to the material things of the world and its lusts out of our love for God. May we use everything in measure and not cling to food, clothing or possessions.
God sent Jeremiah to the men of Judah to rebuke them for not accepting God's discipline for their sins at the hand of the Babylonians.
God rebuked His people for not obeying His commandments, while the sons of Rechab obeyed their father in not drinking wine.

He also rebuked them for rejecting the words of the earlier prophets since the days of Moses, and the later ones such as Jeremiah, that they should not worship idols and should turn back from their evil lusts so as to dwell in the land of Canaan. They did not obey, so they deserved the divine discipline, which is the captivity and expulsion from their land.
By this the sons of Rechab were distinguished from the people of God, the children of Israel; that is, the Gentiles from the Jews.
Obedience to God's commandments protects you from many troubles, so do not make light of it, and if you have violated them, return quickly to God with repentance.

Because of the disobedience of God's people to Him, He will punish them with the captivity, and He declares His name the LORD of hosts, that is, the Lord of power, that they might fear Him, perhaps repenting at the last moment.
He specifies the time of the prophecy, which is the fourth year of King Jehoiakim of Judah, that is, the year 605 BC. This king was wicked and hated Jeremiah because he proclaimed the voice of God.

God commanded Jeremiah to write all the prophecies that God had given him, from the days of King Josiah, that is, the year 626 BC, until the time of the writing of the prophecies, that is, 605 BC, a period of 21 years. They include prophecies against the kingdom of Israel, the kingdom of Judah and the other nations. Perhaps the motive for this was the nearness of the time of the captivity and Jeremiah's exposure to being kept away from the temple or imprisoned, which would hinder God's word from reaching the people. So God commanded him to write the prophecies so that they would be preserved, to be carried by the captives to Babylon or by the fugitives to Egypt, or so that a copy of them would remain in Jerusalem for them to read and repent.
God's purpose in these prophecies and in their writing is to move the hearts of His people to repent, so that He turns back from their punishment and saves them.
The roll of a book: thin sheets of skin or papyrus on which one writes, which are rolled up when kept, and when read these rolled-up sheets are opened.

Jeremiah called his disciple, the prophet Baruch, to write for him the prophecies that he would dictate to him. Jeremiah kept them in memory by the power of the Holy Spirit, or he may have written down each prophecy after proclaiming it. So he wrote all the prophecies of Jeremiah on a roll.

Jeremiah was forbidden to approach the temple. This is the meaning of the word “shut up,” and it does not mean that he was shut up in a prison, as is shown by the fact that he was able to flee, as v. 19 makes clear. This was in the year 605 BC, at the time when Babylon defeated Egypt in the battle of Carchemish on the river Euphrates and then began to advance toward Palestine to besiege Jerusalem.

Jeremiah commanded his disciple, the prophet Baruch, the recorder of his prophecies, that after writing all his prophecies he should read them in the hearing of the people gathered in the house of the Lord, those living in Jerusalem and also those coming from the land of Judah to the house of the Lord. This happened in the ninth month of the year 604 BC, that is, the fifth year of King Jehoiakim, so there is a time gap between the time of the writing of the roll and the time of its reading, of more than a year. This was on the day of the public fast.
[2] The public fast (vv. 8-10)

8- And Baruch the son of Neriah did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading in the book the words of the LORD in the LORD'S house. 9- And it came to pass in the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, in the ninth month, that they proclaimed a fast before the LORD to all the people in Jerusalem, and to all the people that came from the cities of Judah unto Jerusalem.

10- Then read Baruch in the book the words of Jeremiah in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the scribe, in the higher court, at the entry of the new gate of the LORD'S house, in the ears of all the people.

Baruch is a Hebrew name meaning blessed. He was a disciple of Jeremiah and recorded his prophecies for him. After this he went to Babylon and wrote a book of his own, which is one of the deuterocanonical books, that is, within the Holy Bible, but the Protestants removed it. He was related to Jeremiah by kinship.
The writing of the prophecies took more than a year, and then Baruch read them in the house of the Lord before the people.

In the ninth month of the ninth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah, which corresponds to the year 604 BC in the month of December, that is, in winter, they proclaimed in Jerusalem a public fast for all the people. It is not one of the religious fasts written in the Law of Moses, but a fast because of the approach of the armies of Babylon to Jerusalem and the sense of danger, so they sought God to deliver them. Sadly this fast was not accompanied by a turning back from their sins.

Gemariah the son of Shaphan: Shaphan was the scribe of King Josiah (2 Kgs 22:3, 8), and his son Gemariah was also the brother of Ahikam, who treated Jeremiah gently (ch. 25:24). Baruch went to the temple and went up to one of the chambers of the temple, the one belonging to Gemariah the son of Shaphan, who sympathized with Jeremiah. He stood and looked out from above from one of the windows of the chamber on the people gathered in the court of the temple and read the prophecies of Jeremiah that he had recorded for him. It appears that they were written in a condensed form, so that all of it could be read in a reasonable time to all the people.

Fasting is an opportunity to offer your love to God by giving up your material attachments, but it must be joined with your repentance, so that it is a pure fast with which God is pleased, and you feel spiritual consolations and blessing in your life.
[3] The reading of the book to the princes (vv. 11-19)

11- When Michaiah the son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan, had heard out of the book all the words of the LORD, 12- Then he went down into the king's house, into the scribe's chamber: and, lo, all the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe, and Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, and Elnathan the son of Achbor, and Gemariah the son of Shaphan, and Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes. 13- Then Michaiah declared unto them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the book in the ears of the people. 14- Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, unto Baruch, saying, Take in thine hand the roll wherein thou hast read in the ears of the people, and come. So Baruch the son of Neriah took the roll in his hand, and came unto them. 15- And they said unto him, Sit down now, and read it in our ears. So Baruch read it in their ears. 16- Now it came to pass, when they had heard all the words, they were afraid both one and other, and said unto Baruch, We will surely tell the king of all these words. 17- And they asked Baruch, saying, Tell us now, How didst thou write all these words at his mouth?
18- Then Baruch answered them, He pronounced all these words unto me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book.
19- Then said the princes unto Baruch, Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah; and let no man know where ye be.

Among those gathered in the court of the temple who heard Baruch's reading of the roll was a young man, Michaiah the son of Gemariah, one of the leaders of the people, whose grandfather was Shaphan, who had been the official scribe of King Josiah.

After hearing the prophecies of Jeremiah from the mouth of Baruch, Michaiah hurried to the royal palace, and there in one of the rooms called the scribe's chamber, where the scribes of the king and the princes used to meet, he found a number of princes, among them his father Gemariah. Michaiah knew from his father Gemariah the place where they met.

Michaiah told the princes of the prophecies of Jeremiah that he had heard from Baruch, and it appears that he was afraid because of the power of the words. This shows that he was a spiritual young man who cared for the word of God and was affected by it.
The princes sent a representative of theirs named Jehudi to Baruch, and asked him to come to them with the roll. Baruch obeyed and went to them in the royal palace.
The princes asked Baruch to read the book to them, and he read it before them.

When the leaders of the people heard Jeremiah's prophecies and God's threats to punish His people, they were very afraid and felt their responsibility to inform the king so that he would move the whole people in the way of repentance. From this we understand that the fear of God was in the hearts of these leaders, while the king, on the contrary, was wicked and did not fear God.
The princes asked Baruch how all these prophecies had been written and gathered from the days of King Josiah until the time of Jehoiakim, that is, a period of 21 years, as we mentioned.
Baruch informed them that the prophet Jeremiah dictated the prophecies to him and he wrote them in the book.

The princes advised Baruch to flee, he and Jeremiah, and hide in an unknown place, because they feared for them from the vengeance of the king and the false prophets. This confirms their love for Jeremiah and Baruch and their fear of God.

The fear of God makes a person care about hearing His word and even obeying it, so he tries to carry out His commandments and, out of his love for God, warns others so that they turn back from their sins. So be strong and be ready every day, setting your only goal as eternal life and remembering also the judgment.

The princes took the roll that Baruch had written and put it in the chamber of Elishama the scribe, who was probably the official scribe of the king. Then they went in to the king and told him what Baruch had done in the house of the Lord and that the roll was in the king's palace in the chamber of Elishama. Elishama was probably with them.

The king probably received this news coldly, and sent one of his aides in the palace, Jehudi, whom the princes had sent earlier, to bring Baruch from the temple (v. 15). Jehudi brought it from the chamber of Elishama and came with it to the king, and read it before him and before the princes standing with him.
The winter house: a house prepared for dwelling in winter, characterized by warmth. This confirms that this matter was in December of the year 604 BC, as we mentioned.

The hearth: a stove that was used for heating or cooking in ancient times and until recently in the twentieth century. Some wood is lit in it, giving a fire for warmth within a small space surrounded by bricks or stones.
Here He confirms the time of the reading of the book, which was in the ninth month, corresponding to December, that is, in winter, and the hearth was burning for warmth in the king's room.
Penknife: a small knife used by the scribe in preparing the wooden pen so that it has a fine point with which to write when it is dipped in ink.

Instead of the king fearing God's anger, he dared to command that the roll be torn with the scribe's penknife, and he could not bear to hear God's word except a few lines of it. He should rather have feared God, torn his clothes and wept over his sins, and God would have had mercy on him and on his people.
The king's stubbornness was so great that he did not listen to the entreaties of his princes not to burn God's word contained in the roll.

King Jehoiakim persisted in his evil and commanded one of his relatives, Jerahmeel the son of the king, that is, of his family, and two others of his aides, to seize Jeremiah and Baruch in order to punish them or kill them.

Do not rush in your anger, doing disturbing things and angering God and those around you. Be long-suffering and listen to the counsel of those around you, and lift your heart in prayer, and you will find your salvation and escape many evils.
[5] The second copy of the scroll (vv. 27-32)

27- Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, after that the king had burned the roll, and the words which Baruch wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah, saying, 28- Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned. 29- And thou shalt say to Jehoiakim king of Judah, Thus saith the LORD; Thou hast burned this roll, saying, Why hast thou written therein, saying, The king of Babylon shall certainly come and destroy this land, and shall cause to cease from thence man and beast? 30- Therefore thus saith the LORD of Jehoiakim king of Judah; He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David: and his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost. 31- And I will punish him and his seed and his servants for their iniquity; and I will bring upon them, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and upon the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them; but they hearkened not. 32- Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah; who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words.

After King Jehoiakim burned the roll, after a period that may have been a few months, God commanded Jeremiah to prepare a new roll and write in it all the prophecies previously written in the first roll. This shows the inclination of God and His children toward positive action, which is recording the word of God, and not thinking about the evil of the wicked, that is, the evil of Jehoiakim and those with him.

God sent King Jehoiakim a message by the tongue of Jeremiah, whether he wrote it in the roll or sent it with someone, in which God rebukes Jehoiakim because he refused to listen to God's punishment, namely the coming of the king of Babylon to Jerusalem and his taking it and destroying it and destroying men and animals, and he showed his stubbornness toward God in his burning of the roll.
God sent Jehoiakim a threat of punishment as a result of his sins, which includes two matters:
1- None of his sons will reign over the kingdom of Judah, as is the custom with his fathers, but his son Jehoiachin will reign for a few months, and then his uncle Zedekiah.

2- Jehoiakim will be killed at the hand of the Babylonians and his corpse thrown on the ground, and no one will bury him with honor like the rest of the kings, as a declaration of God's anger against him.
And God confirms the words of the roll, that He will punish Jerusalem and its inhabitants and the offspring of King Jehoiakim for their many evils.

Jeremiah obeyed and brought a roll and dictated to Baruch the prophecies previously written in the first roll, and added some further details of the prophecies, among them God's word about His punishment of Jehoiakim mentioned in (vv. 30, 31). Thus God preserved His word however much the wicked tried to remove it, for whoever stands before God or tries to remove His word, God of course laughs at him.
Obey God's word even if it is hard, and keep away from sin however attractive it is, and do not try to interpret God's word according to your desires, for then God will have mercy on you.
Jeremiah in the cistern

After Josiah died, killed in the battle of Megiddo, his son “Jehoahaz” reigned for three months, and then the king of Egypt took him captive, and his brother “Jehoiakim” reigned in his place. After “Jehoiakim” the son of Josiah was killed by the king of Babylon, his son “Jehoiachin,” who is also called “Jeconiah” or “Coniah,” reigned for a short time, three months, and then “Nebuchadnezzar” took him captive to Babylon, and his uncle “Zedekiah,” the brother of “Jehoiakim” and the son of “Josiah” the righteous king, reigned in his place. In the reign of “Zedekiah” Jerusalem was destroyed, the temple burned, and the Babylonian captivity began, for Zedekiah was the last king of the kingdom of Judah.
It is noticeable that from (chs. 37-44) Jeremiah relates to us many events of his history.

It is made clear here that Zedekiah, like his brother Jehoiakim, turned away from the way of God and that both refused to obey Jeremiah, the prophet of God. Although Zedekiah sometimes asked about the word of God, he did not obey it, for his personality was weaker than that of his brother Jehoiakim. Yet both were far from God, and no righteous king arose over the kingdom of Judah after Josiah.
Zedekiah was in perplexity whether to ally himself with the king of Egypt or submit to the king of Babylon, so he sent two of his aides to Jeremiah to pray for him and guide him.
At this time Jeremiah enjoyed freedom of movement among the people and spoke to them the word of God, that is, he had not yet been cast into prison.

If you have a position or leadership or authority, do not forget that it is God who gave you all this. So seek Him and obey His commandments, and you will live in reassurance and lead those with you in the straight way.
[2] The siege of Jerusalem (vv. 5-10)

5- Then Pharaoh's army was come forth out of Egypt: and when the Chaldeans that besieged Jerusalem heard tidings of them, they departed from Jerusalem. 6- Then came the word of the LORD unto the prophet Jeremiah, saying, 7- Thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel; Thus shall ye say to the king of Judah, that sent you unto me to enquire of me; Behold, Pharaoh's army, which is come forth to help you, shall return to Egypt into their own land. 8- And the Chaldeans shall come again, and fight against this city, and take it, and burn it with fire.
9- Thus saith the LORD; Deceive not yourselves, saying, The Chaldeans shall surely depart from us: for they shall not depart.

10- For though ye had smitten the whole army of the Chaldeans that fight against you, and there remained but wounded men among them, yet should they rise up every man in his tent, and burn this city with fire.

The army of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem in the year 588 BC, and “Hophra” king of Egypt, the son of Necho, was afraid of Babylon's attacking Egypt. So he moved with his armies, not out of love for the Jews but in defense of his own country, and came out to attack the army of Babylon besieging Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar feared fighting two armies, the army of Egypt and the army of Jerusalem, and preferred to fight each of them separately so that victory over it would be easy for him, and for this reason he withdrew at that time from fighting Jerusalem. This left King Zedekiah in perplexity as to which was stronger, so as to ally himself with it and submit to it: the king of Egypt or the king of Babylon?
God sent Jeremiah a prophecy answering the question of King Zedekiah, and he told his envoys that the army of Egypt would withdraw and move away from Jerusalem and return to Egypt.
Then Jeremiah added in his prophecy that the army of Babylon had left Jerusalem temporarily and would return to besiege it, take it, destroy it and burn it with fire.

The fall of Jerusalem and its captivity

This chapter tells us how Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem. In this verse it declares that the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar began in the tenth month of the ninth year of King Zedekiah, which is in the year 588 BC.

The Babylonian siege of Jerusalem continued from January of the year 588 BC until the summer of the same year, when they were forced to lift the siege for a short time because of the movement of the army of Egypt. Then Nebuchadnezzar triumphed over Egypt in the battle of Carchemish in Iraq, and after that Nebuchadnezzar returned and besieged Jerusalem, which had become very weak from hunger, thirst and disease, and he entered it and took it in the summer of the year 587 BC, in the month of July, that is, about a year and a half after the beginning of the siege. This was in the fourth month of the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.

The middle gate: probably the main gate of Jerusalem, which was built on five hills, the most important of which were a hill in the north and another in the south with a deep valley between them. This gate led to this valley, which divides the city into two parts, so it is called the middle gate. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard who led the army, attacked the city of Jerusalem and stormed it, and the princes of the army of Babylon entered and sat in the main gate of the city of Jerusalem, declaring their capture of this city. They did not enter into its depths lest harm come to them from one of the people, but the soldiers of Babylon moved to seize whomever they wished throughout the city, and they took the best of the people captive to Babylon. As for King Nebuchadnezzar, he waited in the city of Riblah to prevent any forces coming to the aid of Jerusalem. The princes mentioned here are some of the princes who entered Jerusalem and not all of them, and the functions of some are mentioned: one of them was the chief of the eunuchs, who work as servants for the king of Babylon, and another was the chief of the magi, that is, the wise men and counselors of the king of Babylon. Other names of the princes are mentioned in (v. 13).
The king's garden: large gardens belonging to King Zedekiah beside the pool of Siloam.
The gate betwixt the two walls: a gate of Jerusalem lying on its south side. The plain: the deep valley of the Jordan north of the Dead Sea, which leads to the Arabian desert near Egypt.

When King Zedekiah saw the Babylonian forces beginning to enter Jerusalem, he hurried to flee, he and the men of war, that is, his special guard and the commanders of the army. They took cover by night so that no one would see them, and went out by the way of the king's garden to one of the gates of Jerusalem that lies in its south and is called the gate betwixt the two walls, which leads to the valley of the plain, from which they could flee to Egypt and take refuge in it.
The plains of Jericho: the plains of Jericho extending between Jericho and the river Jordan and also extending south as far as Jerusalem.
Riblah: a city lying in the land of Hamath, north of the city of Damascus, the capital of Syria.

While King Zedekiah and his fighting men were fleeing from Jerusalem in the plains of Jericho, the eyes of the king of Babylon were watching them and searching for them. They learned of their flight and pursued them until they overtook them, and seized them in these plains beside the river Jordan, and took them to Nebuchadnezzar, who was staying in the city of Riblah, which he had taken before.

Nebuchadnezzar commanded the killing of Zedekiah's sons, whom his men had seized with their father, and they killed them before Zedekiah's eyes to humiliate him and frighten him. Then he also commanded, and they killed the nobles of the kingdom of Judah who had been fleeing with Zedekiah. Thus Zedekiah felt complete helplessness after the killing of his children, his nobles and the fighters who defended him.

Nebuchadnezzar also commanded that Zedekiah's eyes be put out, in vengeance on him for not submitting, then bound him with fetters of brass, that is, very strong, from which he could not free himself, and they led him away captive to live as a captive in Babylon after he had lost all his strength and even his sight.

Do not rely on your strength and capabilities, nor on the opinions of people, for they are all weak and cannot protect you. Rather obey God and hold fast to His commandments, even if they seem heavy, trusting in His ability to help you, protect you and save you from every evil.

After they had killed the leaders of the kingdom of Judah and taken the rest of them captive, Jerusalem was left without a force to defend it, and this was about a month after its capture. Here Nebuchadnezzar commanded the burning of the king's palace and likewise the palaces of Jerusalem, so as to humiliate the city and leave it destroyed.

That fell to him: they fled and surrendered themselves to the armies of Babylon. The captain of the guard: the one responsible for security in Babylon. After that the armies of Babylon seized all the Jews fit for work, and also those who had fled from Jerusalem and surrendered themselves to the armies of Babylon, and took them captive, bound as slaves, to Babylon. All this was by the command of the commander of the Babylonian armies, Nebuzaradan.
Nothing remained in Jerusalem but the poor and weak of the Jews, and Nebuzaradan gave them the fields around Jerusalem to cultivate. He intended by this:
1- To preserve these fields so that the Babylonians could take from them and make use of them when they wished in the form of taxes.
2- That there should be in Jerusalem only the weak, unable to resist Babylon.
3- To honor these poor, whom the nobles and rich of the Jews had exploited, and by this to win them over so that they owe loyalty to Babylon and not to their homeland.

These two verses make clear that “Nebuchadnezzar” charged the commander of his armies, Nebuzaradan, to release Jeremiah, care for him and give him the freedom to do what he wished, that is, complete freedom.

It is understood from this that Nebuzaradan brought him out of the prison in which King “Zedekiah” had imprisoned him and gave him his freedom in Jerusalem. But on referring to (Jer 40:1-2) we find that Jeremiah had been seized and taken captive to Babylon, and on the way, at a city called Ramah, the command came from Nebuchadnezzar to Nebuzaradan to release him and return him to Jerusalem a free man. There is no contradiction between the two chapters, for they brought him out of his prison and sent him to Babylon with the captives, but it appears that news reached Nebuchadnezzar from the captive Jews that Jeremiah was the prophet of God who had been calling the king and the people to submit to Babylon. So Nebuchadnezzar felt that he was not an enemy of his and released him and honored him as mentioned in this chapter, and he returned from Ramah to Jerusalem.
Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan: he was cooperative with the Babylonians, who afterward appointed him governor over Jerusalem and its surroundings.

Nebuzaradan and the princes of Babylon carried out the commands of King Nebuchadnezzar and released Jeremiah from the prison, and handed him over to Gedaliah, who was to become governor over Jerusalem, to care for him and settle him among the people in Jerusalem, and to move about with complete freedom.

This goes back to mention a prophecy that God gave Jeremiah when he was imprisoned in Jerusalem, before Nebuzaradan released him.

God sent this prophecy by the mouth of Jeremiah to “Ebedmelech the Ethiopian,” one of the servants of “Zedekiah” king of Judah, among the counselors close to him, who had done a kindness to Jeremiah when he interceded for him before Zedekiah so that he would not die in the cistern full of mire, not afraid of the princes of the king of Judah who had put him in the cistern. He took a command from Zedekiah and brought Jeremiah out of the cistern and put him in a better prison (ch. 38:7-13). This divine message to Ebedmelech declares that God's word, of the destruction of Jerusalem and the killing and captivity of those in it, would be fulfilled quickly and “Ebedmelech” would see it.
This message also contained good news for Ebedmelech that God would deliver him from the hand of his Babylonian enemies so that they would not seize him.

The third matter that this message contained is that God would deliver him from death so that the Babylonians would not kill him, and this was because of his faith in God and his trust in Him, for he feared God and took pity on His prophet Jeremiah and rescued him from death, so God delivers him from death. Thus God preserved three:
(1) His prophet “Jeremiah,” because of his obedience to God and his proclaiming His voice to all the people.
(2) “Ebedmelech,” who represents the Gentiles who fear God and do mercy.
(3) The poor of the Jews to whom the Babylonians gave the fields and vineyards to cultivate and eat from, who represent the weak who rely on God.

If you obey God and fear Him and rely on Him, God will keep you and deliver you from evil, not only in this life but He will give you the glories of eternal life. So hold fast to God's commandments even if everyone keeps away from them, and do not forget your only goal, which is “the love of God.”
The release of Jeremiah

Ramah: a city lying 6 miles north of Jerusalem and 2 miles south-west of Mizpah. Perhaps what is meant by the word of God to Jeremiah is the decision of Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard of the kingdom of Babylon, to release Jeremiah and his return to the captivity, to Mizpah, since he was among the captives whom the Babylonians took from Jerusalem and walked with toward Ramah. Orders came from Nebuchadnezzar to Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, to release Jeremiah, perhaps because he had heard from the Jews of Jeremiah's prophecies calling for submission to the king of Babylon, so he regarded him as a friend and not an enemy. This was by the provision of God to free Jeremiah.

Nebuzaradan uttered an important spiritual truth, namely that the destruction of Jerusalem was because of the Jews' disobedience to God's commandments. Perhaps this idea helped the Babylonians to destroy Jerusalem, but sadly the Jews did not understand this truth.

Take care lest the people of the world know spiritual truths that you do not know, just as Christ in the parable of the unjust steward asked us to learn wisdom from the children of this age. In proportion as you are submissive to God in prayer, He will guide you even through the mouths of the people of the world and not only through the mouths of the spiritual teachers in the Church.
Nebuzaradan issued an order to release Jeremiah, then left to him the choice of the place where he would stay, which was:
1- Going to Babylon, where care and attention from Nebuzaradan awaited him.
2- Going to any place he chose in the world.

Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan: “Shaphan” was the official scribe of King Josiah and shared with him in the religious reforms, so he was a pious man, and his son “Ahikam” is “Gemariah,” one of the princes of King Jehoiakim, who feared God and tried to prevent the king from tearing up Jeremiah's prophecies (Jer 36:25). So Gedaliah was from a pious family, and his name is a Hebrew word meaning “Jehovah is great.” Nebuchadnezzar had appointed him as his deputy and governor of the kingdom of Judah after he took it.

Mizpah: it is eight miles from Jerusalem to its north-west, and very close to Ramah, so it was easy for Jeremiah to return to Mizpah, where Gedaliah the governor was. It is clear that Mizpah had not been destroyed by Babylon like Jerusalem.

Before Jeremiah decided where to stay, Nebuzaradan continued his talk with Jeremiah and said to him: go to Gedaliah, who is the governor of Judah, and he will care for you and you will stay among the people there. So Jeremiah obeyed and returned to Mizpah to live among his poor and weak people, after Nebuzaradan gave him a gift and provisions for the road and took care of him.

When Babylon attacked the kingdom of Judah, a large number of Jews fled to the surrounding mountains, such as the Ammonites, Moab and Edom. After the destruction of Jerusalem and many lands around it and Babylon's capture of the kingdom of Judah, it appointed Gedaliah governor over it to pay tribute to it. When the leading men among the Jews, who were probably soldiers, heard of what had happened, they returned to the land of Judah. It calls them the princes because they were strong and not like the weak who remained in Judah. It mentions some of them, such as Ishmael, who had fled to the land of the Ammonites and was a wicked man and made a pact with the king of the Ammonites to take the kingdom of Judah. It also mentions two pious brothers, Johanan and Jonathan, sons of Kareah, and others.

Gedaliah was affected by the word of God through the mouth of Jeremiah, so when he received these princes mentioned in (v. 8) he said to them: submit to the king of Babylon and dwell in peace in the land.

Gedaliah continued his words by saying that he would remain in Mizpah as a deputy for Babylon to meet the envoys of Nebuchadnezzar and pay him the tribute and all the reports required. As for them, he invited them to dwell in their cities where they had lived in the kingdom of Judah, and to cultivate the fields and gather fruits as they wished, of grapes, figs, olives and all the fruits of the field.

All the Jews who had fled to the countries surrounding the kingdom of Judah also heard of Gedaliah's appointment as governor amid a settled state of security and the return of normal life, so they returned to their land and began to cultivate their lands.

How beautiful it is to live in peace so that you can practice your spiritual life and enjoy God. So keep away from conflict with others as much as you can, and seek peace in order to devote yourself to life with God.

Some of the princes, that is, Jewish officers such as Johanan the son of Kareah, discovered a plot to assassinate Gedaliah the governor. This plot was an agreement between “Ishmael,” who was of the royal line, and “Baalis,” king of the Ammonites, to whom Ishmael had fled when Babylon attacked the kingdom of Judah. It appears that the aim of this plot was for the king of the Ammonites to take the kingdom of Judah and resist Babylon. So Johanan and those with him of the officers and soldiers came and told Gedaliah of the plot, but sadly he did not believe them and considered their words slander and false accusation. Thus Gedaliah rushed to judge by his own opinion and did not return to God in prayer or consult the prophet Jeremiah, who was staying beside him.

Take refuge in prayer in every matter that is presented to you, especially in great decisions, so that you hear His voice and He guides you and you keep yourself from the snares of the devil. God is near to you; He wants to lead your life in peace, so seek Him and persist before Him, and you will hear His voice.

Johanan had pity on Gedaliah and was concerned to preserve the land of Judah, which had begun to settle under Gedaliah's leadership. So he asked Gedaliah's permission to go and kill Ishmael, and thus deliver him from this plot.

Gedaliah rejected Johanan's counsel and accused him of lying. So he lost an opportunity sent to him by God for deliverance, because he relied on his own opinion. Perhaps he felt his strength when he became governor. Despite his piety, he was weak in this situation and was compelled to pay a costly price, which was his whole life.
The assassination of Gedaliah, governor of Judah

Ishmael went with ten men to visit Gedaliah, the governor of Judah, who was living at Mizpah. With him were also some of the royal court of King Zedekiah, whom Babylon had taken captive. Gedaliah welcomed them all and hosted them, and they ate with him at a great feast that he made for them. This shows Gedaliah’s love, his kindness of heart and his generosity.

It seems that Ishmael was jealous of Gedaliah and envied him the office of governor that he had received, and perhaps he had made a pact with the king of the children of Ammon to help him take the rule. So his visit to Gedaliah was for an evil purpose, and in the midst of the feast and the rejoicing he rose up and killed Gedaliah, the governor of Judah, whom the king of Babylon had appointed. This was not an ordinary murder, but carried two meanings:
1- The killing of the head of the kingdom of Judah, which stirred up unrest among the people.
2- A challenge to the king of Babylon, who had appointed Gedaliah.

The men of the palace were alarmed and afraid at the surprise, so Ishmael carried his evil further and struck down all the Jews, the men of Gedaliah, and all the Chaldeans who were assisting Gedaliah on behalf of Nebuchadnezzar. This shows Ishmael’s cruelty and wickedness, his boldness in evil, and also his deceit in exploiting hospitality and love as an opportunity for harm and evil.

The Jews grieved greatly over the killing of Gedaliah, and they appointed a fast for this in the seventh month (Zech 7:5; 8:19). This was most likely a year after Babylon’s seizure of Jerusalem and Judah, that is, in 586 BC.

May you thank everyone who shows you love, and repay good with good. If evil thoughts against someone fight against you, reject them and find an excuse for him, so that you keep your love for him and do not wrong anyone, even unintentionally. And if it happens, apologize quickly and make up with great love to the one you have wronged. [2] The capture and killing of the rest of the people (vv. 4-10):

4- And it came to pass the second day after he had slain Gedaliah, and no man knew it, 5- That there came certain from Shechem, from Shiloh, and from Samaria, even fourscore men, having their beards shaven, and their clothes rent, and having cut themselves, with offerings and incense in their hand, to bring them to the house of the LORD. 6- And Ishmael the son of Nethaniah went forth from Mizpah to meet them, weeping all along as he went: and it came to pass, as he met them, he said unto them, Come to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. 7- And it was so, when they came into the midst of the city, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah slew them, and cast them into the midst of the pit, he, and the men that were with him. 8- But ten men were found among them that said unto Ishmael, Slay us not: for we have treasures in the field, of wheat, and of barley, and of oil, and of honey. So he forbare, and slew them not among their brethren. 9- Now the pit wherein Ishmael had cast all the dead bodies of the men, whom he had slain because of Gedaliah, was it which Asa the king had made for fear of Baasha king of Israel: and Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with them that were slain. 10- Then Ishmael carried away captive all the residue of the people that were in Mizpah, even the king’s daughters, and all the people that remained in Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam: and Ishmael the son of Nethaniah carried them away captive, and departed to go over to the Ammonites.
Shechem: a city lying north of Jerusalem at a distance of 31.5 miles, at Mount Gerizim, and 5.5 miles south-east of Samaria.
Shiloh: 17 miles north of Jerusalem. It was the dwelling place of the Ark of the Covenant of God in the days of Eli the priest and for 300 years before that.
Samaria: the capital of the northern kingdom of the Jews, which is called Israel and which comprises ten tribes. It lies about 35 miles north of Jerusalem.
Rent clothes: tearing the clothes is one of the signs of grief.
Cut themselves: wounded with deep cuts. Cutting the body to please the gods was one of the pagan customs.

After Ishmael killed Gedaliah, he and those with him hid his body in the palace, so that no one knew and the city would not be stirred up against him. On the day after the killing of Gedaliah, 80 men of the Jews happened to arrive from various places, namely Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria, which are Jewish places lying north of Jerusalem. They were going down south toward Jerusalem and reached Mizpah because it was on their way to Jerusalem. They were in mourning over the destruction of Jerusalem, as is proved by their tearing their clothes, but sadly they had been influenced by pagan worship and had cut their bodies. They wished to go to Jerusalem to present offerings to the Lord at the place where the temple of the Lord had been.

Ishmael went further in his evil and deceit. He went forward to meet these Jews who were coming in sorrow to visit the ruins of the temple of the Lord, and he too pretended to grieve over the destruction of the temple. He invited them to rest with Gedaliah at Mizpah and then continue their journey to Jerusalem.
The pit: a deep hole, which may hold water or mud, or may be dry.

Ishmael lured the 80 men into the middle of the city and surrounded them there with his men and began to kill them. He killed most of them and threw them into a pit that was near the middle of the city. It seems that the reason for their murder was to rob them of the goods they carried. This confirms Ishmael’s wickedness and greed, in contrast to the godly Gedaliah, who wanted to gather the scattered Jews and preserve them and their stability.

What confirms Ishmael’s greed is that ten of these eighty men noticed Ishmael plundering their possessions before killing them, so they asked him not to kill them in return for showing him their storehouses in their land, full of God’s good gifts, of crops and their produce. Ishmael agreed to satisfy his greed, whether these men were telling the truth or deceiving him, but by these words they were able to escape death.

Here the account tells us that the pit into which Ishmael threw the bodies of the men he had killed in the middle of the city had been made by King Asa, king of Judah, when he built the city of Mizpah after he prevailed over King Baasha, king of the kingdom of Israel (1 Kgs 15:22; 2 Chr 16:6).

The king’s daughters: all the women of the royal line who remained after the captivity of Zedekiah king of Judah and those with him and their deportation to Babylon. They may also have been of the household of Gedaliah, that is, his daughters and sisters, meaning the relatives of Gedaliah, the governor of the kingdom of Judah.

After Ishmael grew strong by killing many and the people feared him, he seized the men and women in Mizpah and took them captive. They went behind him as he left Mizpah and went to the kingdom of the children of Ammon. Among those he took captive were the princesses, the king’s daughters, that is, he took all the great ones of the city. This shows that he wanted to become king or governor. He went to the king of the children of Ammon to gain strength with the help of its king (Baalis).
Do not use your intelligence for evil to reach your goals, and let your means be sound in order to reach sound goals.
[3] The rescue by Johanan (vv. 11-18):

11- But when Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces that were with him, heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done, 12- Then they took all the men, and went to fight with Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and found him by the great waters that are in Gibeon. 13- Now it came to pass, that when all the people which were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces that were with him, then they were glad. 14- So all the people that Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah cast about and returned, and went unto Johanan the son of Kareah. 15- But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the Ammonites. 16- Then took Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces that were with him, all the remnant of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, from Mizpah, after that he had slain Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, even mighty men of war, and the women, and the children, and the eunuchs, whom he had brought again from Gibeon: 17- And they departed, and dwelt in the habitation of Chimham, which is by Bethlehem, to go to enter into Egypt, 18- Because of the Chaldeans: for they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had slain Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon made governor in the land.
Gibeon: a city about five miles north of Jerusalem. The great waters: a deep pool more than ten meters deep.

The news reached Johanan the son of Kareah, the godly Jewish commander who had warned Gedaliah of the plot to assassinate him at the hand of Ishmael. Sadly, Gedaliah did not believe Johanan, and Ishmael killed him (ch. 40:13-16). Johanan gathered the captains of the Jewish forces, that is, the senior officers, and their soldiers, and advanced toward Mizpah to rescue his people from the hand of Ishmael. He overtook him before he reached the kingdom of the children of Ammon, at the city of Gibeon, which is about three miles from Mizpah, and met him at the deep pool of Gibeon.

When the captive Jews whom Ishmael had seized saw Johanan and the soldiers with him, they rejoiced and took courage. When Johanan, who had come to their aid, signaled to them, they left Ishmael, turned around all together and went after Johanan. As for Ishmael, he was in great fear when he saw Johanan and the army with him.

Since Ishmael feared Johanan and found with him only eight of the wicked men who followed him, he fled quickly to the children of Ammon. Thus the story of Ishmael, his plots and his evils came to an end.
Geruth Chimham: a Hebrew expression meaning “lodging place”. It is a place of hospitality established beside the city of Chimham, which is near Bethlehem, lying south of Jerusalem.

Johanan and the captains who followed him feared the wrath of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, when he would hear the news of the killing of his deputy Gedaliah, whom he had appointed governor over Judah. They had not wronged Gedaliah, but they feared Nebuchadnezzar’s fury against all the inhabitants of the kingdom of Judah. So they fled with those who were with them to Egypt, away from Nebuchadnezzar, and rested on the way at Geruth Chimham. This was a weakness in Johanan despite his godliness. He ought to have prayed and asked Jeremiah, or recalled the words of Jeremiah, who had warned against taking refuge in Egypt. He should have believed in God and remained in his faith so that God would protect him.

Always take refuge in God through prayer and by asking the spiritual fathers, however logical your thinking may be, so that you do not slip onto a wrong path, and God will keep you and protect you in all your ways.
The descent into Egypt

The leaders of the Jews and all the people, that is, a great multitude, came forward and went to Jeremiah the prophet so that he would pray for them, confessing their weakness, for they had become few in number after having been a great nation, because many had died at the hand of Babylon.

They also asked Jeremiah to guide them as to where they should go, whether to Egypt, or to Babylon, or remain in their land. Despite the appearance of concern to hear the voice of God, in truth they had already decided to go down to Egypt, as is evident from the previous chapter (ch. 41:17).

Jeremiah agreed to pray for them so that God would guide them as to where to go. Although they had said to him in (v. 2) “the LORD thy God”, Jeremiah answers them in (v. 4) “the LORD your God”, to teach them to be followers of their God, holding fast to Him and submitting to Him as His people.

They declared their obedience to the word of God that He would speak to Jeremiah, and their readiness to hear His voice, whether God’s opinion seemed good or hard to them. But sadly, all this was a superficial obedience, while the heart insisted on going down to Egypt.
May you believe that God’s choice is the best thing in your life, so that you obey God and the guidance of the Church, however hard it may be or contrary to your own opinions.
God waited ten days and then answered Jeremiah, for the following reasons:
1- So that Jeremiah would pray and prepare to hear the voice of God and enjoy fellowship with Him.
2- So that the people would prepare to hear the word of God, make ready to obey it, and be sure of their submission to Him.
Jeremiah sent for and called the leaders of the Jews, led by “Johanan”, and all the people who followed him.
Jeremiah told them that God had answered him concerning the counsel they had asked of him, whether to remain in the land or go down to Egypt.
God directed them to remain in their land and promised them the following:
1- That He would build them and plant them, that is, establish them and make them grow, so that they would increase in strength and number.
2- He also promises them that He would not pull them down or pluck them up, that is, that they would be established in the land and not be exposed to being driven out of it.
The third promise: if they remained in the land, the king of Babylon would not harm them, but they would live in tranquility and peace.
The fourth promise: that they would receive mercy and kindness from the king of Babylon. The fifth promise is that he would permit those whom he had taken captive to return to their land.
If you obey God’s commandments, you will enjoy mercies and blessings you cannot imagine, and you will live in peace and also grow in His love.

entries.section: (3) The punishment for going down to Egypt

paragraphs.text: The sound of the trumpet: and exposure to death.

God warned them against going down to Egypt, thinking that there was safety there away from the hand of Babylon, because in their eyes Egypt was strong and would protect them, and they would not be exposed to wars or hunger but would live rejoicing in abundant good things.

entries.section: (3) The punishment for going down to Egypt

paragraphs.text: God tells them the truth, which is that if they flee to Egypt they will be exposed to death by the sword that they think they are escaping by leaving their land, and they will also be exposed to death by hunger and will not find the abundant good things they expect in Egypt.

entries.section: (3) The punishment for going down to Egypt

paragraphs.text: Thus by going down to Egypt they will be exposed to death, whether by the sword, by hunger or by disease.

entries.section: (3) The punishment for going down to Egypt

paragraphs.text: God warns them that if they go down to Egypt they will be exposed to the wrath of God, who chastened Jerusalem and Judea by destruction and killing, and that He will chasten them in Egypt in the same way, that is, punish them for their disobedience and lack of repentance.

May you trust in God and not in the passing powers of the world. God’s commandment protects you, and trust in Him supports you however much troubles rise against you. On the contrary, all the powers of the world that you think support you collapse little by little before you.

entries.section: (4) A warning against going down to Egypt

paragraphs.text: God forbids them, with a clear warning, to go down to Egypt, so that they would not perish.

entries.section: (4) A warning against going down to Egypt
