paragraphs.text: He reminds them of their sin, which was lying and deceit when they asked God’s counsel about going down to Egypt or remaining in their land, while they were insisting in their heart on going down to Egypt.

entries.section: (4) A warning against going down to Egypt

paragraphs.text: He repeats His warning to them of death if they continue to insist on going down to Egypt.
If you sin, repent quickly and do not persist in the snare, because God loves you and repeats His call to you to repent, so that you may save yourself by returning to Him.
Jeremiah in Egypt and his prophecy about it

After Jeremiah told the leaders and the people the word of God that they had asked of him, telling them to remain in their land and not go to Egypt lest they die, the leaders of the people accused him of lying, because his word did not agree with their desire.
They also made two other accusations against him:
1- That he was being led by the words of his disciple Baruch and was not telling them the word of God; that is, they accused him of a weak character and of being led by others.
2- That by having them remain in their land he intended the Babylonians to kill them.
The leaders refused and stirred up the people to reject the word of God and not to remain in the kingdom of Judah.

Johanan led the leaders, the people and all those who had fled to the surrounding countries such as Moab, the children of Ammon and Edom, whether officers, or members of the king’s family, the princesses, or the notables of the people. They set out to leave the land of Judah, carrying off with them by force Jeremiah the prophet and his disciple Baruch the prophet. Why did they take Jeremiah with them although they rejected his word?
1- Either out of fear of him, lest his word prove true and the woes he spoke of come upon them, so they thought that his presence with them would protect them from these woes.
2- Or out of fear that if he remained in the land of Judah he would ally himself with Babylon and they would attack them in Egypt.
Tahpanhes: a large fortified city with a palace of the king, lying in the east of Egypt, ten miles west of El Qantara.
This caravan traveled under the leadership of Johanan and reached Egypt, at fortified Tahpanhes, to secure protection for their dwelling there from any Babylonian attacks.

Do not trust in the arm of man or in your own mind more than in God, lest you be exposed to many troubles. Obey His commandments before your mind and be reassured, for He is able to carry out His promises to protect you and care for you.

Jeremiah did not yield to the Jews’ compulsion to come to Egypt by becoming afraid and silent, but considered it an opportunity to declare the word of God, and a prophecy came to him from God whose aim was the repentance of His people.
The clay (mortar): the clay from which they make bricks.
The brickkiln: the place where clay is kneaded to make slabs of mud brick.

This prophecy was accompanied by visible actions that God required, confirming the meaning of the prophecy. He asked Jeremiah to bury large stones in the clay before the king’s palace. These represent the great power of Babylon, whose strength neither the children of Israel nor the Egyptians could grasp; in their eyes it was unseen and buried in the clay, yet it was strong and able to shatter Egypt, and it does not fear Pharaoh, since Jeremiah buried it before the gate of the king’s palace.
Royal pavilion (brocade): the royal garments of silk.
He shall spread his royal pavilion upon them: he will take control of the region and occupy it.
The prophecy, which the buried stones confirm, declares that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon will attack Egypt and defeat it. This happened in 568 BC.
When the king of Babylon strikes Egypt, he will kill some and take others captive.
The land of Egypt: he will take control of it easily and quickly, as a shepherd puts on his garment.
In his attack Nebuchadnezzar will burn the pagan temples of Egypt, crush and seize the land, and after his victory return to his country triumphant.
Images: the obelisks.
Egypt was famous for the worship of “Ra”, the sun god, and the king of Babylon will burn his temples and break the obelisks set up to glorify him, and will generally burn the temples he comes upon.
The shattering of Egypt’s power calls man to trust in God, for He is the only constant, lasting power in the world. The punishment of those who migrated to Egypt
Migdol: a city lying in the north-east of Egypt, in the region of Suez (Ex 14:2; Num 33:7). Tahpanhes: lies west of El Qantara, ten miles from it, and had a palace of the king.
Noph: a city lying about 12 miles south of Cairo, which was at some time the capital of Egypt.
Pathros: this is Thebes, that is, present-day Luxor, which was for a time the capital of Egypt.

It is understood from this verse that the Jews who fled from the kingdom of Judah spread throughout Egypt from its north to its south, and in the last migration they carried Jeremiah with them. The word of God to him was directed to the Jews scattered through all the land of Egypt, and especially the places mentioned here.

God speaks with power, declaring His name to be the LORD of hosts, that is, the God who is able to do all things, who chastened His people in Jerusalem and all the kingdom of Judah by destroying their cities and killing many of them, so that the cities became a desolation in which no one dwells.
The reason for this chastening is the people’s worship of idols, of gods whom neither they nor their fathers had known, but which were the gods of the peoples around them.
The abominable thing: the evil and filth that God hates.

In His longsuffering God sent many prophets, from the days of Moses until Jeremiah, to teach them to worship God and to turn away from the worship of strange gods, which is an uncleanness and an evil that God greatly hates.
Sadly the people did not listen to the words of the prophets and persisted in worshiping idols.
Because of these evils God chastened them by destroying their cities.

God warns them that their continuing in the worship of idols will lead to their destruction, great and small. This did indeed happen, for the Jews in Egypt died and only a few remained who were able to return to the kingdom of Judah.

The Jews completed their evils by worshiping idols in Egypt, in defiance of God and to provoke Him. The result is that He will chasten them so that they become extinct as a people, that is, become a very weak people, so as to be an example of disgrace and shame among the nations, since the curse of their God, whom they angered, came upon them.

God reminds them of the evils of their fathers and the sins of their kings and their wives, such as Jezebel the wife of Ahab, and the wives of Solomon who turned his heart away from the worship of God, and the evils of all the peoples, and how their divine chastening came by the destruction of their cities and the killing of many of them.

It would have been natural, in the face of the divine chastening, for the people to humble themselves in repentance and fear God, and so obtain His mercies. But sadly they continued in the worship of idols, and even increased in it when they came to Egypt, which was full of pagan gods, and no one returned to the law of God and His worship.

Remember how much your old sins did to you, wearied you and distanced you from God, so that today you may be careful of the sources of evil that make you fall into sin and keep away from them; and if you fall, repent quickly and return to God and enjoy His forgiveness, His love and His care.
God declares His decision to destroy His people, so that they see the face of God angry with them, and He allows them to be killed because of their sins.
A curse (oath): they will become an example of the divine chastening, and people will swear by what happened to them. That is, they will become a lesson before all the peoples.
An astonishment: people will marvel at the severity of the chastening that came upon them because of the multitude of their evils.

The divine chastening strikes those who migrated to Egypt, that is, the remnant of the Jews who remained after the Babylonian captivity and sought protection by coming to Egypt instead of obeying God, trusting in Him and remaining in their land as Jeremiah had told them. God will destroy them visibly, so that they become, before all the peoples, an example of divine chastening as a result of their rebellion and disobedience.

The divine punishment will fall on the Jews who worship idols in Egypt, as it fell on the Jews who worshiped idols in Jerusalem and the kingdom of Judah through Babylon’s attack on them. As Babylon attacked Jerusalem, so it will attack Egypt also.
The Jews who migrated to Egypt will perish and will not return to their land except a small number who were able to escape. God preserved this remnant so that perhaps it would repent and worship Him.

In His tenderness God is longsuffering toward you and gives you an opportunity to repent, even if He allows troubles and some things in your life to be held up. But you still have strength to return to Him, so that your soul may live and enjoy fellowship with Him.

entries.section: (3) Persistence in the worship of idols

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah was speaking to the Jews living in Pathros, that is, present-day Luxor, and calling them to repentance and to return to God, as is clear from the preceding verses of this chapter. But the answer was strange from the men and women who were gathered around Jeremiah in a great assembly to hear the voice of God.

entries.section: (3) Persistence in the worship of idols

paragraphs.text: All of them refused to hear the word of God from the mouth of Jeremiah, in clear defiance of God and complete disobedience.

entries.section: (3) Persistence in the worship of idols

paragraphs.text: They declared that they would continue to worship the queen of heaven, which is either Ashtaroth the goddess of the Assyrians, or Baal, or any gods they take from the heavens, such as the sun, the moon, the stars and the storms. Their proof and encouragement for worshiping them was the comfort and prosperity they supposed they had while worshiping them in the kingdom of Judah, for they attributed their prosperity to the worship of the gods of heaven and not to God, who was longsuffering toward them. This shows the extent of their rebellion and persistence in evil.

If you have grown weak and sinned, return to God, for He is tender and merciful. But do not justify your sins, persisting in them and defying God. Who are you that you should stand before God and disobey Him?! Apologize to Him and to those around you with humility, and you will regain your sonship to Him.

entries.section: (3) Persistence in the worship of idols

paragraphs.text: Drink offerings: they used to pour out wine and oil to please the gods.
We have wanted all things: we have lacked all material needs, that is, we became poor.

They attributed prosperity to the worship of the gods of heaven and attributed poverty to their not worshiping them, whereas in truth the prosperity was from God’s longsuffering toward them, and the poverty was a divine chastening to bring them back to Him. Thus, through their distance from God, they did not understand His purposes and persisted stubbornly in their evils.

entries.section: (3) Persistence in the worship of idols

paragraphs.text: The women declared that their worship of the gods of heaven, by making cakes and pouring out drink offerings, was with the consent and even the help of their husbands; that is, all of them, men and women, were insisting on the worship of idols.

entries.section: (4) The confirmation of the divine punishment

paragraphs.text: God was longsuffering toward the rebellious people and sent them His word a second time through Jeremiah.

entries.section: (4) The confirmation of the divine punishment

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah reminded them of their evils in burning incense to idols in Jerusalem and the land of Judah, which greatly provoked and troubled God, for it came from all the people, and the kings and the leaders.

entries.section: (4) The confirmation of the divine punishment

paragraphs.text: God could not bear their evils any longer, since He found in them no inclination to repent, so He chastened them by destroying Jerusalem and the land of Judah. Here Jeremiah makes clear that the poverty and the ruin were because of their sins against God, and not because of their turning away from the worship of the gods of heaven, as they had supposed.

entries.section: (4) The confirmation of the divine punishment

paragraphs.text: He affirms that the cause of the shame and humiliation they are in is their sins against God by burning incense to idols.

entries.section: (4) The confirmation of the divine punishment

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah told them the word of God and the punishment coming upon them because of their burning incense to the gods of heaven and offering vows to them; all this confirms their faith in them and not in God.

entries.section: (4) The confirmation of the divine punishment

paragraphs.text: Because of their evils God will prevent His name from being mentioned by the mouths of the wicked Jews, because they mention His name and at the same time worship the idols that are against Him, so He will allow them to be killed at the hand of Babylon because of their persistence in evil.

entries.section: (4) The confirmation of the divine punishment

paragraphs.text: God decides that He will destroy His people, so that they die by the sword of the king of Babylon, and those who do not die by the sword will die by hunger, contrary to what they imagined of good things for them in Egypt.

Do not think that your comfort lies in your material ambitions, for they are not guaranteed, but changeable and passing. Rather seek first to live with God and regain your peace, and enjoy joy on earth and then in heaven.

entries.section: (4) The confirmation of the divine punishment

paragraphs.text: Whose words shall stand: whose word of any of us shall stand, whether the word of God or the word of the Jews.

When the king of Babylon attacks Egypt and kills many of the Egyptians and with them the Jews, it will be shown whose word is true: the word of God, who carried out His word and punished them by killing most of them, so that only a few escaped and returned to their land, or the word of His rebellious people, who think they are under the protection of the gods of heaven and enjoy the protection and good things of Egypt. That is, events will prove that the word of God is the true one and not the word of the rebellious idol worshipers.

entries.section: (4) The confirmation of the divine punishment

paragraphs.text: God gave a sign of the fulfillment of His word, which is the death of most of His people who came to Egypt, that Pharaoh of Egypt, whose name is Hophra, would die at the hand of the king of Babylon. This indeed happened, for this Hophra is of the twenty-sixth dynasty, being its fourth king, and he died in 546 BC. This is a clear sign that the king of Babylon, who seized Zedekiah king of Judah, would kill Hophra king of Egypt. The consolation of Baruch

God declares His punishment and chastening of Jerusalem and Judea because of their evils, in order to call everyone to repentance, so that He pulls down His people whom He had formed, and drives them out and plucks them up from the Promised Land in which He had planted them.

It seems that Baruch hoped to obtain a position in the state, because his brother Seraiah became chief of the camp in the days of Zedekiah (ch. 51:59). So God forbids him to be attached to positions and the high demands of the world, because all of them are passing; Jerusalem and all the surrounding countries will be destroyed and many will die. But God’s love for Baruch shows in that He delivers him from evil, so that no harm touches him.

Do not be attached to the passing things of this world, but care for the salvation of your soul, so that you are not defiled by its evils and may reach the Kingdom. If you fall, rise quickly; and if you obtain material things, thank God the Giver and use them for His glory.
The chastening of Egypt

From this chapter begin the prophecies about the nations, to the end of the book. It is concerned with the chastening of the nations, because God is the Creator of all peoples and desires their salvation. If He chastens them severely, it is so that they may repent, and then He blesses them with a great blessing, like Egypt, which He chastened with one defeat after another, with poverty and humiliation until it repented, and then gave it a blessing, so that it became a strong Church of God until now.

Pharaoh Necho: the second king of the twenty-sixth dynasty, representing the end of the strong kings in Egypt; he reigned from 609 to 583 BC. Carchemish: its meaning is the fortress of Chemosh, the chief god of Moab, and it lies on the river Euphrates, in the chariot. The first prophecy mentioned in this chapter is about the defeat of Pharaoh Necho king of Egypt at the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon in the battle of Carchemish, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah, that is, in 605 BC.

Although Necho had held Carchemish for 4 years and had fortified it and taken all the lands before it in Syria, he was defeated at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar and all his authority over this region was lost. So do not be proud, however great your strength, and know that every strength you have is a grace from God; thank Him for it and use it faithfully for His glory.
[2] The fall of proud Egypt (vv. 3-12)

3- Order ye the buckler and shield, and draw near to battle. 4- Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with your helmets; furbish the spears, and put on the brigandines. 5- Wherefore have I seen them dismayed and turned away back? and their mighty ones are beaten down, and are fled apace, and look not back: for fear was round about, saith the LORD. 6- Let not the swift flee away, nor the mighty man escape; they shall stumble, and fall toward the north by the river Euphrates. 7- Who is this that cometh up as a flood, whose waters are moved as the rivers? 8- Egypt riseth up like a flood, and his waters are moved like the rivers; and he saith, I will go up, and will cover the earth; I will destroy the city and the inhabitants thereof. 9- Come up, ye horses; and rage, ye chariots; and let the mighty men come forth; the Ethiopians and the Libyans, that handle the shield; and the Lydians, that handle and bend the bow. 10- For this is the day of the Lord GOD of hosts, a day of vengeance, that he may avenge him of his adversaries: and the sword shall devour, and it shall be satiate and made drunk with their blood: for the Lord GOD of hosts hath a sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates. 11- Go up into Gilead, and take balm, O virgin, the daughter of Egypt: in vain shalt thou use many medicines; for thou shalt not be cured. 12- The nations have heard of thy shame, and thy cry hath filled the land: for the mighty man hath stumbled against the mighty, and they are fallen both together.
Buckler: a weapon of war for defense, like the shield.
Shield: a wooden disc with a handle, which the soldier wears on his arm and moves before him to protect himself from arrows.
The commanders of the Egyptian army call their soldiers to prepare their weapons and advance to fight the army of Babylon in the battle of Carchemish.
Harness the horses: put the saddle on the backs of the horses. The saddle is the seat on which the horseman sits on the back of the horse.
Helmets: a helmet is a metal covering placed on the soldier’s head to protect him from blows. Furbish: clean them so that they become sharp and pointed and strike the enemies.
Brigandines (coats of mail): what the soldier wears on his chest, down to above his knees, made of metal to protect him from blows.
God continues His call to their soldiers to prepare the instruments of war and put them on to enter the battle with the Babylonians.

Turned away back: hastening in flight backward in great sorrow. Jeremiah sees, by the spirit of prophecy, the soldiers of Egypt fleeing before the might of the Babylonian army, in great fear, hastening to save their lives.

Flee away: escape. Jeremiah also sees that the soldiers distinguished by lightness and speed cannot escape from the face of the army of Babylon. Likewise the strong Egyptian mighty men fall slain, and so the Egyptian army was defeated in the north, that is, at Carchemish on the river Euphrates.
Its waters: its waters and its waves.
The Egyptian army was confident of its strength, like the river Nile full of life, and the army was sure that it would triumph over Babylon.

Ethiopians (Cush): Abyssinia. Libyans (Put): a region in Libya or Somalia. Lydians (Lud): the rest of the inhabitants of Libya. The Egyptian army was relying on mercenaries from neighboring countries such as Libya and Africa, and also Abyssinia, and these mercenaries were trained in shooting arrows with the bow. So the Egyptian army advanced with confidence that it would win because of its great strength.

The day of the battle of Carchemish was the day of the Lord’s vengeance on proud Egypt, which had humiliated His people in the days of Moses and troubled them in later ages. God uses Babylon as an instrument to chasten Egypt, for God is the Avenger, to humble the Egyptians so that perhaps they would repent and return to Him and not rely on their pagan gods. In this battle many of the Egyptians were killed and their blood flowed.

Gilead: a region lying east of the river Jordan, which the children of Israel seized and settled in. Balm: a plant consisting of tall smooth trees with small leaves; from the trunk of the tree comes a liquid used for treating many diseases, and it grew in Gilead and Abyssinia. Medicines: drugs. Cure (bandage): a piece of cloth wrapped on wounds, like what we call gauze today. The phrase “thou shalt not be cured” means there is no remedy for you.

He likens Egypt to a weak woman, borrowing for her the name “virgin”, that is, a weak young girl, whom the armies of Babylon have struck, and who seeks medicines to treat her wounds, but in vain, because she has been shattered before Babylon.

He declares the defeat of Egypt, which began to cry out at the horror of the defeat at Carchemish, and the surrounding nations heard of it; for although Egypt was strong like a mighty man, Babylon was stronger than it, and struck it like a mighty man and shattered it.

If you have met troubles and pains, do not look for your remedy in the world, for your only remedy is knowing Christ and living with Him. He is the One who heals you of all your pains of soul and body and restores your spiritual strength.
[3] The attack of Babylon on Egypt (vv. 13-17:)

13- The word that the LORD spake to Jeremiah the prophet, how Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon should come and smite the land of Egypt. 14- Declare ye in Egypt, and publish in Migdol, and publish in Noph and in Tahpanhes: say ye, Stand fast, and prepare thee; for the sword shall devour round about thee. 15- Why are thy valiant men swept away? they stood not, because the LORD did drive them. 16- He made many to fall, yea, one fell upon another: and they said, Arise, and let us go again to our own people, and to the land of our nativity, from the oppressing sword. 17- They did cry there, Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise; he hath passed the time appointed.

After Babylon’s victory over Egypt in the battle of Carchemish in 605 BC, the armies of Babylon moved and besieged Jerusalem. The armies of Egypt advanced to help Jerusalem, and the Babylonian army withdrew by military wisdom, in 588 BC, and the armies of Egypt returned to Egypt. Then the armies of Babylon moved to attack Egypt, about 17 years after their victory over them at Carchemish, and destroyed the power of Egypt, then returned to besiege Jerusalem, and took it and struck it in 587 BC.
Jeremiah, by the spirit of prophecy, calls to Egypt with its various places that were spoken of before in (ch. 44:1), to prepare for the Babylonian attack coming upon it.

The mighty men and giants of the Egyptian army fell slain before the Babylonian army, and Jeremiah makes clear that this was by God’s permission to chasten them for their pride, that perhaps they would repent, as is shown by his saying, “because the LORD did drive them”.

Likewise the mercenary soldiers whom Egypt had added to its army from the countries of Africa, when they saw Egypt’s weakness for the second time before Babylon, which attacked Egypt in its own land, and some of them fell slain with the Egyptian soldiers before Babylon, said, “Arise, and let us go again to our own people”, to save themselves, because Egypt had become weak and the dominant power in the world had become Babylon.

The mercenary soldiers, and the Egyptians also, cried out that Pharaoh the king was exposed to destruction, and that the time had passed in which Egypt was the great power of the world before Assyria and Babylon.

In another translation, such as the Jesuit, the word “destroyed” is translated “uproar”, that is, “noise”, and the meaning is that they cried to Pharaoh that Egypt had been filled with uproar because of the Babylonian attack, and that Egypt’s dignity was lost and weakened.

Do not rely on your strength in facing the world, for you are a man, and however great your strength, it is liable to change. But rely on God, who does not change, so you will not fear the power of the world, and keep your peace even if troubles pass over you, so that you are reassured at all times.
[4] The destruction of Egypt by Babylon (vv. 18-26)
18- As I live, saith the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts, Surely as Tabor is among the mountains, and as Carmel by the sea, so shall he come.
19- O thou daughter dwelling in Egypt, furnish thyself to go into captivity: for Noph shall be waste and desolate without an inhabitant.

20- Egypt is like a very fair heifer, but destruction cometh; it cometh out of the north. 21- Also her hired men are in the midst of her like fatted bullocks; for they also are turned back, and are fled away together: they did not stand, because the day of their calamity was come upon them, and the time of their visitation.
22- The voice thereof shall go like a serpent; for they shall march with an army, and come against her with axes, as hewers of wood.
32- They shall cut down her forest, saith the LORD, though it cannot be searched; because they are more than the grasshoppers, and are innumerable.

24- The daughter of Egypt shall be confounded; she shall be delivered into the hand of the people of the north. 25- The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, saith; Behold, I will punish the multitude of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with their gods, and their kings; even Pharaoh, and all them that trust in him: 26- And I will deliver them into the hand of those that seek their lives, and into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of his servants: and afterward it shall be inhabited, as in the days of old, saith the LORD.
Tabor: a high mountain, 1,800 feet in height, lying beside the Valley of Jezreel in the north of the land of the Jews.
Carmel: also a high mountain, 1,700 feet in height, lying in the north of Lebanon, close to the Mediterranean Sea.
He likens Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to a high mountain like Mount Tabor or Mount Carmel, which lie in the north of Palestine, so Nebuchadnezzar moves and comes to attack Egypt.

Furnish thyself to go into captivity: preparing to travel and leave the place, so that a person gathers his necessary belongings. He likens Egypt to a girl of weak strength and calls her to prepare to flee from Nebuchadnezzar. She had been dwelling in security, but Babylon’s attack on her makes her flee before it. Noph, which was at one time considered a capital of Egypt and lies in the region north of Giza and Helwan, that is, south of Cairo, becomes waste from the Babylonian attack, and its inhabitants leave it.

He also likens Egypt to a heifer fair to look at, which Nebuchadnezzar devours, slaughters and eats, because she worshiped the calf Apis, so the king of Babylon crushed her, that perhaps she would repent and believe in the true God. Nebuchadnezzar came from the north and attacked Egypt.

Fatted: fat. Egypt hired mercenary soldiers from Africa to strengthen its army, but when they saw its weakness and that they would be slaughtered like fatted calves with the Egyptian army defeated before Babylon, they fled to their countries to save themselves. Thus Egypt became weak before the nations of the world, because it was proud and did not know God, the Creator of heaven and earth.

He likens the Egyptian army to the serpent, whose voice, the hissing, is a very weak sound before the cry of the strong Babylonian army. And as the head of the serpent is cut off with an axe, Jeremiah likens the power of the armies of Babylon to men cutting wood with their axes, so that they break the power of Egypt.

He likens the multitude of the Babylonian army to locusts in their number, attacking Egypt, which is likened to a forest, that is, a deserted place with many trees, and the king of Babylon cuts them down and overcomes all these trees because of the multitude of his numbers.
By the defeat of Egypt before Babylon, which came from the north, shame and disgrace came upon it.

Amon of No: the city of Amon, that is, Thebes, the capital of Egypt, which is the city of Luxor. God declares that He will punish the pride of the Egyptians and their many gods, the greatest of which is Amon, whose center is in Thebes, so He will destroy it and lay waste the cities of Egypt and shatter their gods at the hand of the king of Babylon. For God is the mover of the affairs of the world, to call Egypt to humility and to return to Him.

After Nebuchadnezzar shatters Egypt, it is inhabited again, but with a better building than material building, which is the entry of the faith at the hand of St. Mark, so that Egypt becomes Christian and leaves the worship of idols.

If troubles and the ruin of your material life lead to the firmness of your faith, accept it, for it is the way of salvation for you, because God loves you and plucks you out of the evils of the world so that you may live to Him.
[5] The salvation of Israel (vv. 27, 28:)

27- But fear not thou, O my servant Jacob, and be not dismayed, O Israel: for, behold, I will save thee from afar off, and thy seed from the land of their captivity; and Jacob shall return, and be in rest and at ease, and none shall make him afraid. 28- Fear thou not, O Jacob my servant, saith the LORD: for I am with thee; for I will make a full end of all the nations whither I have driven thee: but I will not make a full end of thee, but correct thee in measure; yet will not leave thee wholly unpunished.

As God chastens Egypt, which humiliated His people for long years, He gives good news to His people, whom Babylon took captive, that they will return from captivity, so they should not fear the might of Babylon or Assyria. As Egypt and Assyria were shattered, Babylon and the empires after it will be shattered; indeed God uses the kings of Media and Persia, who shatter Babylon, to bring back His people to rebuild Jerusalem and Judea. This is a symbol of the return to God and faith in Christ in the fullness of time.

If God may destroy the great empires that humiliated His people, He promises to preserve them; and if He will chasten them for their sins so that they repent, He then returns and has mercy on them when they believe in Christ and live with Him forever.

God’s promises are beautiful and strengthen the soul however much hardships surround it, and even His chastenings of His children are in small measure so that they repent, and then He gives them many mercies. So let your heart be reassured, my brother, and remember His promises, and do not fear any troubles.
The devastation of Palestine and its allies

entries.section: (1) The striking of Palestine by Egypt and Babylon

paragraphs.text: The book sets the time of this prophecy as before Pharaoh Necho’s striking of Gaza. This time is not known exactly, but it is in the late seventh century and the beginning of the sixth century BC. This king of Egypt may have struck it on his way to Carchemish on the river Euphrates, or on his return from it after his defeat at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, or on his return from the attempt to rescue Jerusalem when the king of Babylon struck it in 587 BC. This Palestine entered into wars with the people of God in the days of Samson, in the days of Samuel and in the days of David the prophet, so it bore enmity toward the children of Israel. God, who was patient with it for many years, now allows its chastening and destruction, so that its people may be humbled, turn away from their violence and believe in God. This indeed happened, for many of them believed in Christ.
The striking of Gaza is the striking of a famous Philistine city, and what is meant by it is the striking of Gaza itself, or the beginning of the striking of all the cities of Palestine.

entries.section: (1) The striking of Palestine by Egypt and Babylon

paragraphs.text: The prophecy is about Babylon’s attack on Palestine. He likens Babylon to a sweeping flood of water coming from the north, because they have the great river Euphrates; it comes upon the land of Palestine and destroys it with all that is in it and kills those who dwell in it, and the Philistines cry out with bitter weeping at the horror of the destruction.

entries.section: (1) The striking of Palestine by Egypt and Babylon

paragraphs.text: Rushing and rumbling (noise of the stamping and rattling): the sound of the iron of the chariots rubbing against each other, and the sound of the chariot wheels scraping the ground. Feebleness of hands (slack hands): great weakness and fear. Babylon attacks with its horsemen and war chariots and kills and destroys the cities of Palestine, and the Philistines flee in great panic, so that in their weakness they leave their children behind them.

Do not be harsh in your dealings with those around you, relying on your strength, for it is liable to pass away. Know that God is just and able to chasten you severely, but He is longsuffering toward you, that perhaps you may repent and have mercy on those around you and forgive them their faults.
[2] The destruction of the allies (v. 4:)

4- Because of the day that cometh to spoil all the Philistines, and to cut off from Tyrus and Zidon every helper that remaineth: for the LORD will spoil the Philistines, the remnant of the country of Caphtor.

The day that cometh: the day of Babylon’s attack on Palestine and its allies. Tyre: a city in Lebanon lying on the Mediterranean Sea, an important commercial port. The meaning of the word Tyre is “rock”, because it is built on rocks.
Sidon: a city in Lebanon lying on the Mediterranean Sea, south of Tyre. The meaning of the word is “a place of fishing”, because it is famous for fishing.
Caphtor: the island of Crete.

In Babylon’s attack on the Philistines to lay waste their land, they also attacked their allies Tyre and Sidon, and also the island of Crete, from which the Philistines came to the land named after them. With the destruction of the allies, the Philistines find no help against the Babylonian attack.
Let your reliance be on God and not on the powers of the world, for they are passing and weak however strong they appear. Take refuge in God by prayer in all your needs.
[3] The pagan gods do not benefit Palestine (vv. 5-7:)

5- Baldness is come upon Gaza; Ashkelon is cut off with the remnant of their valley: how long wilt thou cut thyself? 6- O thou sword of the LORD, how long will it be ere thou be quiet? put up thyself into thy scabbard, rest, and be still. 7- How can it be quiet, seeing the LORD hath given it a charge against Ashkelon, and against the sea shore? there hath he appointed it.

entries.section: (1) The striking of Palestine by Egypt and Babylon

paragraphs.text: Cut thyself: you wound your body. Their valley: the valleys surrounding the cities. He likens Gaza to a girl on whose head baldness has come, so that she lost her hair; what is meant is that she lost her standing and became weak like a girl in her bodily weakness, and the strong cities of Palestine such as Ashkelon were destroyed. Palestine tried to seek help from its pagan gods and to cut its body to please them, but in vain, for its gods did not help it against the Babylonian attack.

entries.section: (1) The striking of Palestine by Egypt and Babylon

paragraphs.text: Scabbard: the sheath in which the sword is placed. He calls Babylon the sword of the LORD, which chastens the Philistines, and the prophet sees the cruelty of the destruction or killing that Babylon carries out on Palestine, so the prophet is moved and calls on the LORD to stop this destruction or killing.

entries.section: (1) The striking of Palestine by Egypt and Babylon

paragraphs.text: God answers in the prophecy that the sword will continue to kill, because God has commanded it so, as a chastening of the Philistines for their violence.

Since the world is changeable and you can lose your strength at any time, be detached from material things and use them in measure, for asceticism is beautiful against the violence of changes. Be satisfied with the love of God, and you will live happily and prepare your soul for eternity.
Prophecies about Moab

God declares the ruin of Moab, which lies east of the river Jordan, north of the children of Ammon. He mentions its famous cities as a symbol of all Moab. The city of Nebo lies beside Mount Abarim, east of the Jordan opposite Jericho, and beside it are the cities of Kiriathaim and Misgab.
Babylon’s attack on Moab destroys their capital Heshbon, and the sword of Babylon kills the people of Moab in the Moabite city of Madmen.
As a result of the destruction of the Moabite city of Horonaim and the killing of many, the rest of the Moabites cry out at what has happened to them.
As a result of the ruin of Moab, its little ones cry out in fear and terror at what is happening to them.

Here he also mentions two Moabite cities, the ascent of Luhith and Horonaim, which lies in a valley beside it. From these cities bitter weeping is heard, for the sorrow of their peoples over the ruin of their land. Because of the corruption of Moab and the spread of evil lusts in it, ruin came upon it at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, and that was in 582 BC. The Moabites are the descendants of Lot, that is, relatives of the children of Israel, and had a relationship with the people of God in the days of the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Then after the children of Israel settled in the Promised Land, there were disputes and wars between them until David subdued the Moabites. Then Moab was destroyed by Assyria, and when it afterward tried to regain its strength, it was destroyed by the Moabites of whom Jeremiah speaks here; then it submitted afterward to Persian rule and after that to the Arabs.
Do not go on and on in your lusts, lest divine justice come upon you and your end be destruction, but sanctify your senses and your thoughts to be for God, and you will live in reassurance.
[2] The flight of Moab (vv. 6-10:)

6- Flee, save your lives, and be like the heath in the wilderness. 7- For because thou hast trusted in thy works and in thy treasures, thou shalt also be taken: and Chemosh shall go forth into captivity with his priests and his princes together. 8- And the spoiler shall come upon every city, and no city shall escape: the valley also shall perish, and the plain shall be destroyed, as the LORD hath spoken. 9- Give wings unto Moab, that it may flee and get away: for the cities thereof shall be desolate, without any to dwell therein. 10- Cursed be he that doeth the work of the LORD deceitfully, and cursed be he that keepeth back his sword from blood.

Heath: a shrub that grows in the desert, with small leaves, which goats eat; it is a symbol of the man who trusts in men, for he loses his strength as the heath loses its leaves when animals eat them. Jeremiah calls the Moabites to flee from the Babylonian attack, and when they reach the desert the Babylonians neglect them, but they are in distress, isolation and weakness like the heath plant.
Chemosh: the god of the Moabites, to whom human sacrifices of children were offered. Solomon introduced his worship into Jerusalem, and King Josiah afterward removed it.

He rebukes the cities of Moab, which trusted in their strength and their circumstances, for their shame will appear when the Babylonians destroy them and drive out their inhabitants, who go out carrying the images of their god Chemosh in weakness and shame, and thus the priests of Chemosh and the princes of Moab are humbled when Babylon takes them captive.
The valley: a vale. Babylon destroys all the cities of Moab, whether those on the heights or in the valleys, because God is the One who commanded this as a chastening of Moab.
Jeremiah expresses the Moabites’ fear of Babylon, for they need speed in running, as a bird flies, because the Babylonian attack will be violent and kill everyone it meets.

God calls the army of Babylon to kill the Moabites and do the work of the LORD, that is, the destruction of Moab, with all zeal and energy, so that the Babylonians do not slacken in killing the Moabites by the sword. The destruction of Moab is considered the work of the LORD, because they provoked Him with their evil lusts, so He chastens them by the hand of Babylon.

All your works, especially if they are service to those around you and care for the salvation of their souls, are the work of the LORD. May you do it with care, because it is the work of the LORD, and offer it to Him before offering it to people. And as Christ cared for the salvation of your soul and accomplished it with all seriousness, so that He died for you, do His work with all energy, however great the sacrifice.
[3] The weakness of Moab (vv. 11-13:)

11- Moab hath been at ease from his youth, and he hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither hath he gone into captivity: therefore his taste remained in him, and his scent is not changed. 12- Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will send unto him wanderers, that shall cause him to wander, and shall empty his vessels, and break their bottles. 13- And Moab shall be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel their confidence.
Lees: the remains of fermented grapes, that is, the sediment found at the bottom of wine bottles.
Settled on his lees: this means that Moab is at ease like the wine sediment that does not move at the bottom of the bottles, because no one dares to stir it, that is, to attack Moab.
Not emptied from vessel to vessel: the Moabites were not moved from place to place, that is, from their land to another land in captivity.

He explains the state of the Moabites, who were living in reassurance inside their land, and likens them to the sediment at the bottom of the wine vessel. No one took them captive except a small number in the days of the Assyrian attack, until the Babylonian attack came and took most of the Moabites captive. That is, Moab lived in peace and ease like wine whose scent is in it and whose taste has not changed, until Babylon attacked it and turned it into a bad state; the bad vessel from which all its goods were poured out was then broken, that is, its goods were taken away and it was shattered.

Wanderers that shall cause him to wander (pourers who pour him out): workers, that is, smiths who shape it, and what is meant is that they turn it into a bad vessel. Jeremiah warns Moab that days will come, the days of the Babylonian attack, when they will drive the Moabites from their land and destroy their cities. He likens the cities of Moab to wine vessels, which Babylon overturns, and the wine is spilled and they stir the sediment at the bottom, then break the vessels, that is, destroy the cities. In sum, Babylon will take away Moab’s peace, drive out its inhabitants and destroy its cities.

Moab feels its weakness, and the weakness of its god Chemosh, before Babylon, and is ashamed as the kingdom of Israel was ashamed, that is, the northern kingdom whose capital was Samaria, when it trusted in the images that King Jeroboam set up in Bethel when he separated with the ten tribes from the kingdom of Judah and Jerusalem. The weakness of these images appeared, for they did not protect the people from the Assyrian attack and captivity.

Trust in God in all your works, for He is able to protect you, and do not trust in your money and your abilities, lest your weakness and shame appear. Use these capacities for God’s sake and with His help, and they will be beneficial to you. [4] The shame of Moab (vv. 14-25:)

14- How say ye, We are mighty and strong men for the war? 15- Moab is spoiled, and gone up out of her cities, and his chosen young men are gone down to the slaughter, saith the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts. 16- The calamity of Moab is near to come, and his affliction hasteth fast. 17- All ye that are about him, bemoan him; and all ye that know his name, say, How is the strong staff broken, and the beautiful rod! 18- Thou daughter that dost inhabit Dibon, come down from thy glory, and sit in thirst; for the spoiler of Moab shall come upon thee, and he shall destroy thy strong holds. 19- O inhabitant of Aroer, stand by the way, and espy; ask him that fleeth, and her that escapeth, and say, What is done? 20- Moab is confounded; for it is broken down: howl and cry; tell ye it in Arnon, that Moab is spoiled, 21- And judgment is come upon the plain country; upon Holon, and upon Jahazah, and upon Mephaath, 22- And upon Dibon, and upon Nebo, and upon Beth-diblathaim, 23- And upon Kiriathaim, and upon Beth-gamul, and upon Beth-meon, 24- And upon Kerioth, and upon Bozrah, and upon all the cities of the land of Moab, far or near.
25- The horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm is broken, saith the LORD.

Jeremiah marvels at the boasting of the men of Moab in their strength in war, when they have been crushed before the Babylonian attack. This is what he sees by the spirit of prophecy: its people fled from their cities in the plains and went up to the mountains to hide in them, but the sword of Babylon reached them and brought them down slain to the ground. This is the chastening and command of God concerning Moab. In God is all power, so He is called the LORD of hosts, who shatters every evil power on earth that stands in His face, as Moab did.
He also declares that the destruction of Moab is very near, so Jeremiah’s prophecy will be fulfilled quickly by Babylon’s attack on Moab.

Bemoan him: speak words of lament in which you show its virtues, and weep over it. God calls the cities and nations around Moab to grieve over it, for despite its former greatness it has now been shattered by Babylon. He likens its strength to the golden staff that the king holds, or the rod of authority; that is, it will lose its glory and greatness among the nations and be in great shame before Babylon.
Thirst: dry, thirsty land. Dibon: the Moabite city in which stands the god Chemosh, the god of the Moabites; it lies north of the river Arnon, that is, east of the Dead Sea.

He declares to Moab that it will come down from its glory and be in hunger and thirst that lead it to death, and its god Chemosh, whom they have set in the city of Dibon, will not profit it, because the army of Babylon, the destroyer of Moab, has attacked its cities and gone up on its walls and fortresses and demolished them.
Aroer: a Moabite city north of the river Arnon, which lies east of the Dead Sea; it is 12 miles from the Dead Sea and south-east of Dibon.

He shows how amazed the Moabites were at the speed of the Babylonian attack on them. He calls the inhabitants of the city of Aroer to go out onto the roads leading to the rest of the cities of Moab, so that they see people running in flight and ask then what is the reason for their flight, and learn that it is the violent Babylonian attack.

Then he calls the Moabites to tell all the cities around the river Arnon, which lies inside the land of Moab, and let them know of the Babylonian attack, so that they flee far away. Thus weeping and fear cover the people of Moab, and they are scattered in flight everywhere.

He shows the sweeping of the Babylonian attack over all Moab, and here mentions the most famous cities of Moab that were ruined, to show Babylon’s reaching all the cities of Moab, far and near, and shattering them.
Cut off: broken.

The sum is the shattering of Moab’s power before Babylon, which is symbolized by the horn that is broken and the arm that is shattered; the horn and the arm are the strength with which an animal or a man defends or attacks in war.

Consider the situations in which you trusted in your strength and the troubles that befell you, so that you take refuge in God and rely on Him, and neither Satan nor all the powers of the world will prevail against you.
[5] The pride of Moab (vv. 26-32:)
26- Make ye him drunken: for he magnified himself against the LORD: Moab also shall wallow in his vomit, and he also shall be in derision.

27- For was not Israel a derision unto thee? was he found among thieves? for since thou spakest of him, thou skippedst for joy. 28- O ye that dwell in Moab, leave the cities, and dwell in the rock, and be like the dove that maketh her nest in the sides of the hole’s mouth. 29- We have heard the pride of Moab, (he is exceeding proud) his loftiness, and his arrogancy, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart. 30- I know his wrath, saith the LORD; but it shall not be so; his lies shall not so effect it. 31- Therefore will I howl for Moab, and I will cry out for all Moab; mine heart shall mourn for the men of Kir-heres. 32- O vine of Sibmah, I will weep for thee with the weeping of Jazer: thy plants are gone over the sea, they reach even to the sea of Jazer: the spoiler is fallen upon thy summer fruits and upon thy vintage.

He shows the lowliness of Moab before the Babylonian attack, so that it becomes like a drunkard who staggers and has lost his balance and his greatness. He asks the army of Babylon to make him drink the wine, that is, to make him stagger from fear as the drunkard staggers, and from his great drunkenness he vomits what is inside him, so his humiliation increases as he wallows in the vomit he has thrown up, and all the surrounding peoples mock him. All this is because of his pride and his magnifying himself against God and against His people Israel, for Moab used to mock the people of God when distress came upon them or enemies attacked them.

Skippedst (you shook the head): you shake your head in mockery and contempt. God rebukes Moab in its shame and declares to it that the cause of this shame is its mocking of the people of God and despising them as though they were wicked thieves, so it used to speak of them with mockery and move its head in contempt of them in their troubles.

Leave: vacate, flee and abandon the cities. He calls the Moabites to flee from their cities to the mountains and hide among the rocks, that perhaps they may escape from the hand of Babylon, and likens them to a weak dove that cannot nest safely among the branches of trees but flees to make itself a nest among the rocks in the mountains.
Here he affirms that all the surrounding peoples know Moab’s great pride, and because of it this shame came upon it before Babylon.

God declares that the wrath of Moab, which used to terrify those around it, is nothing, and its weakness and shame have appeared before Babylon. And all the words of pride that Moab kept repeating are lies, as proved by the shame it received before Babylon.
Kir-heres: a Moabite city lying east of the Dead Sea and its southern part.

The fatherhood of Jeremiah appears in his weeping over Moab, for he is like his God, who wants the salvation of all and not only of the people of God. He is deeply moved, so he weeps and howls and then cries out with a loud voice because of the ruin of Moab, and within himself he also groans, pained for its sake. He mentions here one of the cities of Moab as a symbol of all the cities of Moab.
Jazer: a Moabite city lying north of Moab, ten miles west of Rabbah of Ammon.
Sibmah: a Moabite city beside the city of Heshbon, the capital of the Moabites, in the north of the land of Moab; Sibmah was famous for its vineyards.
Vine: a grapevine.
Summer fruits: the fruits gathered from the harvest.

Jeremiah continues his feelings of fatherhood toward Moab and weeps over its land, famous for its wealth, such as Jazer and Sibmah, for all its good things, from the clusters of grapes with their branches and the various fruits, were seized by the Babylonians and carried over the sea, that is, the rivers, so that they might enjoy them, after they had destroyed the land of Moab and left its inhabitants who remained after the killing in great poverty.

Your pride separates you from God, so you are deprived of His mercies and Satan attacks you, and thus you find no one to help you. Therefore humble yourself quickly and offer repentance before God, and He will forgive you and save you from the enemy.
[6] The humiliation and poverty of Moab (vv. 33-39:)

33- And joy and gladness is taken from the plentiful field, and from the land of Moab; and I have caused wine to fail from the winepresses: none shall tread with shouting; their shouting shall be no shouting. 34- From the cry of Heshbon even unto Elealeh, and even unto Jahaz, have they uttered their voice, from Zoar even unto Horonaim, as an heifer of three years old: for the waters also of Nimrim shall be desolate. 35- Moreover I will cause to cease in Moab, saith the LORD, him that offereth in the high places, and him that burneth incense to his gods. 36- Therefore mine heart shall sound for Moab like pipes, and mine heart shall sound like pipes for the men of Kir-heres: because the riches that he hath gotten are perished. 37- For every head shall be bald, and every beard clipped: upon all the hands shall be cuttings, and upon the loins sackcloth. 38- There shall be lamentation generally upon all the housetops of Moab, and in the streets thereof: for I have broken Moab like a vessel wherein is no pleasure, saith the LORD. 39- They shall howl, saying, How is it broken down! how hath Moab turned the back with shame! so shall Moab be a derision and a dismaying to all them about him.

Shouting (uproar): noise and clamor. Since the Babylonians seized the good things of Moab and its gardens full of fruitful trees, the Moabites were in great sorrow, for they no longer had vineyards, and the enemies also demolished the winepresses. Instead of hearing in Moab the shout of joy at gathering the harvests, pressing the vines and drawing out the wine, the noise of weeping will be heard, especially since the men who tread the grapes in the winepresses have died at the hand of Babylon.
Heshbon: the capital of Moab, lying in its north.
Elealeh: a Moabite city lying on a hill north of Heshbon.
Jahaz: a Moabite city lying east of the Dead Sea.
Zoar: beside Sodom and Gomorrah, and it was not burned with them because Lot took refuge in it; it lies south-east of the Dead Sea.
Horonaim: a Moabite city lying in a plain beside Zoar. The waters of Nimrim: many springs lying south-east of the Dead Sea.
Heifer of three years old: a heifer three years of age.

Weeping and sorrow filled the Moabites, as cries of distress rose from the various places of Moab, from the capital of Moab, Heshbon, and from all the land, however rich in its good things, for the enemy had plundered all these good things.

The Moabites lost their hope in their gods, since they did not help them in Babylon’s attack on them, so they abandoned the worship of idols in despair of them, but they did not return to God. Thus no incense was offered in the temples of the idols, and no worship on the high places to the pagan gods.
Jeremiah expresses his sorrow over the cities of Moab, such as Kir-heres, by sounding like a sad pipe for them because they have lost their riches.

The sorrow of Moab appears in the shaving of the men’s hair; those who shaved used to do this to captives. They also shave their beards, which symbolize dignity, that is, the Moabites become humbled and abased.

Weeping and sorrow filled the houses of the Moabites, where they went up and wept on their roofs; instead of offering pagan worship on the roofs, they offered weeping and humiliation, and the streets were filled with weepers. For God had broken Moab by means of Babylon, and He likens Moab to an old vessel unfit for use, which its owner breaks.

The pride of Moab turned into weakness and lowliness. They fled before Babylon and gave it their backs, and Moab became an example of mockery before those around it, and also of terror and fear, for how was the mighty one shattered, so that all the cities feared Babylon’s violence against them if it attacked them.

When troubles press on you, do not give way to despair, but take refuge in God, rejecting everything you relied on, and you will experience the power of God in your life, and He will rescue you from your troubles.
[7] Babylon’s invasion of Moab (vv. 40-47)

40- For thus saith the LORD; Behold, he shall fly as an eagle, and shall spread his wings over Moab. 41- Kerioth is taken, and the strong holds are surprised, and the mighty men’s hearts in Moab at that day shall be as the heart of a woman in her pangs.

42- And Moab shall be destroyed from being a people, because he hath magnified himself against the LORD. 43- Fear, and the pit, and the snare, shall be upon thee, O inhabitant of Moab, saith the LORD. 44- He that fleeth from the fear shall fall into the pit; and he that getteth up out of the pit shall be taken in the snare: for I will bring upon it, even upon Moab, the year of their visitation, saith the LORD. 45- They that fled stood under the shadow of Heshbon because of the force: but a fire shall come forth out of Heshbon, and a flame from the midst of Sihon, and shall devour the corner of Moab, and the crown of the head of the tumultuous ones. 46- Woe be unto thee, O Moab! the people of Chemosh perisheth: for thy sons are taken captives, and thy daughters captives. 47- Yet will I bring again the captivity of Moab in the latter days, saith the LORD. Thus far is the judgment of Moab.
He likens the army of Babylon, in its swift attack and its swooping on Moab, to the eagle that swoops swiftly from the sky on its prey.

A woman in her pangs: the woman at the hour of her childbirth. Kerioth: a fortified Moabite city lying south of the river Arnon. By Babylon’s attack they seized the fortified cities and all the land of Moab, and the strong Moabite soldiers were in great weakness, like the woman who writhes at the hour of her childbirth.
The reason for the destruction of Moab and the perishing of its people is its pride against God and His people, the children of Israel.

The Moabites are struck with great fear and die of fear, and whoever escapes death by fear falls, as he flees from Babylon, into pits found on the road and dies; and whoever is able to escape these pits falls into the snares that Babylon made for them to make them fall, and they perish also. This is because God commanded their punishment for the multitude of their evils at this time, that is, this year.
When the Moabites fled from the village of Moab, they took refuge in their capital Heshbon, and were surprised to find it burning at the hand of Babylon, so their escape was lost.
The sum is the perishing of the Moabite people who worship Chemosh, with their men and women, at the hand of Babylon.
What is meant by the bringing again of the captivity of Moab is not the establishment of a state for them, but the faith of the captive Moabites in Christ, so that they live a new life in the faith.

The devil, with his great power and the speed of his swooping on men, cannot do anything if he has no place in them. So beware, my brother, of sin, lest you fall into it, and if you fall, turn back from it by repentance, and the devil will fear you and keep away from you.
Prophecies about the children of Ammon, Edom, Damascus, the Arabs and Elam

The prophet Jeremiah marvels at the enmity of the children of Ammon toward the children of Israel. The tribe of Gad dwelt east of the river Jordan, where the kingdom of the children of Ammon lies, north of the kingdom of Moab. The children of Ammon were distinguished by enmity toward the people of God throughout the generations, from the days of the judges until near the birth of Christ. So Jeremiah grieves that the king of the children of Ammon advanced and seized some of the land of the tribe of Gad, that is, of the people of God. In some translations “Malcham” is written instead of “their king”, and Malcham is the god of the children of Ammon, to whom human sacrifices were offered; what is meant is that the people of the children of Ammon seize and dwell in the cities of the children of Israel.
Rabbah of the children of Ammon: the capital of the children of Ammon, which is now Amman, the capital of Jordan.

Because of the enmity of the children of Ammon toward the people of God, God chastens them by means of Babylon, so the noise of war is heard in their capital Rabbah. The army of Babylon makes Rabbah known as a heap, and they burn her daughters with fire, that is, they kill the inhabitants of Rabbah. What is meant by Israel’s inheriting those who were his heirs is Babylon’s seizing their cities; that is, God chastens the enemies of the people of God.
Ai: either a Moabite city or a word meaning destruction, and what is meant is the destruction of the cities of the children of Ammon.

Heshbon: the capital of Moab, which was mostly in the possession of Moab and sometimes in the possession of the children of Ammon. Jeremiah calls to it to weep over the city of Ai, which belonged to the children of Ammon. He also calls the women of the city of Rabbah, the capital of the children of Ammon, to cry out in sorrow over their slain, and asks them to put on coarse clothes such as sackcloth, as a sign of great grief; they used to wear it especially on the middle and below, that is, the loins. Then they utter words of lament, that is, wailing, for the ruin that came upon them, and they also run to and fro among the walls of the temples seeking the help of the gods, but there is no helper, because the Babylonian captivity has taken the king, the priests and the leaders, and the remaining people of the children of Ammon are in great humiliation.

Valleys: the valleys. The people of the children of Ammon boasted of their fertile plains, which gave good crops and many good things, so the prophet calls on them to cease their boasting, after the valleys were filled with the blood of their slain, because of their turning away from God, their worship of idols, and their reliance on their wealth and good things, which will be destroyed at the hand of Babylon.

When the army of Babylon attacks the inhabitants of the children of Ammon, it fills their hearts with fear and they flee, leaving their lands, and Babylon takes their men captive and moves them to other distant lands. In the end the land of the children of Ammon is emptied of its inhabitants and its people are scattered in many lands, and they are unable to return and gather again in their land.

(v. 6): Jeremiah gives them the good news that they will return from captivity. The book of Nehemiah tells us that Tobiah the Ammonite was a leader of the children of Ammon, and that was during the captivity of Media and Persia. This verse is also a prophecy of the return of the children of Ammon to the faith, that is, their faith as Gentiles in Christ, for Christ came for the sake of the Jews and the Gentiles.

Do not rely on your wealth and good things, for they are changeable, but rely on God, the Giver of these good things, and thank Him every day for His kindnesses. He gave them to you as proof of His love, so that your heart may cling to Him, to set out in prayers, meditations and service to Him.

7- Concerning Edom, thus saith the LORD of hosts; Is wisdom no more in Teman? is counsel perished from the prudent? is their wisdom vanished? 8- Flee ye, turn back, dwell deep, O inhabitants of Dedan; for I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him, the time that I will visit him. 9- If grapegatherers come to thee, would they not leave some gleaning grapes? if thieves by night, they will destroy till they have enough. 10- But I have made Esau bare, I have uncovered his secret places, and he shall not be able to hide himself: his seed is spoiled, and his brethren, and his neighbours, and he is not. 11- Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive; and let thy widows trust in me. 12- For thus saith the LORD; Behold, they whose judgment was not to drink of the cup have assuredly drunken; and art thou he that shall altogether go unpunished? thou shalt not go unpunished, but thou shalt surely drink of it. 13- For I have sworn by myself, saith the LORD, that Bozrah shall become a desolation, a reproach, a waste, and a curse; and all the cities thereof shall be perpetual wastes. 14- I have heard a rumour from the LORD, and an ambassador is sent unto the heathen, saying, Gather ye together, and come against her, and rise up to the battle. 15- For, lo, I will make thee small among the heathen, and despised among men.

16- Thy terribleness hath deceived thee, and the pride of thine heart, O thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, that holdest the height of the hill: though thou shouldest make thy nest as high as the eagle, I will bring thee down from thence, saith the LORD. 17- Also Edom shall be a desolation: every one that goeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss at all the plagues thereof. 18- As in the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighbour cities thereof, saith the LORD, no man shall abide there, neither shall a son of man dwell in it. 19- Behold, he shall come up like a lion from the swelling of Jordan against the habitation of the strong: but I will suddenly make him run away from her: and who is a chosen man, that I may appoint over her? for who is like me? and who will appoint me the time? and who is that shepherd that will stand before me? 20- Therefore hear the counsel of the LORD, that he hath taken against Edom; and his purposes, that he hath purposed against the inhabitants of Teman: Surely the least of the flock shall draw them out: surely he shall make their habitations desolate with them. 21- The earth is moved at the noise of their fall, at the cry the noise thereof was heard in the Red sea. 22- Behold, he shall come up and fly as the eagle, and spread his wings over Bozrah: and at that day shall the heart of the mighty men of Edom be as the heart of a woman in her pangs.

Edom: this is Esau, and the word Edom means red. He dwelt in the mountains of Seir, which lie south of Palestine, and its capital was Sela. It resisted the children of Israel greatly and sometimes submitted to them, and King Herod in the days of Christ was an Edomite.

Teman: its meaning is the south. It is one of the most important cities of the Edomites and was named after a grandson of Esau; it lies north-east of the land of Edom, and its people were distinguished by wisdom and the speaking of proverbs.
Jeremiah marvels at the fall of Teman and the land of Edom at the hand of the Babylonians, and asks where their wisdom is, which did not help them to defend themselves before Babylon.
Dedan: a son of Abraham by Keturah; he dwelt south-east of Edom and was subject to it, and his people were distinguished by trade.

Dwell deep: hide. He calls the land of Dedan, which was subject to Edom and neighboring it, to flee and look right and left as they flee for fear of the Babylonian enemies, and to hide as far as they can, because God’s wrath on Edom has come upon them also.
Gleaning grapes: the few fruits remaining on the cluster of grapes or on the branches of the tree.

The prophet is astonished at Babylon’s destruction of the land of the Edomites, because it is customary that the grapegatherers, when they gather the fruits, leave some berries or a few fruits, and thieves, when they steal, take what suffices them and leave the rest, but Babylon shattered Edom completely.

This is what happened to Edom at the hand of Babylon: complete destruction of his seed, his brethren and his neighbors, that is, all his inhabitants and those of the neighboring peoples on whom he relies. The enemy left nothing of the possessions of Edom without seizing and shattering it, so Edom was completely stripped, and nothing precious was left to him hidden or concealed.

God turns back and gives hope to Edom, that after the killing of its men He will call and preserve its orphan children and its widowed women. For God does not intend the destruction of the nations but their return to Him by faith and repentance when they hear Jeremiah’s prophecies about them, and also when some of them die and the rest believe.

What is meant by the cup is the cup of divine wrath, and those whose judgment was not to drink of the cup are the people of God. That is, if God has allowed His people to be chastened for their sins so that they repent, then all the more the wicked Edom, which worships idols and is proud, ought to drink the cup of God’s wrath, because the just God judges him and does not acquit him.
Bozrah: a main city in Edom, which was for some time its capital.

God declares the destruction of the most important city of Edom, Bozrah, so that whoever passes by it is astonished at its ruin after it was a great city; it becomes a proverb of reproach and curse, because it does not rise or get built again.
God shows what will happen to Edom, which is the gathering of the nations, that is, the armies of Babylon, against it to destroy it.
After Edom’s destruction it does not remain a strong people but becomes small and despised among the peoples.
The clefts of the rock: caves among the rocks, in which the Edomites used to dwell, fortified in the rocks, in hiding places where they felt that no one could reach them because of their strength.

The hill: the mound or plateau. He rebukes Edom for its pride and its terrifying the peoples around it, because it is strong and dwells above the mountains in fortified caves, and God says to it that if you liken yourself to the eagle, the strongest of the birds of prey, which cannot be reached, God by His power brings it down to the ground and destroys its land at the hand of Babylon.
Because of the destruction of Edom, which was a great country, everyone who passes by it marvels, and even hisses in mockery of it because of its ruin.
He likens the destruction of Edom to the ruin of Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighboring cities, that is, a total destruction, so that no man can dwell there but it becomes completely deserted.

The swelling of Jordan: the waters of the river Jordan when they overflow with force and pride. He likens the army of Babylon, in its attack on Edom, to the lion, the king of the beasts in his strength, and likens it also to the flood of the waters of the Jordan, which attacks Edom, which was fertile pastures. But God winks at it, that is, signals to it, so it turns back from Edom and does not kill everyone in it, so it runs away from it, that is, Babylon runs and moves away from Edom. Then God speaks with power, describing Himself as the shepherd who has full authority over all the earth, so He commands Babylon and it attacks Edom, and then He stops it and turns it back from it, because God is the Ruler of all.

God declares His judgment on the land of Edom, one of whose most famous cities is Teman, that it will become very weak after the Babylonian attack, so that flocks of weak sheep drag them away after the destruction of its cities.

He shows the extent of Edom’s calamity and the cry of its sorrowing people: from the violence of the Babylonian attack they will cry out so loudly that their voice is heard in the Red Sea, and so their cry reaches Egypt, and all the lands of the peoples around Edom tremble and shake because of its calamity.

He likens the army of Babylon to the strong eagle that spreads its wings over the land of Edom, that is, attacks it and destroys its cities, symbolized by Bozrah, its capital, and no strong man remains to defend Edom, but its mighty ones become weak and in pain like a woman when she gives birth.

If pride is the cause of many evils and brings God’s wrath, then humility is the shortest way to the heart of God. So declare your repentance before Him and plead with Him in reverence, and you will obtain mercies; your true humility appears when you humble yourself and bear with those around you.
[3] Concerning Damascus (vv. 23-27:)

23- Concerning Damascus. Hamath is confounded, and Arpad: for they have heard evil tidings: they are fainthearted; there is sorrow on the sea; it cannot be quiet. 24- Damascus is waxed feeble, and turneth herself to flee, and fear hath seized on her: anguish and sorrows have taken her, as a woman in travail. 25- How is the city of praise not left, the city of my joy! 26- Therefore her young men shall fall in her streets, and all the men of war shall be cut off in that day, saith the LORD of hosts. 27- And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall consume the palaces of Benhadad.

Damascus: the capital of the land of the Arameans, that is, Syria; it is an ancient and strong city. Hamath and Arpad: great Syrian lands that come after Damascus in Aram, which is Syria. When the land of the Arameans heard the news of the Babylonian attack, it was very afraid and fell into shame, because of its weakness before the power of the enemies, and was troubled like the raging sea.
Damascus and the lands around it were alarmed and became terrified before Babylon, in pain like a woman when she gives birth.
Damascus was distinguished by corruption and the pleasures of various lusts, but all this joy was lost by Babylon’s attack on it and the killing of its young men and all its men of war.
Benhadad: a title of the kings of Damascus.
The city of Damascus shelters behind its high walls, but when Babylon attacks it, its walls are burned, a sign of its ruin.

The pleasure of sin is temporary, but the pleasure of virtue is lasting. So hold fast to the love of God and delight in fellowship with Him, so that your peace and joy endure and the devil, the enemy, cannot shatter you.
[4] The Arabs (vv. 28-33:)

28- Concerning Kedar, and concerning the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon shall smite, thus saith the LORD; Arise ye, go up to Kedar, and spoil the men of the east. 29- Their tents and their flocks shall they take away: they shall take to themselves their curtains, and all their vessels, and their camels; and they shall cry unto them, Fear is on every side. 30- Flee, get you far off, dwell deep, O ye inhabitants of Hazor, saith the LORD; for Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon hath taken counsel against you, and hath conceived a purpose against you. 31- Arise, get you up unto the wealthy nation, that dwelleth without care, saith the LORD, which have neither gates nor bars, which dwell alone. 32- And their camels shall be a booty, and the multitude of their cattle a spoil: and I will scatter into all winds them that are in the utmost corners; and I will bring their calamity from all sides thereof, saith the LORD. 33- And Hazor shall be a dwelling for dragons, and a desolation for ever: there shall no man abide there, nor any son of man dwell in it.

Kedar: the most famous of the tribes of the land of Arabia; the word means black. They dwell in tents and not in cities, that is, they are Bedouin, and they owned many cattle and were rich. Hazor: lies south of the Euphrates, that is, in the north of the Arabian Peninsula; they are Bedouin tribes who dwell in tents or in unwalled villages.
Jeremiah’s prophecy calls the armies of Babylon to attack the tribes of Kedar, who dwell in the east of Egypt.
Curtains: pieces of cloth attached to the tents to enlarge them.

When Babylon attacks Kedar, it seizes their tents, their sheep, their curtains and their vessels, so the inhabitants of Kedar are afraid and try to flee, for they feel the Babylonian attack besieging them from every side. Babylon did not take them captive, feeling that it had no need of them, and was content to plunder their possessions.

Likewise the tribes of Hazor feared because of the command of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to attack them, and from their fear they tried to flee to escape from his hand and to hide, after they felt their defeat and weakness before him.

Those that are in the utmost corners (with the hair cut round): they used to please their gods by cutting their hair round, leaving some hair on top of their heads, and what is meant here is the people of Hazor.

The tribes of Hazor were rich in many cattle and camels, so the Babylonians plundered them and their inhabitants, with their hair cut round, fled, and the Babylonians killed many of them, and thus they were scattered as the farmer scatters the chaff with the winnowing fork, that is, it flies in the air.
Dragons (jackals): a predatory animal whose size is between the fox and the wolf, which lives in deserted places.
The land of Hazor becomes a ruin in which people do not dwell but the animals that live in deserted places, such as jackals.

Do not resemble the people of the world in appearance, and let your trust be in God and not in the multitude of your material possessions. In proportion to your care, you will enjoy a pure relationship with God and experience His love. [5] Elam (vv. 34-39:)

34- The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet against Elam in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, saying, 35- Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Behold, I will break the bow of Elam, the chief of their might. 36- And upon Elam will I bring the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and will scatter them toward all those winds; and there shall be no nation whither the outcasts of Elam shall not come. 37- For I will cause Elam to be dismayed before their enemies, and before them that seek their life: and I will bring evil upon them, even my fierce anger, saith the LORD; and I will send the sword after them, till I have consumed them: 38- And I will set my throne in Elam, and will destroy from thence the king and the princes, saith the LORD. 39- But it shall come to pass in the latter days, that I will bring again the captivity of Elam, saith the LORD.

Elam: a strong country lying east of Babylon, distinguished by shooting arrows. It submitted to Assyria and then Babylon, but its strength afterward helped in shattering Babylon and the rise of the kingdom of Media and Persia. The time of this prophecy is fixed as the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, the last of the kings of Judah.
God declares the defeat of Elam before Babylon and the shattering of their power, which appears in their skill in shooting arrows with the bow.

When Babylon attacks Elam, it attacks them from every side and drives out its inhabitants, and they are scattered over the whole earth as the farmer scatters the chaff, so that it flies in the air in every place.
